Handbook

Start Here

What this handbook is

A visual, structured study system for Product Management, built from your 55-lecture course study guide and extended to the 12 Product Core modules. It is designed for three jobs: learning, applying, and interview preparation.

Source integrity

  • Content marked "From your course notes" is preserved from your PDF study guide, with the guide's own corrections applied.
  • Content marked "Hypothetical example" uses invented numbers for teaching. It is never presented as real company data.
  • Company examples use only widely known public facts and are labelled as illustrative. Nothing here claims a real company's results.
  • Lectures 44 and 54 had no recordings; this handbook says nothing about their content.
  • The curriculum screenshot did not arrive, so module titles come from your brief and are provisional.

How each topic is taught

Three depths, marked by colour:

  • Level 1 · Beginner — plain English.
  • Level 2 · Working PM — how you use it in daily work.
  • Level 3 · Senior PM — strategy, trade-offs, money and risk.

Around those you will find worked examples, visuals, common mistakes, interview angles, exercises with model answers (hidden until you click), key takeaways and a short quiz.

Suggested path

  1. Modules 1 → 3: role, strategy, discovery.
  2. Modules 4 → 7: framing, UX, communication, analytics (the highest-leverage skills in interviews).
  3. Modules 8 → 9: growth and technical fluency.
  4. Modules 10 → 12: AI foundations, building with AI, agentic systems.
  5. Throughout: use the Framework Library, Case Studies and Interview Handbook; complete the Projects for your portfolio.

Using the HTML version

  • Search with / from anywhere.
  • Progress, quiz scores and theme are saved in this browser only.
  • Mark module complete on each module page; the dashboard shows status.
  • Print any page with your browser, or use the PDF downloads.
Module 1

Fundamentals of Product Management

What a product is, what a PM actually does, how a PM thinks and decides, and how product work is organised.

≈ 6 h study

1.1 How to read this module

Each topic is taught at three depths. Look for the coloured boxes:

Level 1 · Beginner

The idea in plain English, no jargon.

Level 2 · Working PM

How you use it in a sprint, a roadmap review or a stakeholder meeting.

Level 3 · Senior PM

Strategy, organisational constraints, money and risk.

From your course notes

Content preserved from the 55-lecture study guide (page references in the module header). Where the guide itself flagged a lecture statement as inaccurate, the corrected version is taught here.

Hypothetical example

Invented numbers for teaching. They are not real company data.

1.2 What is a product?

A product is anything a person or organisation uses to achieve a goal, delivered in a repeatable way. For a PM the useful definition is:

A product is a bundle of value (the job it does for someone) and experience (how it feels to get that job done), sustained by a business model (why the organisation can afford to keep providing it).

Level 1 · Beginner

A food-delivery app is a product. Its value is "I get lunch without cooking or leaving my desk." The experience is browsing, ordering, paying, tracking and receiving. The business model is the commission and fees the company earns. If any of the three is broken, the product fails: great value with a terrible experience loses customers; a lovely experience with no business model runs out of money.

Kinds of product you will meet

Type Example (illustrative) What the PM mainly optimises
Consumer app A food-ordering or ride-hailing app Activation, repeat usage, trust
B2B SaaS A team-collaboration or CRM tool Adoption inside accounts, renewals, expansion
Marketplace Buyers and sellers, riders and drivers Liquidity: balanced supply and demand
Platform / API A payments API used by other developers Developer experience, reliability, ecosystem
Internal tool An operations dashboard Employee productivity, error reduction
AI product A support assistant Answer quality, safety, cost per resolution

1.3 What is Product Management?

Product management is the discipline of deciding which problems are worth solving, for whom, and how the team will know the solution worked, then guiding the team to deliver it. The PM does not “own” the product alone; they own the clarity of the problem and the quality of the decisions.

From your course notes (Lecture 2)

  • Products deliver value by solving user needs; a feature should trace back to a real need.
  • PMs balance user needs, technical feasibility and business goals, and collaborate with designers, engineers and stakeholders. This does not automatically give a PM formal authority over everyone.
  • Specialisations differ by company: Technical PMs (platforms, infrastructure), Data PMs, Growth PMs (acquisition → revenue), Business PMs. An AI-enabled PM uses AI tools in their work; an AI PM manages a product whose functionality depends on AI. One person may do both.
  • Product–market fit is not proven simply because a market exists or some demand exists.

1.3.1 The three circles — and the fourth risk

A good product sits where three things overlap: desirable (people want it), feasible (the team can build and run it) and viable (it works for the business). Marty Cagan frames the same idea as four risks a PM must retire before and during building: value risk, usability risk, feasibility risk and business-viability risk.

1.3.2 What a PM is responsible for

  1. Problem definition — who has the problem, how often, how painful, what they do today.
  2. Strategy and focus — saying “not now” so the team works on the highest-value problem.
  3. Discovery — talking to users, reading data, running cheap experiments.
  4. Requirements and alignment — turning understanding into artefacts the team can build from (PRDs, user stories, acceptance criteria).
  5. Delivery partnership — removing blockers, making scope trade-offs, protecting quality.
  6. Launch and learning — go-to-market coordination, metrics, post-launch review.
  7. Stakeholder communication — keeping leadership, sales, support, legal and operations informed.

Level 2 · Working PM

On a typical week you might: review last week's funnel, run two customer calls, refine the next sprint's stories with an engineer, answer a sales request with data about why you won't build it this quarter, and update a one-page decision note. The through-line is decisions made with evidence, written down so others can challenge them.

Level 3 · Senior PM

Seniority is less about more features owned and more about bigger ambiguity and cost of being wrong: choosing which market to enter, how to price, whether to build vs buy vs partner, how to sequence a multi-team programme, and how to say no to a powerful stakeholder without losing the relationship.

1.4 How a PM thinks: trade-offs, evidence and outcomes

PMs make decisions with incomplete information. Good ones follow a loop, not a gut feel:

Trade-offs you will make daily

Tension Example Question to ask
Speed vs quality Ship a payment retry now or harden the flow first? What is the cost of a failure here — money, trust, regulation?
Short-term vs long-term Quick revenue feature vs platform investment What does this make cheaper or harder next quarter?
New users vs existing users Onboarding polish vs power-user requests Which segment drives the metric we are accountable for?
Breadth vs depth Ten shallow integrations vs one excellent one Where do customers actually get stuck today?
Customer ask vs customer need “Add an export button” vs “I need to share results with finance” What job is behind the request?

Worked example · reading a request as a problem

A sales lead asks for “a PDF export on the dashboard.” The PM asks what happens after the PDF is created? and learns the customer pastes the numbers into a monthly slide for their boss. Options now include a scheduled email summary, a shareable link, or a PowerPoint export — each has a different cost and risk. The PM picked the problem (“managers need to share monthly numbers”), not the solution.

Interview perspective

When asked “how do you make product decisions?”, describe the loop above, give one real example with a trade-off you explicitly named, and say what you would measure to know you were right. Interviewers listen for evidence, trade-offs and learning, not frameworks by name.

1.5 PM versus adjacent roles

Role boundaries differ by company. These are typical emphases, not rules; always ask “who makes the final call on X?” in a new team.

From your course notes (Lecture 12)

Product Managers, Product Owners and Business Analysts may divide discovery, requirements and prioritisation differently across companies. Product management focuses on value and outcomes; project and program management emphasise delivery coordination at different scopes. Exact responsibilities vary.

Common confusion

“PM = Product Owner” is true in some teams and false in others. In Scrum, the Product Owner is one person accountable for maximising the value of the product and managing the Product Backlog. A PM may be that person, or may work above the team setting strategy while a PO handles day-to-day backlog detail.

1.6 PM specialisations and career paths

From your course notes (Lecture 2)

A possible progression is Associate PM → PM → Senior PM → Group PM / Director → VP Product → Chief Product Officer. Domain expertise, communication, analytical thinking and case-study practice can support a transition into PM. Career paths vary.

Specialisation Focus Typical metrics
Growth PM Acquisition, activation, retention, monetisation experiments Conversion, retention, CAC, LTV
Technical / Platform PM APIs, infrastructure, developer tools Reliability, latency, API adoption, developer satisfaction
Data PM Data products, pipelines, analytics tooling Data quality, adoption, time-to-insight
Business / Strategy PM P&L ownership, partnerships, pricing Revenue, margin, contribution
AI PM Model-powered features, evaluation, safety Answer accuracy, cost per task, escalation rate

1.7 Product lifecycle versus product development lifecycle

Two different lifecycles are easy to mix up.

  • Product Life Cycle (PLC) — how a product's market life evolves: introduction → growth → maturity → decline. It guides strategy: invest to find fit and acquire in introduction; scale and defend in growth; optimise margin and extend in maturity; decide to harvest, reinvent or retire in decline.
  • Product Development Lifecycle (often the SDLC for software) — how a piece of work moves from idea to release: discover → plan → design → build → test (QA/UAT) → release → learn.

1.7.1 Waterfall, Agile, Scrum, Kanban, SAFe — what to know as a PM

From your course notes (Lecture 12)

  • Waterfall: sequential phases; late changes are costly. Agile: iterative delivery and learning from feedback; the best choice depends on context.
  • Scrum organises work into sprints. A sprint is at most one month; it does not have to be two weeks. Scrum defines accountabilities, events and artefacts — read the official Scrum Guide.
  • Kanban manages and improves flow, including limiting work in progress (WIP) — it is not simply a mix of Scrum and XP.
  • SAFe coordinates work across many teams; XP emphasises engineering practices. Scrum and SAFe are not the only Agile approaches, and Agile existed well before the mid-2010s.
  • UAT checks whether the solution meets acceptance needs; it cannot guarantee zero production issues.
  • Definition of Ready (criteria a team may use before starting work) and Definition of Done (shared quality criteria for completed work) are different things.

Level 2 · What you do in Scrum as a PM or PO

You keep an ordered Product Backlog, write items so the team can ask good questions, attend Sprint Planning to propose a Sprint Goal, answer questions during the sprint, and use the Sprint Review to gather stakeholder feedback. You do not tell developers how to build it, and you do not treat story points as individual productivity.

1.8 Product operating models

An operating model is how the organisation turns ideas into shipped product: who decides, how teams are formed, how funding and priorities flow.

Model How it works Strengths Failure mode
Project-based / feature factory Business hands requirements to delivery; success = “shipped on time” Predictable scope and cost Output without outcome; teams don't own results
Product-based (project-to-product) Long-lived teams own a product area and its metrics Continuity, learning, accountability Needs strong product leadership and trust
Empowered product teams Teams get problems to solve with measurable outcomes, not solutions Faster learning, higher morale, better ideas Requires capable PM/design/engineering trio and clear strategy
Platform + feature teams Platform team builds reusable capabilities; feature teams assemble them Reuse, consistency Platform becomes a bottleneck or builds what nobody uses
Matrix / functional Reporting by function; work organised by project Deep craft Hand-offs, diluted ownership

Level 3 · Senior PM

Operating-model problems often masquerade as product problems. If every initiative arrives as a solution from the top and teams are measured on delivery, no amount of discovery skill will help. Senior PMs diagnose the model, then change incentives and decision rights — e.g., replacing a feature roadmap with outcome-based goals and quarterly reviews of learning.

1.9 Vision, mission and strategy (overview)

  • Mission — why the organisation exists and what it does.
  • Vision — the future you want to create for users.
  • Strategy — the choices about whom to serve, which problem to solve and how to win sustainably (including what not to do).
  • Roadmap — a communicated plan of outcomes and likely work over time; not a promise of dates.

From your course notes (Lectures 10, 13; Extra topic 1)

A vision need not serve every person on earth, and it can evolve. A roadmap can be feature-based or goal-based; build it with engineering, design and stakeholders; treat it as an evolving plan, not a guarantee.

1.10 Product–market fit

Product–market fit (PMF) means a product satisfies a real market need strongly enough that customers keep using, paying for and recommending it. Marc Andreessen's often-quoted framing is being “in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market.”

Signals of fit (use several, never one):

  • Retention curves that flatten rather than decay to zero (see Module 7).
  • Growing share of new users arriving by word-of-mouth or referral.
  • The “very disappointed” survey test (popularised by Sean Ellis): if roughly 40%+ of active users say they would be very disappointed if the product disappeared, that is a commonly used signal of fit. It is a heuristic, not a law.
  • Customers pulling the product faster than you can serve it; sales cycles shortening.
  • Unit economics that work at the margin (Module 7).

Not evidence of fit

A large TAM, a polished prototype, a high survey intent score, or “people said they'd use it.” The course notes make the same point: a survey preference is not proof of purchase, and picking the largest segment alone does not prove fit.

1.11 Customer value versus business value

  • Customer value — benefit the customer gets relative to what it costs them (money, time, effort, risk).
  • Business value — what the organisation gains: revenue, margin, retention, strategic position, cost savings, learning.

Good products create value for customers first, then capture a fair share. Both must be positive or the product is not sustainable.

Situation Customer value Business value Verdict
Clear fee display at checkout High (trust, fewer surprises) Medium–high (fewer abandons) Win–win
Hidden fees revealed at the last step Negative Short-term gain, long-term trust loss Reject — exploits users
Deep discount to win users High for now Negative contribution margin Only as a bounded experiment
Heavy personalisation on sensitive data Possible Possible Gate by consent, privacy and regulation

1.12 Output versus outcome

  • Output — what the team produces: features shipped, tickets closed, story points.
  • Outcome — the change in user behaviour or business results that follows: higher checkout completion, fewer support contacts, better retention.

From your course notes (Companion ch. 1, Extra topic 2)

“A feature is something the team builds; an outcome is the change in user behaviour or business results. Neither a polished screen nor a shipped story alone proves value.” In OKR terms: if the release happens but completion does not improve, the initiative shipped but the key result has not been achieved.

Hypothetical worked example · feature factory vs outcome focus

A food-ordering team ships 12 features in a quarter. Checkout completion is 70.0% before and 70.4% after. Another team ships 3 changes: show the delivery fee early, add a retry for failed payments, remove one form field; completion rises from 70.0% to 76.0% and complaints do not increase.

Output: Team A 12, Team B 3. Outcome: Team A +0.4 pts, Team B +6.0 pts. The relevant question is not “how much did we build?” but “what changed for users and the business?”

Level 3 · Why leaders care

Outputs are cheap to count and easy to inflate; outcomes are what pay for the organisation. Senior PMs translate roadmaps into outcome language for executives: “reduce failed payments by 30% this quarter,” not “build payment retry screen.” They also protect against Goodhart's law — when a metric becomes a target it stops being a good metric — by pairing each outcome with guardrails.

1.13 Product discovery versus product delivery

  • Discovery — deciding what to build: understanding the problem, testing value and usability, estimating feasibility and viability.
  • Delivery — building, testing and releasing it reliably.

In dual-track teams both happen continuously: discovery de-risks the next items while delivery builds the current ones.

When not to over-discover

If a change is small, reversible and cheap (a label, a default), just ship it behind a flag and measure. Reserve heavy discovery for costly, hard-to-reverse bets.

1.14 Stakeholder management (introduction)

A stakeholder is anyone affected by or able to affect the product: leadership, sales, support, legal, compliance, finance, operations, partners, and users.

Four habits cover most of it:

  1. Map them — who has influence and who has interest? (Module 6 covers the power–interest grid.)
  2. Align on the goal first — agree the outcome before debating solutions.
  3. Make trade-offs visible — one page: options, cost, benefit, risk, recommendation.
  4. Close the loop — record the decision, the owner and a review date.

From your course notes (Extra topic 11)

A large customer wants an export this week while the team is fixing payment failures. Compare user impact, revenue risk, urgency, engineering effort and operational risk; present a time-limited workaround or staged plan; record who decided and when to revisit.

1.15 Product sense and product thinking

Product sense is the ability to quickly see a product through the user's eyes and the business's, spot what matters, and propose sensible improvements. Product thinking is the habit of starting from the user problem and outcome rather than from a feature or technology.

Build it deliberately:

  • Critique products you use, writing: who is it for, what job, what works, what frustrates, what would you test, what could go wrong.
  • Watch real people use something — your own app or someone else's.
  • Read teardowns and case studies, then predict the metric they would have moved.
  • Practise estimation and metric reasoning (Modules 3 and 7).

From your course notes (Lectures 4, 19)

A critique should explain the user, the task, the difficulty and the expected benefit — not “the app is bad.” Separate observations from assumptions; an outsider can't know a company's internal data or reasons.

Worked example · a 90-second product critique (illustrative)

Product: a grocery-delivery app. User: a busy parent ordering weekly staples. Job: “Restock the kitchen without a store trip.” Works: saved baskets make repeat orders fast. Pain: delivery fee and minimum basket value are discovered late. Hypothesis: showing the fee and “add ₹X to avoid fee” in the cart reduces abandonment without hurting order value. Metric: checkout completion; guardrail: complaints and refund rate. Risk: the fee varies by distance — show an honest estimate or say “unavailable”, never an invented number.

1.16 Growth model and customer relationship: PLG versus SLG

Product-led growth (PLG) Sales-led growth (SLG)
Main acquisition engine The product itself: self-serve sign-up, free tier or trial, virality Sales team: outbound, demos, negotiation
Typical buyer experience Try → get value → upgrade Talk to sales → proof of concept → contract
Best for Lower price points, easy individual adoption, bottom-up spread High price/complex purchases, long procurement, heavy integration
PM focus Activation, time-to-value, in-product conversion Enterprise features, security/compliance, integrations, sales enablement
Key metrics Activation rate, free→paid conversion, expansion Win rate, sales cycle, ACV, net revenue retention
Risk Big deals need sales-assist Product neglected in favour of custom asks

Most mature B2B companies blend the two (“product-led, sales-assisted”). Module 8 develops growth loops and PLG in detail.

1.17 B2B versus B2C product management

Dimension B2C B2B
Buyer vs user Usually the same person (sometimes different — e.g., a parent buys, a child uses) Often different: buyer, admin, end-user, and approver
Volume Large, fast feedback and statistical A/B tests Fewer customers; qualitative depth matters more
Success metrics Activation, retention, engagement, ARPU Adoption within accounts, renewal, expansion, NRR
Sales cycle Minutes to days Weeks to months
Risk of customisation Low High — one large customer can steer the roadmap
Compliance Privacy, consumer protection Security reviews, SLAs, contracts, data residency

From your course notes (Lecture 20)

For B2B, the buyer and the actual end-user may be different people — test with both.

1.18 Platform products versus feature products

  • A feature product solves a bounded job for end-users (a scheduling app).
  • A platform provides capabilities others build on (payments API, identity service, internal developer platform). Its customers are often developers or other teams.

Platform PMs optimise developer experience (clear docs, fast integration, stable APIs, predictable pricing), reliability and ecosystem growth, and must manage backwards compatibility — breaking an API breaks someone else's product.

Platform trap

Building a platform before you have two or three real consumers usually produces abstractions nobody wants. Prove the use case with a feature first, then generalise.

1.19 Common Product Management mistakes

Mistake Why it hurts Fix
Starting with a solution You optimise the wrong thing Write the problem statement and evidence first
Confusing activity with progress Shipping ≠ impact Define the outcome metric before building
Treating stakeholder requests as requirements Roadmap becomes a request queue Ask for the underlying job; show trade-offs
Skipping discovery because “we know our users” Confirmation bias Do 5–8 interviews; watch behaviour
Over-relying on data (or on gut) Blind spots either way Combine quantitative “what” with qualitative “why”
Vague success metrics Can't tell if you won Define numerator, denominator, period, guardrails
Too many priorities Nothing ships well Limit WIP; make “not now” explicit
Weak relationships with engineering/design Surprises, rework Involve them early; ask for estimates and risks, don't dictate dates
No post-launch review No learning Schedule a review before launch
Inventing numbers Loses credibility Label assumptions; say “not measured” when true

Integrity note from your course

The guide repeatedly flags that candidates should not misrepresent job titles, invent metrics or claim work they did not do. Present course or personal projects as such, label assumptions, and say plainly when you did not measure a result. This is both ethical and practical: interviewers probe.

1.20 Source-flagged misconceptions (corrected)

  • A sprint is ≤ 1 month — not necessarily two weeks.
  • MVP ≠ prototype ≠ public launch. An MVP is the smallest useful version or experiment that teaches you something important; it must still be safe and fit its test.
  • Kanban is flow management with WIP limits, not a Scrum–XP hybrid.
  • A focus group is a moderated research discussion, not another name for a target audience.
  • There is no universal rule that every product has two or three personas.
  • A unicorn is a private company valued at ≥ US$1 billion, not one with $1 billion revenue.
  • Product–market fit is not proven by market size alone.

1.21 Practice and model answers

Exercise 1 · Role clarity

Your company has a Product Owner, a Project Manager and you (PM). A VP asks for a new report “by end of next month.” Write who should decide (a) whether the report is worth building, (b) the scope for the first release, (c) the delivery plan and dates.

Model answer

(a) PM with the VP: this is a value/priority decision tied to outcomes. (b) PM/Product Owner with design and engineering: scope is a trade-off between value and effort. (c) Project Manager with engineering: schedule, dependencies, risks. The PM stays involved by monitoring scope trade-offs. State the assumption that these decision rights are typical, and confirm them with the team.

Exercise 2 · Turn an output into an outcome

“Build a chatbot for support” is on the roadmap. Rewrite it as an outcome with a metric, a baseline and a guardrail.

Model answer

Outcome: “Resolve common order-status questions without agent contact.” Metric: self-service resolution rate for order-status queries, baseline 35% (assumption — must be measured), target 55% in one quarter. Guardrails: customer satisfaction of bot-handled chats ≥ baseline; escalation-to-human success; incorrect-answer rate from sampled review.

Exercise 3 · Critique in 90 seconds

Pick an app you use daily. Using the structure user → job → what works → pain → hypothesis → metric → guardrail → risk, write a critique in under 150 words.

Model answer outline

Any app works; assess your answer against the structure above and the Level-1 test: could a non-expert understand the user and the problem? Did you separate observation from assumption? Did you include a guardrail?

1.22 Interview perspective

“What does a Product Manager do?” — 60-second answer

“A PM decides which problems are worth solving for which users, and defines how we'll know the solution worked. Day to day I talk to users and look at data to understand the problem, work with design and engineering to shape and deliver a solution, and align stakeholders on trade-offs. I'm accountable for outcomes — for example, improving checkout completion — not just for shipping features. I try to make decisions with evidence, write them down, and review results afterwards.”

“How is a PM different from a Project Manager or Product Owner?”

What the interviewer tests: role clarity and humility about variation. Structure: define each by core question; note overlap; give a team example. Answer: “A project manager owns delivery of a defined scope on a timeline; a PM owns the problem, the outcome and the priority. A Scrum Product Owner manages the Product Backlog and its value for a team; in some companies the PM does that too. In my last team I treated the roles as decision rights: I'd confirm who decides scope, who decides dates, and who decides priority.” Mistake to avoid: claiming PMs “manage” engineers or that titles mean the same everywhere.

1.23 Key takeaways

  • A product is value + experience + business model.
  • A PM's job is to choose and clarify the problem and be accountable for the outcome, working through influence, not authority.
  • Retire the four risks — value, usability, feasibility, viability — as cheaply as possible.
  • Output ≠ outcome. Define the metric and guardrails before building.
  • Discovery and delivery run together in good teams.
  • Role names vary; decision rights are what matter.
  • Be honest: label assumptions and don't invent results.

1.24 Check your understanding

Check your understanding

A team ships 12 features but checkout completion barely moves. Which statement is most accurate?

  1. They did great work because output was high.
  2. They produced high output but low outcome.
  3. Checkout completion is not a valid metric.
  4. They should ship more features.
Why: Output counts what was built; outcome measures the change in user or business results. High output with flat outcome is the feature-factory pattern.

In Scrum, how long can a sprint be?

  1. Exactly two weeks
  2. At most one month
  3. At least one month
  4. Any length, including quarterly
Why: The Scrum Guide sets sprints at one month or less; two weeks is a common choice, not a rule.

Which is NOT strong evidence of product–market fit?

  1. Retention curves that flatten
  2. Rising organic referrals
  3. A very large estimated TAM
  4. Many users saying they'd be very disappointed to lose the product
Why: Market size says there could be demand; fit requires evidence that real customers keep using and valuing the product.

Which risk does a usability test mainly reduce?

  1. Value risk
  2. Usability risk
  3. Feasibility risk
  4. Viability risk
Why: Usability tests check whether users can figure out how to use the solution. Value, feasibility and viability need other evidence.

A sales lead asks for a PDF export. What should the PM do first?

  1. Add it to the sprint
  2. Refuse the request
  3. Ask what the customer does with it and what outcome they need
  4. Ask engineering for a date
Why: Requests are solutions; the underlying job determines the best option and the cost-benefit.

Which model most strongly encourages empowered teams?

  1. Feature factory
  2. Project-based delivery with fixed scope
  3. Teams assigned problems and outcomes
  4. Waterfall
Why: Empowered teams are given problems to solve and measurable outcomes, not a list of solutions.

1.25 Recommended resources

  • The Scrum Guide — official rules for Scrum.
  • Atlassian: Product management — practical overviews (from your course reference list).
  • Silicon Valley Product Group articles — Marty Cagan on empowered teams and the four risks.
  • Product Talk (Teresa Torres) — continuous discovery habits.
  • Lenny's Newsletter — practitioner essays and PM career guidance.
Module 2

Product Strategy and Strategic Thinking

Turn business objectives into focused product choices — markets, positioning, moats, pricing, OKRs and go-to-market.

≈ 10 h study

About examples

Company names appear only as widely known illustrations of a concept. Numbers in worked examples are hypothetical. Never quote them as facts about a real business.

2.1 What strategy is (and is not)

Strategy is a set of choices about where to play (which customers, problems, markets), how to win (why customers pick you over alternatives) and what not to do — backed by the capabilities and economics to sustain it. A strategy that does not exclude anything is not a strategy.

Level 1 · Beginner

Strategy answers: Who are we helping? With what? Why us rather than the alternatives? And how will we know it is working? A list of features is not a strategy.

From your course notes (Lecture 10)

Product strategy involves choices: whom the product serves, which problem it addresses, why customers would choose it, and how it can achieve business outcomes. Use user research and competitor research to inform those choices. A vision is the future you hope to create; strategy is the choice of whom to serve, which problem to solve and how to win sustainably; a roadmap turns strategic choices into planned outcomes and work. Test whether the segment actually has the need, then track whether the choice delivers value and supports the business.

2.1.1 Vision, mission, strategy, roadmap

Layer Question Time horizon Example (hypothetical food app)
Mission Why do we exist and what do we do? Enduring “Make everyday meals easy and trustworthy.”
Vision What future are we trying to create? 3–10 years “Nobody is ever surprised by the price of dinner.”
Strategy Where do we play and how do we win? 1–3 years “Win budget-conscious urban households with transparent total prices and reliable delivery.”
Objectives / OKRs What measurable results show progress? Quarter/year “Raise checkout completion from 70% to 76% without raising complaints.”
Roadmap What outcomes and bets, in what likely order? Next 2–4 quarters “Q1 price transparency; Q2 reliability of payments; Q3 repeat-order shortcuts.”

2.1.2 Strategy versus roadmap

A roadmap is derived from strategy; it is not strategy. A strategy says “we will win on trust and price clarity”; the roadmap lists the bets that express it. If a roadmap can be read as a list of unrelated requests, the strategy is missing.

From your course notes (Lecture 13; Extra topic 1)

A roadmap communicates priorities and direction over time. The class distinguishes a feature-based roadmap from a goal-based (outcome-based) one. Build it collaboratively with engineering, design, stakeholders and customers; discuss dependencies, capacity, estimates and risks. It is an evolving plan, not a guarantee. The lecturer sometimes described vision as unchanging and cross-functional input as unnecessary — in practice strategy and vision can evolve and involvement depends on the organisation.

2.2 From business objective to product decision (the cascade)

PMs translate company goals into product choices through a cascade. Worked example:

Method: (1) restate the business objective with a number; (2) diagnose the biggest lever (funnel, cohort, unit economics); (3) choose a segment and problem; (4) define the strategic bet; (5) set outcome metrics and guardrails; (6) pick the cheapest experiment that reduces the biggest risk.

2.3 Market analysis

Market analysis answers: how big, how fast, who competes, what is changing, and where are the gaps. Use secondary research (reports, filings, company databases, news) to frame the landscape and primary research (interviews, surveys) to learn what customers actually do.

From your course notes (Lecture 6)

Primary research gathers new evidence directly (interviews, surveys, moderated focus groups); secondary research analyses existing information (reports, articles, company databases such as Crunchbase and Tracxn). Ask an AI research tool a specific question, specify geography, stage and audience, and open and verify the cited sources and dates. The claim that “surveys don't work in India” or that “90% of responses are biased” was not substantiated; sampling, incentives and question design can introduce bias but do not make surveys invalid.

2.3.1 Market sizing: TAM, SAM, SOM

  • TAM — total addressable market: demand if you captured everything your product could serve.
  • SAM — serviceable available market: the part you can actually serve with your offering, geography and channels.
  • SOM — serviceable obtainable market: what you can realistically win in a stated period.

Prefer bottom-up sizing (users × frequency × price) over “1% of a huge market”.

Worked example — bottom-up market sizing for a meal-planning app (hypothetical, one city)

Step Assumption Value
Households in the city assumed 2,000,000
Smartphone-using households that order or cook regularly 60% 1,200,000
TAM (all of them, annual price ₹1,200) 1,200,000 × ₹1,200 ₹144 crore ≈ ₹1.44 billion
Households within the service area and income band that fit 25% of 1,200,000 300,000
SAM 300,000 × ₹1,200 ₹36 crore ≈ ₹360 million
Realistic capture in year 1 (marketing reach, conversion) 4% of SAM households 12,000
SOM 12,000 × ₹1,200 ₹1.44 crore ≈ ₹14.4 million

State the unit (₹/year), the time period and each assumption. Then show a low and high case (e.g., 2% and 6% capture → ₹0.72 crore to ₹2.16 crore). The weakest assumption is usually the capture rate — validate it with a pilot.

From your course notes (Extra topic 8; Lecture 6)

A hypothetical city with 100,000 potential users: if 20,000 are in the delivery area and fit the criteria, they may form the serviceable market; if you assume 2,000 could be acquired in a period, document the evidence and constraints. Avoid multiplying an enormous market by an arbitrary one-percent share without evidence. The shampoo figures in class were illustrative, not verified. A unicorn is a private company valued at $1 billion or more, not one with $1 billion revenue.

2.4 Competitive intelligence

From your course notes (Lecture 9)

The goal is to understand the market and find meaningful gaps — not to copy every feature. Direct competitors offer closely comparable solutions to similar users; indirect competitors solve the same need differently; substitutes compete for the same outcome, time or budget (streaming vs cinema vs games vs sleep). Classification depends on the need being analysed. A different channel can still be a threat (gift buyers choosing a quick-commerce item over waiting for a watch). Compare the alternatives, not only your own product.

Process: (1) define the customer job; (2) list alternatives incl. “do nothing”, spreadsheets, manual workarounds; (3) compare on a few user-relevant dimensions; (4) record evidence and date; (5) ask “which differences actually matter to customers?”

2.4.1 SWOT

SWOT organises Strengths and Weaknesses (internal) and Opportunities and Threats (external). It is a summary tool, not an analysis: each item needs evidence, and the real value is the so-what — which strengths address which opportunities, which weaknesses expose which threats.

From your course notes (Lecture 9)

Support claims with evidence and flag unknowns. The instructor noted that one group's SWOT described Ola but missed a direct side-by-side competitor comparison.

2.4.2 Porter's Five Forces

Porter's Five Forces assesses the structural attractiveness of an industry: rivalry among existing competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers, and bargaining power of suppliers. High force intensity → lower profit potential.

Worked example — Five Forces for food-delivery marketplaces (hypothetical, qualitative)

Force Assessment Why (illustrative) Product implication
Rivalry High Few large players; promotions and speed compete directly Differentiate beyond discounts (reliability, trust)
New entrants Medium Software is easy; supply density and brand are hard Win density in chosen micro-markets
Substitutes High Cooking, offline dining, grocery delivery Anchor on convenience and price clarity
Buyer power High Low switching costs for consumers; multi-homing Build habit loops, loyalty, saved preferences
Supplier power Medium–high Restaurants and delivery partners can multi-home Better tools and fair economics for partners

Limitation: Five Forces is a static industry snapshot; it ignores complements and fast technology change. Use it to frame, then validate with data.

From your course notes (Lecture 24)

Porter's Five Forces was announced but not substantially taught in the recording; this section is independent reference material.

2.4.3 PESTLE

PESTLE scans the macro environment: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental.

2.5 Segmentation, Targeting and Positioning (STP)

  • Segment — divide the market into groups with shared needs/behaviours (not just demographics).
  • Target — choose which segment(s) to serve first, based on need severity, size, strategic fit, reachability and ability to pay.
  • Position — define how the product sits in the target's mind relative to alternatives.

From your course notes (Lectures 3, 26; Extra topic 9)

Segment beyond demographics: package size, affordability, distribution, brand perception, motivations. These are hypotheses to research, not assumptions that apply to everyone in a place or income group. Positioning explains which users a product serves, the problem it solves and why it may be a better choice than relevant alternatives; competitors include doing nothing, a spreadsheet or asking a person. Validate whether users care about the proposed difference and whether it is accurate before presenting it as fact.

Positioning statement: For [target customer] who [need/job], [Product] is a [category] that [key benefit]. Unlike [primary alternative], [Product] [reason to believe / differentiator].

Example (hypothetical)

For busy parents who need predictable weekly food costs, PlanPlate is a meal-planning app that shows an accurate weekly grocery estimate. Unlike collecting recipes and prices by hand, PlanPlate does it in one tap — reason to believe: price estimates refresh from partner stores daily (to be validated).

2.5.1 Value propositions

A value proposition states the benefit a customer gets and why it beats alternatives. The Value Proposition Canvas pairs the customer profile (jobs, pains, gains) with your value map (products/services, pain relievers, gain creators). Fit exists when your relievers and creators address the pains and gains that matter most.

2.6 Business models: Business Model Canvas and Lean Canvas

The Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder) describes nine building blocks. The Lean Canvas (Ash Maurya) adapts it for startups: it replaces Key Partners, Key Activities, Key Resources and Customer Relationships with Problem, Solution, Key Metrics, Unfair Advantage.

2.7 Differentiation, competitive advantage and moats

Differentiation gives customers a reason to choose you that rivals cannot easily copy. A competitive advantage is durable only if it resists imitation; such protective features are often called moats.

Source of advantage What it means How it works Fragility
Network effects Product becomes more valuable as more people use it Direct (messaging) or cross-side (riders ↔ drivers; buyers ↔ sellers) Local not global; can reverse; multi-homing weakens it
Switching costs Cost (money, time, data, learning) of changing Integrations, data lock-in, workflows, contracts Customers resent lock-in; regulators may require portability
Economies of scale Unit costs fall with volume Purchasing, infrastructure, density Needs sustained volume
Brand and trust Customers prefer you under uncertainty Reliability, safety, reputation One incident can damage it
Data advantage More usage → better model/personalisation Learning from behaviour Only if data is proprietary, relevant and used well
Proprietary tech / IP / regulation Legal or technical barriers Patents, licences Time-limited; can be designed around
Distribution Cheap access to customers Embedded in other products, partnerships Platform risk

Level 3 · Senior PM

“Network effects” is an overused claim. Test it: does the marginal user make existing users better off, and is that effect strong enough to beat a rival's promotions? In marketplaces, the effect is usually local (density in a city), so a global user count hides weakness. Ask what happens if a rival subsidises both sides for a quarter.

2.7.1 Blue Ocean Strategy

Blue Ocean Strategy (Kim & Mauborgne) advises creating uncontested market space by making competition irrelevant, using a strategy canvas: plot competitive factors on the x-axis and offering level on the y-axis, then use the Eliminate–Reduce–Raise–Create grid to reshape value.

2.8 Build, buy or partner

Option Choose when Advantages Risks
Build Core differentiator; unique requirements; long-term control matters Control, IP, tailored experience Slow, costly, maintenance burden
Buy (license / acquire) Commodity capability; speed matters; mature vendors exist Fast, proven Vendor lock-in, integration cost, ongoing fees, limited customisation
Partner Capability sits outside your core; shared upside; distribution access Faster market access, shared risk Dependency, revenue share, misaligned incentives

Decision questions: Is it core to our differentiation? How fast do we need it? What is the total cost of ownership over 3 years (including maintenance and vendor fees)? What is the switching cost if the vendor fails? What data and compliance obligations apply? Could we start by buying and later build once learning proves the need?

Example (hypothetical)

A food-delivery startup considers building its own maps and routing. Verdict: buy/partner (commodity, huge fixed cost), and build its own order-batching logic because that is where its cost advantage lives.

2.9 Strategic trade-offs

Strategy is about saying no. Typical explicit trade-offs: growth vs profitability; breadth vs depth; speed vs quality; acquisition vs retention; customer-specific requests vs platform consistency; exploit the core vs explore a new bet. A useful practice: write “We will not…” statements (e.g., “We will not compete on discount depth; we will compete on transparency and reliability”).

From your course notes (Lecture 24, Extra topic 11)

For any strategic choice, describe the target, evidence, costs, risks and what would make you change your mind. Stakeholders have different incentives; clarify the shared outcome, evidence, constraints and decision rights instead of promising every request.

2.9.1 Growth options: the Ansoff matrix

From your course notes (Lecture 24)

Existing product/existing market = market penetration; new product/existing market = product development; existing product/new market = market development; new product/new market = diversification. The distinction is relative to the company; examples can be debatable. The instructor initially gave inconsistent quadrant labels; this is the standard mapping.

2.10 Pricing and monetisation strategies

  • Pricing — how much and on what terms customers pay. Monetisation — the broader way the product earns revenue.
  • Anchor on value to the customer, then check cost, competitor prices, willingness to pay and trust. Cost-plus alone ignores value.
Model How it works Best when Watch out for
One-time purchase Pay once Simple tools; low ongoing cost No recurring revenue; support cost continues
Subscription Recurring access fee Ongoing value; predictable costs Churn; need steady value delivery
Freemium Free tier + paid upgrades Viral/low marginal cost products Free users cost money; conversion often small — model it
Usage-based Pay for consumption Value scales with use (APIs, cloud) Unpredictable bills; metering complexity
Tiered Good/Better/Best plans Different segments value different features Poor tier design confuses or leaves money on the table
Marketplace / transaction fee Take rate on transactions Two-sided platforms Disintermediation; fee fairness
Advertising Advertisers pay for attention Large audiences Conflicts with user experience; privacy
Licensing / enterprise Per-seat, per-usage or per-deal B2B with high value Long sales cycles; custom demands
Affiliate Paid for referred outcomes Content/recommendation products Trust and disclosure

From your course notes (Lecture 26; Extra topic 5)

The class compared subscriptions, freemium, advertising, affiliate, usage-based, licensing and transaction/marketplace models; models can be combined. Tiered pricing and hybrid monetisation are different but can coexist. License fees can be per user, usage-based or otherwise structured; cloud pricing is not universally per seat. White-labelling concerns branding another supplier's product; dropshipping concerns fulfilment directly by a supplier — they are not the same. A free trial should disclose when payment begins and how to cancel. Do not interpret stated willingness to pay as guaranteed purchases. A data product requires appropriate legal, security and privacy protections.

Worked example — a simple price-test decision

Plan A: ₹99/month; Plan B: ₹149/month. In a pilot of 2,000 visitors each: A converts 5.0% (100 payers → ₹9,900/month), B converts 3.5% (70 payers → ₹10,430/month). B earns ₹530 more revenue per month but with 30 fewer customers. If monthly churn is higher for B or support cost per customer is fixed, A may be better long-term; if costs are per user, B wins. The pilot is a signal; it needs a significance check (Module 7) and a view on churn and strategy (market share vs margin).

2.11 Objectives and Key Results (OKRs)

An objective is a qualitative direction; key results are measurable changes that indicate progress; initiatives are the work you believe might move the key results. OKRs are not a task list or an automatic performance score.

Tips: 3–5 objectives max; 2–4 KRs each; stretch but plausible (many teams aim for ~70% achievement on ambitious KRs); review weekly; separate committed deliverables from aspirational goals; pair outcomes with guardrails.

2.12 Product portfolio strategy

Larger organisations manage multiple products and must allocate resources across them.

  • BCG growth-share matrix — classifies products by market growth and relative market share into Stars (high/high), Cash cows (low growth/high share), Question marks (high growth/low share) and Dogs (low/low). It guides investment but oversimplifies and depends on how markets are defined.
  • Three Horizons — H1 optimise the core, H2 build emerging businesses, H3 explore future options; allocate effort and expectations differently (the commonly cited “70/20/10” split is a rule of thumb, not a law).
  • Portfolio questions: Which products share customers or infrastructure? Where do we cannibalise ourselves? Which should we sunset to free capacity?

2.13 Go-to-market (GTM) strategy

GTM is the plan for getting a product to the right people and helping them use it. Module 8 covers launch plans in depth; here are the strategic pieces.

From your course notes (Lecture 23; Extra topic 10)

GTM is the plan for reaching and serving a market — for a new product, an existing product entering a new market, or another launch. Start with the business case and timing (why now, who benefits, market conditions, seasonality, competition). Define the audience and proposition (personas, positioning, differentiators, messaging, pricing and rationale). Plan distribution and launch support (channels, sales and support readiness, onboarding, budget, owners). Set measurable success metrics and adjust the roadmap using feedback. In the cricket-equipment exercise, the instructor challenged learners to consider partner incentives, sponsorship costs and likely return — not just list channels. Pilot with a small group before a public launch; assign owners and a rollback owner.

2.14 Strategy in practice: a worked mini-case

Hypothetical: choosing a segment for a budgeting app

Context. A small team can build one thing this quarter. Three candidate segments: students, young professionals, freelancers. Evidence (hypothetical). 12 interviews per segment; pain severity (1–5): students 4.1, young professionals 3.2, freelancers 4.5. Estimated serviceable users: students 200k, professionals 500k, freelancers 80k. Reachability: students via campus (high), professionals (medium), freelancers via communities (medium). Willingness to pay (stated; to be validated): ₹0, ₹100/month, ₹250/month. Scoring (1–5 scores, weights: pain 35%, size 20%, reach 20%, willingness to pay 25%). Pain is the interview score above; the other criteria are converted to 1–5 — size: students 3, professionals 5, freelancers 1; reach: 5, 3, 3; willingness to pay: 1, 3, 5. Students: 4.1×.35 + 3×.2 + 5×.2 + 1×.25 = 1.435 + 0.6 + 1.0 + 0.25 = 3.29. Professionals: 3.2×.35 + 5×.2 + 3×.2 + 3×.25 = 1.12 + 1.0 + 0.6 + 0.75 = 3.47. Freelancers: 4.5×.35 + 1×.2 + 3×.2 + 5×.25 = 1.575 + 0.2 + 0.6 + 1.25 = 3.63. Decision. Start with freelancers (pain and willingness to pay are highest) while the small serviceable base is acceptable for a first version; plan a second wave for professionals. Risks: small market; stated willingness to pay is unreliable — test with a priced pilot. What would change our mind: if pilot conversion is below 3% or if freelancers churn after tax season.

2.15 Source-flagged corrections

  • Strategy ≠ roadmap ≠ vision; they are layers.
  • Ansoff labels: see above.
  • Five Whys and first principles are related but different (Module 4).
  • A survey preference is not proof of purchase; PMF needs behavioural evidence.
  • Segmenting by largest size alone does not prove fit.

2.16 Exercises with model answers

Exercise 1 · Size a market

Estimate the annual SOM for a language-learning app in one city: 3,000,000 residents; 40% aged 18–40; 20% of those would consider paying for an app; annual price ₹2,000; you believe you can win 5% of the considering users in year one. Show TAM, SAM, SOM and name the shakiest assumption.

Model answer

Residents aged 18–40: 3,000,000 × 0.40 = 1,200,000. Considering payers: 1,200,000 × 0.20 = 240,000. SAM (users who would consider): 240,000 → ₹2,000 × 240,000 = ₹48 crore. Taking TAM as all 18–40 residents = 1,200,000 × ₹2,000 = ₹240 crore. SOM: 5% × 240,000 = 12,000 users → ₹2.4 crore. Shakiest assumption: the 5% capture rate (and the 20% “would consider” which is stated intent). Run a landing-page test with a real price to refine both. Present a range (3%–7% → ₹1.44–3.36 crore).

Exercise 2 · Positioning

Write a positioning statement for a budgeting app for freelancers, naming the alternative it competes with.

Model answer (example)

For freelancers who struggle with irregular income, IncomeSmooth is a budgeting app that forecasts cash flow across months. Unlike spreadsheets and bank apps that assume a fixed salary, IncomeSmooth builds a safe monthly allowance from your average income and warns you before tax and low-income months. Reason to believe: forecasts use the user's own 12-month history (to be validated with beta users).

Exercise 3 · Build, buy or partner

A fintech wants in-app identity verification. Recommend and justify.

Model answer

Buy/partner with an established KYC provider: identity verification is regulated, commodity-like and expensive to build and maintain; speed to market matters. Retain control of the onboarding UX and data handling, check vendor compliance and uptime SLA, plan for vendor switching (abstraction layer), and review data-protection obligations. Revisit building in-house only if unit cost at scale or differentiation justifies it.

2.17 Interview perspective

“What is your product strategy for X?” — structure
  1. Clarify the company goal and stage. 2. Choose the segment and the problem (with evidence). 3. State the positioning and why you win (differentiation/moat). 4. Name the top 2–3 bets and what you won't do. 5. Define the North Star, outcome metrics and guardrails. 6. Highlight biggest risks and how you'd test them. 7. Note what evidence would change your mind. Keep it to 2–3 minutes before drilling down.
“How would you decide between building and partnering?” — 60-second answer

“I start with whether it's core to differentiation. If it's commodity or regulated, I lean to buy or partner for speed and lower risk, and compare three-year total cost, vendor lock-in, data/compliance obligations and the cost of switching later. If it's what makes us different — like our routing logic — I build. I'd often start with a partner to learn, keep a clean abstraction layer, and revisit once volume or differentiation justifies building.”

2.18 Key takeaways

  • Strategy = choices (who, what, why us, what not). Roadmaps follow strategy.
  • Use frameworks (SWOT, Five Forces, PESTLE, STP, canvases) to organise thinking, then validate with evidence.
  • Size markets bottom-up, show a range and name the weakest assumption.
  • Moats are specific: network effects, switching costs, scale, brand, data — test each claim.
  • Price on value, check unit economics, and run price tests with significance and churn in view.
  • OKRs: objective (direction) + measurable key results + guardrails; not a task list.
  • Always write down what would change your mind.

2.19 Check your understanding

Check your understanding

Which best describes a roadmap?

  1. A guarantee of dates for specific features
  2. A communicated plan of outcomes and likely work, derived from strategy
  3. The company's mission statement
  4. A list of all customer requests
Why: A roadmap communicates priorities and direction over time; it is evolving and follows strategy.

In the Ansoff matrix, selling the current product to a new market is…

  1. Market penetration
  2. Product development
  3. Market development
  4. Diversification
Why: Existing product + new market = market development.

Which sizing approach is preferred?

  1. 1% of a huge market
  2. Bottom-up: users × frequency × price, with a range
  3. The biggest number you can cite
  4. Competitor revenue only
Why: Bottom-up estimates expose assumptions you can test. Arbitrary percentages of a giant market are not evidence.

A strong network effect exists when…

  1. Many people have downloaded the app
  2. Each additional user makes the product more valuable for existing users, enough to resist rivals
  3. The product is popular on social media
  4. The company has many partners
Why: Network effects mean marginal users add value to others; they are often local and can be weakened by multi-homing.

Which is a well-formed key result?

  1. Launch the new checkout
  2. Improve conversion
  3. Increase checkout completion from 70% to 76% for new users this quarter, complaints ≤ 1.3%
  4. Make the team happy
Why: A key result has a baseline, target, population, time frame and often a guardrail.

Which is a substitute rather than a direct competitor?

  1. Another food-delivery app
  2. Cooking at home instead of ordering
  3. A rival's identical subscription
  4. A copy-cat app with same features
Why: Substitutes meet the same need (a meal) in a different way and compete for the same outcome, time or budget.

2.20 Recommended resources

  • Strategyzer: Business Model Canvas and Value Proposition Canvas.
  • Harvard Business Review: The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy (Michael Porter).
  • Blue Ocean Strategy — official site.
  • Lean Canvas (Ash Maurya).
  • Atlassian: Product management — roadmap and strategy guides.
  • What Is OKR? — Google re:Work.
Module 3

Problem Discovery and Market Research

Find problems worth solving: research methods, interviews and surveys, personas, jobs-to-be-done, journeys, synthesis and evidence quality.

≈ 10 h study

About examples

Personas, quotes, review counts and estimates are invented to teach technique. They are not research findings about any real product or user group.

3.1 What discovery is

Product discovery is the work of learning what is worth building before (and while) building it: who has the problem, how painful it is, how they cope today, and whether your idea would be chosen and used. Customer discovery focuses on understanding customers; problem validation tests that the problem is real, frequent and painful enough to matter.

Level 1 · Beginner

Discovery = talking to people and watching what they do, so you build the right thing. If you can only ask “Would you use my idea?”, you will mostly hear polite yeses.

From your course notes (Lectures 6, 8; Picture lesson)

Validate the problem before investing heavily in a solution. Ask whether the need is real, who experiences it, how people solve it today and whether the opportunity is worth pursuing. A solution is a hypothesis to test, not a guaranteed success. Start with a user and a task; ask about a recent real experience; watch the task where appropriate; look for repeated difficulties. Do not assume an idea is useful simply because someone says it sounds nice.

3.2 Research methods: qualitative and quantitative, primary and secondary

Two different axes — do not confuse them:

Qualitative (why / how) Quantitative (how many / how much)
Primary (you collect it) Interviews, observation, diary studies, usability tests, moderated focus groups Surveys, A/B tests, instrumented behaviour in your own product
Secondary (already exists) Support tickets, app-store reviews, forums, published case studies Market reports, public statistics, company databases, benchmarks

From your course notes (Lecture 6)

Qualitative and quantitative describe the kind of evidence, not alternatives to primary research. Interviews give qualitative insight into why; a well-designed survey can estimate how common a behaviour is. Both can be primary. A focus group is a moderated research discussion — not another name for a target audience. Ten interviews reveal useful clues but do not establish the habits of an entire city.

3.3 Customer interviews

3.3.1 Principles

  1. Ask about the past, not the future. “Tell me about the last time you ordered lunch” beats “Would you use an app that…?”
  2. Seek stories, then specifics: what triggered it, what alternatives they considered, what happened, how they felt, what they did next.
  3. Stay neutral: don't pitch; don't lead; tolerate silence.
  4. Recruit for contrast: include people who tried and churned, people who never tried, power users — not only fans.
  5. Consent and privacy: explain purpose, record only with permission, remove identifying details in notes.
  6. Debrief fast: write observations separately from interpretations within 24 hours.

From your course notes (Lecture 3; Companion ch. 2)

Interview a student who buys lunch. Ask “Tell me about the last time you ordered lunch.” If they say they missed delivery fees, watch where they expected to see the price. Five interviews can reveal problems but cannot establish their population frequency. Recruit a range of users including those who abandoned and those who did not; get consent; avoid leading questions; remove identifying information; compare themes with quantitative data.

3.3.2 Question design

Weak (leading / hypothetical) Stronger (past behaviour, neutral)
“Would you pay for faster delivery?” “Last time you were in a hurry, what did you do about food?”
“Do you find our checkout confusing?” “Walk me through placing your last order. What did you look at first?”
“Don't you hate hidden fees?” “How did you decide whether the total was acceptable?”
“Is price important to you?” “Tell me about a time you decided not to order because of the cost.”
“What features do you want?” “What did you do the last time this didn't work?”

3.3.3 Sample interview script (45 minutes)

Script: ordering food after work (hypothetical study)

Opening (5 min). “Thanks for your time. I'm learning how people decide about dinner on weekdays. There are no right answers; I'm not testing you. May I record audio for my notes only? I'll remove names.” Warm-up (5 min). “Tell me about your typical weekday evening.” Core story (20 min). “Think about the last time you ordered food from an app on a weekday. What was happening before you opened it?” → “What did you do first?” → “What else did you consider?” → “What were you looking at when you decided?” → “Was there a moment you almost gave up?” → “What did you do next?” Probe the friction (10 min). “You mentioned the total changed at the end — what did you expect to see?” → “How did that feel?” → “What did you do?” Wrap-up (5 min). “Is there anything I should have asked?” → “Who else should I speak to?” → thank, explain next steps. Don't: pitch your idea, ask about features, or suggest answers.

3.3.4 Recording the evidence

Use a two-column note sheet: Observation (what they did/said, verbatim where possible) | Interpretation (your hypothesis). Tag each observation with the participant ID and the journey stage.

3.4 Surveys and questionnaire bias

A survey estimates how common something is — if the sample is representative and the questions are neutral.

Common biases and fixes

Bias What happens Fix
Leading question Wording nudges the answer (“How great was…?”) Neutral wording; balanced scales
Double-barrelled Two questions in one (“fast and cheap?”) One idea per question
Social desirability People give flattering answers Anonymity; behaviour (“last week, how many times…?”)
Acquiescence Tendency to agree Mix positively and negatively worded items; use specific choices
Order effects Earlier questions prime later ones Randomise; put sensitive items last
Sampling / self-selection Respondents differ from the population Define the frame; track response rate; compare with known figures
Hypothetical bias Stated intent ≠ behaviour Prefer behavioural questions; validate with a real action
Incentive bias Rewards attract the wrong people Screen carefully; use modest incentives

From your course notes (Lecture 6; Lecture 10)

The claim that “90% of survey responses are biased” was not substantiated; sampling, incentives and question design can introduce bias but do not make surveys inherently invalid. A survey preference is not proof that respondents will purchase.

Sample survey questions (rewritten)

  • Bad: “Do you agree our app is easy and fast to use?” → Good: “In the past 7 days, how many times did you place an order? (0 / 1 / 2–3 / 4+)” and “How easy or difficult was it to find the total price on your last order? (Very difficult … Very easy)”.
  • Bad: “Would you use a feature that tells you about fees?” → Good: “When you last saw a price at checkout, was the total different from what you expected? (Yes, higher / Yes, lower / No / Don't remember)”.

3.5 Customer segmentation and personas

A segment is a group sharing a relevant need or behaviour. A persona is an illustrative profile of a segment — a communication aid, not proof everyone acts alike. Prefer behavioural and need-based segments over purely demographic ones.

From your course notes (Lecture 3)

A target audience is a group a product or message is intended to reach. The buyer and end user can be different (FirstCry: a parent may buy while a child uses). Build and validate personas with research, not guesses. There is no universal rule that every product needs two or three personas, and choosing the largest segment alone does not prove product–market fit. The iPhone-user personas in class were exercise assumptions, not claims about all iPhone users. When needs conflict, consider market size, severity of need, strategic fit, feasibility and reachability; persona overlap is normal.

3.6 Jobs to Be Done (JTBD)

JTBD frames demand as people “hiring” a product to make progress in a particular circumstance. A job statement has the form:

When [situation], I want to [motivation / progress], so I can [desired outcome].
  • Jobs have functional, emotional and social dimensions.
  • The competition is whatever else gets hired for the job — including doing nothing.
  • Uncover jobs from switching stories: what triggered the move, alternatives considered, what pushed them away from the old solution (push), what pulled them to the new one (pull), what anxieties held them back, what habits kept them in place — the four forces.

Example (hypothetical): lunch

When I'm in back-to-back meetings and have 15 minutes, I want to get a filling lunch without leaving my desk or being surprised by the cost, so I can stay focused and not blow my budget. Competing alternatives: order in, ask a colleague to pick up, eat a snack, skip lunch, bring food. Anxieties: “Will it arrive in time? Will the price change?” Implication: reliability and total price clarity matter more than restaurant variety for this job.

From your course notes (Lecture 21)

Jobs to be done asks what progress users want to make in a situation; first-principles thinking breaks a problem down to fundamental assumptions. The recording mainly refers learners to further material for these concepts — this section is independent reference material.

3.7 Pain-point identification

List pains with severity (how bad), frequency (how often), breadth (how many people) and current workaround (the clearest sign of real pain: people already spend effort to solve it). Rank by severity × frequency × breadth, then by whether you can credibly solve it.

3.8 Customer journey mapping and user flows

From your course notes (Lecture 5; Companion ch. 3)

A journey map follows the whole experience, including actions, thoughts and feelings, across touchpoints; a user flow focuses on paths and decisions inside an interface; one journey can contain many flows. A workflow focuses on the sequence of activities, systems and decisions. Start with a concrete task, map the steps and important branches; use the appropriate level of detail. AI can brainstorm a first draft (give it problem, users, features, constraints) — check it against the real product and do not copy it blindly. Add the key branches: valid/invalid address, payment failure, retry, cancellation — and label the desired outcome for each. A remembered login session is not necessarily single sign-on.

3.8.1 Opportunity Solution Trees (OST)

Teresa Torres's Opportunity Solution Tree connects a desired outcome to the customer opportunities (needs, pains, desires) and then to solutions and experiments. It prevents jumping from outcome straight to a favourite feature.

3.9 Competitor research, review mining and support-ticket analysis

Review mining turns public reviews and support tickets into themes and a vocabulary. Method: (1) sample reviews across ratings and dates; (2) code each into themes (one review can have several); (3) count and read representative quotes; (4) note sampling limits; (5) turn themes into hypotheses.

Worked example — coding 40 synthetic app reviews

Theme Mentions Share of 40 reviews
Late delivery 11 27.5%
Fees / total unclear 9 22.5%
Food quality 7 17.5%
App crashes at payment 6 15.0%
Slow support 4 10.0%
Good discounts (positive) 3 7.5%

From your course notes (Lecture 39)

The class sampled a public dataset, asked an AI tool for sentiment and potential themes (reliability, pricing, safety, support). Review individual comments and sampling bias; a small sample cannot establish the full market's sentiment. Public datasets can be real, synthetic or mixed — check provenance and licence. Never upload confidential data without authorisation.

3.10 Behavioural analytics and observation

  • Behavioural analytics (funnels, cohorts, session replays where permitted) shows what people do at scale (Module 7).
  • Observational research — watching users perform tasks (in context if possible) reveals what they cannot articulate: workarounds, hesitations, misreadings. Think-aloud usability testing is a form of observation.
  • Always combine: analytics finds where; observation and interviews find why.

3.11 Research synthesis

3.11.1 Affinity mapping

Write each observation on a note; cluster by similarity (silently first, then discuss); name clusters as insights (“Users distrust totals that change at the end”), not topics (“Pricing”); count participants per cluster.

3.11.2 Assumption mapping and hypothesis generation

List every assumption behind the idea (desirability, usability, feasibility, viability). Plot on importance (how fatal if wrong) vs evidence (how much we know). Test the important, low-evidence assumptions first.

Hypothesis template: We believe that [change/solution] for [segment] will [expected outcome/metric] because [reason/evidence]. We will know we are right when [measurable signal].

3.12 Problem validation and evidence quality

Triangulation means reaching a conclusion from multiple independent kinds of evidence. Grade evidence honestly:

Strength Evidence Example
Strong Observed behaviour at scale; randomised experiments; paid pilots Conversion lift in an A/B test; people paying a real price
Medium Repeated behaviour in small samples; consistent interview themes; usability test patterns 6 of 8 users miss the fee in a task
Weak Stated intent, opinions, single anecdotes, AI-generated claims, “I would use this” Survey says 80% “would try”

From your course notes (Lectures 6, 28, 41)

Label comparisons based on impressions as hypotheses; support material claims with suitable research, sources and methodology. Do not present AI-generated target numbers as evidence — one team acknowledged the tool invented its metrics. A student's own experience is a starting point, not proof of a widespread problem.

3.13 Guesstimates (estimation)

A guesstimate breaks an unknown number into smaller numbers you can explain, state assumptions for, and sanity-check — and gives a range.

From your course notes (Lecture 7)

Clarify the question first (geography, typical day vs special event, ride types, whether cancelled requests count — keep definitions consistent). Break into measurable assumptions; explain and sanity-check each; compare top-down and bottom-up; communicate a range and the assumptions that matter most. The class estimates were practice figures, not verified Uber statistics. There is no single right answer, but arithmetic errors, inconsistent definitions or implausible assumptions make an estimate weak. Simple example: 1,000 students × 60% at school × 50% buying lunch = 300 lunches.

Worked example — daily ride-hailing trips in a large metro (practice numbers, not facts)

Top-down: metro population 20 million → adults 70% = 14.0 million → people who use ride-hailing at least weekly: 8% = 1.12 million → 3 trips per week each = 3.36 million trips/week → ≈ 480,000 trips/day. Bottom-up (supply check): active drivers per day 55,000 × 9 completed trips per driver per day = ≈ 495,000 trips/day. Reconcile: two independent approaches land within ~3% — this raises confidence but both rest on assumptions I invented. Give a range: 450k–500k/day, and name the most uncertain assumptions (share of weekly users, trips per driver). Sanity check: 480k trips/day ÷ 14M adults ≈ 3.4% of adults ride each day — plausible for a big city.

Structure to use in interviews: clarify → choose approach (top-down or bottom-up) → segment → state assumptions → compute → sanity-check → give range → discuss what would change it.

3.14 Product critique and teardown

A teardown studies a product from the outside to understand users, goal, journey, strengths and possible improvements. Separate observations from assumptions; an outsider cannot know a company's internal data.

From your course notes (Lectures 4, 19, 28)

A critique explains the user, the task, the difficulty and the expected benefit. Suggested teardown sequence: product context and problem → vision/purpose → personas → user and market research → journey and pain points → prioritised opportunities → proposed solution → success metrics (adapt it to the question). Each claim needs evidence and each change needs a test. Student proposals in class (Myntra, Amazon, X, ChatGPT, Netflix) were proposals and observations, not verified gaps. Consider constraints such as content rights and contracts.

Teardown skeleton (use for any product)

  1. Product & user: what job; for whom; business model (assumption, label it).
  2. Journey: 5–7 stages; where does it help; where does it hurt (evidence: your own walk-through, reviews, tests).
  3. Opportunity: one problem; evidence; who is affected; size (assumption).
  4. Solutions: 2–3 options incl. a non-AI/simple one.
  5. Choice: impact/effort/risk; recommendation.
  6. Measurement: primary metric; guardrails; experiment.
  7. Risks and unknowns.

3.15 Discovery exercises

Exercise 1 · Rewrite the questions

Rewrite three poor interview questions and explain the bias in each: (a) “Do you think our onboarding is too long?” (b) “Would you pay ₹99/month for this?” (c) “What features would make you love this app?”

Model answer

(a) Leading and closed → “Walk me through your first time setting up the app. Where did you hesitate?” (b) Hypothetical bias → “What do you pay for today to solve this? How did you decide it was worth it?” (c) Solution-seeking; customers aren't product designers → “Tell me about the last time this task went badly. What did you do?”

Exercise 2 · Evidence grading

You have: (1) 8 interviews, 6 mention surprise at fees; (2) a funnel showing a 30% drop at the fee step; (3) a survey where 78% say they “like transparent pricing”. Rank the evidence and state what you would do next.

Model answer

(2) funnel = behavioural, scalable (strong that a drop exists, not why). (1) interviews = medium (consistent reasons, small sample). (3) survey = weak (stated preference, hypothetical). Next: segment the funnel (device, new/returning), run a usability task on the fee screen, then test early fee display in an A/B experiment with a complaint guardrail.

Exercise 3 · Estimate

Estimate how many cups of coffee are sold in a city of 5 million in a day. Show two methods and a range.

Model answer (example)

Top-down: 5M × 70% adults = 3.5M; 55% drink coffee ≈ 1.9M; 1.8 cups/day from cafés/vending/home? Only 35% bought outside → 1.9M × 1.8 × 0.35 ≈ 1.2M purchased cups/day. Bottom-up: 2,500 cafés × 250 cups = 625k + 1,500 kiosks × 300 = 450k + vending/office 100k ≈ 1.18M. Range 0.9–1.4M. Sensitive to share who buy outside and cups per café.

3.16 Source-flagged corrections

  • Qualitative/quantitative ≠ primary/secondary.
  • Focus group ≠ target audience.
  • Persona count is not fixed; personas must be evidence-based.
  • “Surveys don't work in some country” is unsupported; design matters.
  • AI summaries of research need source checking.

3.17 Interview perspective

“How would you validate a problem before building?” — 60-second answer

“I'd start with a clear problem hypothesis and target segment, then interview 8–10 people who've recently experienced it, asking about their last real experience and what they do today. I'd look at available data to size and locate the problem, mine reviews or support tickets for patterns, and write down the assumptions that could kill the idea. For the riskiest assumption I'd run the cheapest test — a prototype or a smoke test with a real price — and decide in advance what result would make me continue, pivot or stop.”

“Tell me about a product you love and how you'd improve it.”

Tests: product sense, empathy, prioritisation, honesty about evidence. Structure: user + job → why it works → one meaningful pain (with evidence you'd gather) → 2–3 solutions → pick one with trade-offs → metric + guardrail + experiment. Mistakes: naming five features, ignoring constraints (content rights, privacy, cost), assuming your own experience is universal.

3.18 Key takeaways

  • Discovery reduces risk by learning before building. Treat solutions as hypotheses.
  • Ask about past behaviour; recruit for contrast; separate observation from interpretation.
  • Match method to question; triangulate (analytics → interviews → experiment).
  • Surveys estimate frequency but suffer from bias — design carefully.
  • Use JTBD, journey maps, OSTs and assumption maps to structure what you learn.
  • Grade evidence honestly; label hypotheses and AI-generated claims.

3.19 Check your understanding

Check your understanding

Which is an example of secondary quantitative research?

  1. A survey you design and send
  2. A published market report with spending figures
  3. Five customer interviews
  4. A usability test
Why: Secondary research uses existing information; quantitative means numeric evidence. A published report fits both.

Which interview question is best?

  1. Would you use an app that shows fees early?
  2. Don't you hate surprise fees?
  3. Tell me about the last time the total changed at checkout.
  4. Which features do you want?
Why: It asks about a specific past experience, is neutral and invites a story.
