In the four forces of switching, 'anxiety' refers to…

  1. Frustration with the current solution
  2. Attraction to the new solution
  3. Worries about trying the new solution
  4. Inertia of habit
Why: Push and pull move people toward switching; anxiety and habit hold them back.

6 of 8 interviewees mention the fee surprise. How should you report it?

  1. 75% of customers dislike hidden fees
  2. 6 of 8 interviewed participants mentioned it; frequency in the population is unknown
  3. It's statistically significant
  4. Ignore it; the sample is too small
Why: Small qualitative samples reveal themes, not population percentages.

On an assumption map, which should you test first?

  1. High importance, low evidence
  2. Low importance, high evidence
  3. Low importance, low evidence
  4. High importance, high evidence
Why: Assumptions that would sink the idea and that you know little about carry the most risk per test.

A guesstimate gives 480k/day top-down and 495k/day bottom-up. The right conclusion is…

  1. The answer is exactly 487,500
  2. Confidence is higher but both depend on assumptions; give a range
  3. Both are wrong
  4. Use the larger number
Why: Agreement of independent methods raises confidence, but communicate a range and the key assumptions.

3.20 Recommended resources

  • Nielsen Norman Group: Heuristic evaluations (from your course list) and user interviews.
  • Product Talk: Opportunity Solution Trees.
  • Rob Fitzpatrick, The Mom Test — asking good questions about past behaviour (book site).
  • Jobs to Be Done — Christensen Institute.
  • Google Cloud / Google: Gen AI glossary for AI-assisted research caveats.
Module 4

Problem Framing and Prioritization

Define the right problem, find root causes, size opportunities, and choose what to build first with defensible frameworks.

≈ 12 h study

About the numbers

All backlogs, scores and costs below are hypothetical (see datasets/rice_backlog.csv). Scores are discussion aids, not facts — the point is the reasoning, not the ranking.

4.1 Problem framing

“A problem well stated is half solved.” Problem framing is turning a vague complaint (“checkout is bad”) into a specific, evidence-backed, measurable statement the team can act on.

Problem statement: For [user/segment], [task] is difficult because [observed barrier]. We know this from [evidence]. We will measure improvement using [metric] and protect [guardrail].

From your course notes (Extra topic 15; Lecture 38)

The problem statement template above is the course's own. A strong statement identifies who has difficulty, what they are trying to do, why it matters and the desired outcome; it does not begin with a tool name. Weak: “Add AI to travel.” Stronger: “Commuters struggle to find reliable platform information before departure; help them find it faster.” Validate the claim with users.

Worked example (hypothetical)

Weak: “Reduce cart abandonment.” (No user, no cause, no number.) Better: “For first-time buyers on mobile, completing checkout is hard because the delivery fee first appears on the payment step. In March, 30% of checkout starters left at the payment step (analytics); 6 of 8 interviewees said the fee surprised them. We will raise checkout completion for first-time buyers from 70% to 76% while keeping complaint rate ≤ 1.3%.”

Framing checks: Is the problem observed (not assumed)? Specific user and moment? Measurable? Solution-free? Do we know how big it is? Is it worth solving now versus alternatives?

4.2 Root Cause Analysis (RCA)

RCA looks for the factors that, if fixed, would prevent a problem from recurring — not just the visible symptom. Use several lenses.

4.2.1 The Five Whys

Ask “why?” repeatedly (typically around five times) to move from symptom to a systemic cause.

From your course notes (Lecture 24)

The lecture contrasted immediately proposing a solution with asking successive “why” questions. Treat both the suspected cause and the proposed solution as hypotheses and test them with evidence. The five whys is a technique, not a guarantee of one true cause or a low-cost fix, and it is related to — but not identical with — first-principles thinking.

Limitations: it can follow a single causal chain and miss parallel causes; answers reflect the asker's knowledge; it needs evidence at each step.

4.2.2 Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram

A fishbone organises possible causes by category (often People, Process, Product, Platform, Policy, Partners) so you don't fixate on the first idea.

4.2.3 Pareto analysis

The Pareto principle (often “80/20”) observes that a few causes typically produce most of the effect. A Pareto chart sorts categories by frequency with a cumulative-percentage line.

4.2.4 First Principles Thinking

First principles thinking breaks a problem into its fundamental truths and rebuilds the solution from there, instead of reasoning by analogy (“competitors do X”). Steps: (1) state the goal; (2) list current assumptions; (3) challenge each (“is this a law of physics or just how it has been done?”); (4) identify what is actually fixed; (5) design from those truths.

Example (hypothetical)

Assumption: “Our delivery promise is 30 minutes because competitors say 30.” First principles: customers choose a time they can rely on; the cost drivers are travel time and wait time at the restaurant. Option: promise a window based on live load and show an honest ETA — reliability beats a faster-but-missed promise.

4.2.5 Systems Thinking

Systems thinking looks at how parts interact through feedback loops and delays. In reinforcing loops change feeds on itself (growth or collapse); in balancing loops change triggers a correcting response. Product problems often involve both — fixing one metric can trigger a hidden loop elsewhere.

Level 3 · Senior PM

The classic failure is a local optimisation with a hidden balancing loop: raising surge prices increases driver supply (good) but also riders' cancellations and mistrust (bad). Mapping the loops before intervening reveals which guardrails to watch.

4.3 Hypothesis-driven product development

Turn every bet into a falsifiable statement with a pre-agreed decision rule.

We believe that [change] for [segment] will [outcome/metric movement] because [reason/evidence]. We will know we are right when [measurable signal] by [date/sample]. We will stop or pivot if [disconfirming signal].

From your course notes (Lecture 27; Extra topic 15)

Experiment template: “We believe [change] will improve [metric] for [eligible users] because [reason]. Compare [control] with [variant] for [planned duration], with [guardrails]. Decide using [pre-agreed criteria].” A hypothesis is a testable prediction. Review sampling and analysis with an analyst. Module 7 covers the statistics.

4.4 Opportunity sizing

Before building, estimate how big the prize could be. Use reach × frequency × value per instance × share you can influence, with explicit assumptions and a range.

Worked example — opportunity size for early fee display

  • Checkout starters per month: 120,000
  • Abandonment at payment step: 30% → 36,000 users
  • Share of those caused by fee surprise (from interviews + analytics; assumption): 20% → 7,200
  • Share we can recover with early display (assumption): 30% → 2,160 additional orders/month
  • AOV ₹400 → extra GMV ≈ ₹864,000/month
  • Contribution per order ₹16 (from Module 7 example) → ≈ ₹34,560/month Low case (10% fee-driven, 20% recovery): 720 orders → ₹11,520 contribution/month. High case (30%, 40%): 4,320 orders → ₹69,120. Even the high case is modest: contribution is thin here, so the strategic value (trust, repeat orders) may matter more than the immediate margin — which is exactly what a PM should flag.

4.5 Prioritisation frameworks

From your course notes (Lecture 17)

Prioritisation means deciding what to do first when you cannot do everything at once. Compare expected value, effort, risk and urgent needs. Safety or legal work can be mandatory regardless of score. A RICE score is a discussion aid: Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort — use consistent units, check assumptions and revisit the decision. Research informs impact; engineers and other specialists help estimate effort, complexity and dependencies.

4.5.1 Impact vs effort (value vs complexity)

Plot candidates on a 2×2 of expected value vs estimated effort: quick wins (high value, low effort), big bets (high/high), fill-ins (low/low), time sinks (low value, high effort).

Use when: early triage, workshops, explaining trade-offs visually. Don't use when: you need a defensible numeric ranking across many items. Limits: subjective, ignores reach/confidence/risk/dependencies.

4.5.2 RICE

RICE score = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort Reach = people (or events) affected in a defined period, e.g. users per quarter Impact = effect per person on the goal: 3 = massive, 2 = high, 1 = medium, 0.5 = low, 0.25 = minimal Confidence = how well supported the estimates are: 100% high, 80% medium, 50% low Effort = total work, in person-months (must be > 0)

From your course notes (Lecture 17) — corrections

The recording said reach minus impact equals churn and that impact must always be numerically lower than reach. That is wrong: reach and impact measure different things, and churn is a proportion of users lost over a defined period. The instructor also initially inverted the effort scale then corrected it: more effort belongs in the denominator and lowers the score. Use consistent units and a nonzero effort. Hypothetical Amazon features scored in class (search, registration, cart, payment) were assumptions, a discussion aid, not research.

Fully worked example (dataset: rice_backlog.csv)

Feature Reach / quarter Impact Confidence Effort (person-months) RICE = R×I×C÷E Rank
Show delivery fee early in cart 40,000 2 80% 2 40,000×2×0.8÷2 = 32,000 1
Order-again shortcut 35,000 1 80% 1 35,000×1×0.8÷1 = 28,000 2
Payment retry on failure 18,000 3 80% 3 18,000×3×0.8÷3 = 14,400 3
Saved addresses 25,000 1 100% 2 25,000×1×1.0÷2 = 12,500 4
Dark mode 30,000 0.5 80% 1.5 30,000×0.5×0.8÷1.5 = 8,000 5
Voice ordering 8,000 2 30%* 8 8,000×2×0.3÷8 = 600 6

*Confidence below 50% is allowed here to show the effect of low evidence.

Sensitivity check (always do this). If confidence in “fee early” falls from 80% to 50%, its score becomes 40,000×2×0.5÷2 = 20,000, and order-again (28,000) moves to #1. If effort for “payment retry” is actually 2 (not 3), its score becomes 21,600 (#3 → still #3 but closer). A ranking that flips with small input changes should be treated as a tie and decided on other grounds (strategy, risk, dependencies).

Beyond the score — decision notes:

  • Dependencies: order-again may require saved payment tokens (security review) → check sequence.
  • Mandatory work: a regulatory or security fix comes off the top regardless of score.
  • Strategy fit: if the quarter's goal is checkout completion, “fee early” and “payment retry” map directly; “order-again” serves repeat orders.
  • Risk: payment retry touches money flows — higher QA and rollback needs.

Use RICE when: comparing many comparable initiatives with some data. Don't use when: items are not comparable (a legal fix vs a feature), reach/impact are unmeasurable, or the exercise is political theatre. Limits: false precision; garbage-in/garbage-out; biased toward high-reach features over deep strategic bets; confidence is subjective.

Defending the decision in a stakeholder meeting (script)

PM: “For Q2 I'm recommending we do three things: fee early, order-again, and payment retry. Fee early scored highest and maps directly to our checkout goal; order-again is cheap and supports repeat orders; payment retry has the biggest per-user impact but costs three person-months and touches payments, so I'm scheduling it after fee early.” Sales: “But our biggest client asked for voice ordering.” PM: “I hear it. It's expensive (8 person-months) and our confidence is low — we've had one request. I'll interview five of their users this month and propose a prototype test; if we see broader demand, it enters the next planning cycle with a better score. Meanwhile, what problem does the client need solved — is it hands-free ordering, or speed?” Why this works: it shows the data, names trade-offs and risks, offers a path for the stakeholder's idea, and invites correction.

4.5.3 ICE

ICE score = Impact × Confidence × Ease (each scored 1–10; some teams average instead of multiplying)

Worked example (same backlog, 1–10 scales)

Feature Impact Confidence Ease ICE (I×C×E)
Show fee early 8 8 7 448
Order-again shortcut 6 8 9 432
Payment retry 9 8 5 360
Saved addresses 5 9 7 315
Dark mode 3 8 8 192
Voice ordering 7 3 2 42

ICE vs RICE: ICE omits Reach and uses a single “Ease” in place of person-months — faster but less discriminating. Use ICE for quick growth-experiment ranking; use RICE when audience size varies a lot. Both inherit subjectivity.

4.5.4 MoSCoW

Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have (for now) — classify scope for a specific release or time-box.

From your course notes (Lecture 17)

Make the scope and release period clear, and agree with stakeholders on why each item belongs in its category.

Use when: negotiating release scope against a fixed date. Don't use when: you need to rank within a category (it doesn't). Limit: everything tends to become a “Must”.

4.5.5 Kano Model

The Kano model classifies features by how they affect satisfaction: Must-be (expected; absence dissatisfies, presence is neutral), Performance / one-dimensional (more is better), Attractive / delighter (unexpected; presence delights, absence is fine), Indifferent, Reverse. Features drift over time: today's delighter becomes tomorrow's must-be.

How to run it: For each feature ask two questions — functional ("How would you feel if the product had X?") and dysfunctional ("…if it did not have X?") — with answers: Like / Expect / Neutral / Live with / Dislike. Map each pair to a category:

Example (hypothetical)

Payment success confirmation → Must-be (expected). Faster checkout → Performance. Surprise free dessert → Attractive. Dark mode for most users → Indifferent; for night-shift users → Performance. Implication: never ship a product missing must-bes to chase delighters.

Limits: survey-based; wording sensitive; categories shift over time; doesn't capture cost or feasibility.

4.5.6 Weighted scoring models

Score options against weighted criteria that reflect strategy, then multiply and sum.

Worked example

Criteria and weights: Customer impact 35%, Revenue 25%, Strategic fit 20%, Ease 20% (scores 1–5, higher is better; ease is inverse of effort). | Initiative | Impact | Revenue | Fit | Ease | Weighted score | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Payment retry | 5 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 5×.35 + 4×.25 + 4×.20 + 3×.20 = 1.75 + 1.00 + 0.80 + 0.60 = 4.15 | | Show fee early | 4 | 3 | 5 | 4 | 1.40 + 0.75 + 1.00 + 0.80 = 3.95 | | Saved addresses | 3 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 1.05 + 0.50 + 0.60 + 0.80 = 2.95 | | Voice ordering | 2 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 0.70 + 0.50 + 0.40 + 0.20 = 1.80 |

Note that the ranking differs from RICE: weighted scoring rewards strategic fit and revenue explicitly, while RICE weights reach. Frameworks encode values — choose the one that reflects the decision you are really making, and say why.

Rules: agree weights before scoring (to avoid reverse-engineering); keep ≤ 5 criteria; use anchored scales (“5 = measurable impact on the quarterly KR”); test sensitivity by changing weights ±10 points.

4.5.7 Cost of Delay and WSJF

Cost of Delay (CoD) is the value lost per unit time by not having something. WSJF (Weighted Shortest Job First) — from the Scaled Agile Framework — prioritises by CoD ÷ job size, so small, valuable, time-critical items go first.

WSJF = Cost of Delay ÷ Job size Cost of Delay = User/business value + Time criticality + Risk reduction or opportunity enablement (each on a relative scale, e.g. Fibonacci 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20)

Worked example (relative scores)

Job Value Time criticality Risk/opportunity CoD Size WSJF Order
C · Fix gateway timeout before sale season 5 13 2 20 3 6.67 1
A · Fee shown early 8 5 3 16 5 3.20 2
B · Redesign loyalty programme 13 8 5 26 13 2.00 3
D · Platform refactor to reduce incident risk 3 2 8 13 8 1.63 4

Job C is small and time-critical, so it jumps to the front even though B has the highest absolute value. CD3 is a related variant (“Cost of Delay Divided by Duration”). If a feature earns ₹50,000/week and a delay of 6 weeks is likely, the delay costs ₹300,000 — a concrete way to argue for staffing.

Use when: many items compete for scarce capacity and timing matters (seasonal launches, compliance dates, competitor moves). Don't use when: you can't estimate relative sizes honestly. Limits: relative scales are subjective; favours small jobs and can starve large strategic ones.

4.5.8 Risk-adjusted prioritisation

Discount value by the probability of success and subtract cost:

Expected value = P(success) × value if successful − cost

Example

Project X — value if successful ₹60 lakh, P = 50%, cost ₹10 lakh → EV = 30 − 10 = ₹20 lakh. Project Y — value ₹25 lakh, P = 90%, cost ₹5 lakh → EV = 22.5 − 5 = ₹17.5 lakh. X has a higher EV but is riskier; a PM might still choose Y first (less variance, funds learning) or split X into a cheaper test that raises its probability estimate. EV is only as good as the probabilities — treat them as ranges.

4.5.9 Choosing a framework

Situation Reach for
Quick triage in a workshop Impact–effort 2×2
Many comparable features, some data RICE (or ICE if reach is similar)
Fixed-date release scope MoSCoW
Understanding customer expectations Kano
Strategy-weighted choice among few big initiatives Weighted scoring
Time-sensitive work with scarce capacity WSJF / Cost of Delay
Choosing between experiments ICE/PIE on the learning value + cost to run

4.6 Dependency mapping and prioritisation under constraints

A dependency is work or a decision that something else relies on. Map them so the ranking reflects feasible sequence.

Prioritising under constraints

  1. Take mandatory work off the top (legal, security, contractual deadlines, incidents).
  2. Reserve capacity for reliability and technical debt (e.g., 15–25% — a guideline, justify with data).
  3. Score the rest, then sequence by dependencies, team skills and risk.
  4. Limit work in progress; finishing beats starting.
  5. Record what you are not doing and why.
  6. Re-plan on a cadence; treat the plan as a hypothesis.

From your course notes (Extra topic 12)

A dependency is work or a decision that another piece of work relies on. Technical debt is the future cost of a technical shortcut or outdated implementation; not every bug or maintenance item is technical debt. Showing an estimated fee depends on a delivery-price service and an agreed fallback — if the service is late, a staged release may show “estimate unavailable” rather than invent a number. Ask engineering to identify system owners, risks and realistic alternatives.

4.7 MVP definition

An MVP (Minimum Viable Product) is the smallest useful version or experiment that lets a team learn about an important assumption with real users. It is defined by the learning goal, not by feature count.

From your course notes (Lecture 20; Lecture 43)

An MVP must still be appropriate and safe for its intended test. Prototype vs MVP: a prototype can be interactive and helps test a concept or flow; an MVP may be a usable early offering or another focused experiment — the boundary depends on the learning goal, and real users can test prototypes too. The recording sometimes equated an MVP with a prototype and implied it must always be a public launch — neither is a universal rule. A pivot is a substantive change in direction, not every small iteration. A payment screen that shows “success” without a real payment provider is a simulation — label it. Record what works, what is mocked and what needs security, accessibility and reliability testing.

MVP checklist: (1) Riskiest assumption named? (2) Success threshold set in advance? (3) Who will use it and are they informed/consenting? (4) Safe — privacy, security, financial, legal? (5) What is simulated vs real, and is that disclosed internally? (6) What decision will the result drive?

4.8 Experiment prioritisation

Rank experiments by expected learning per unit cost: how important is the assumption (importance), how uncertain (evidence gap), how cheap to test, and how long to read out. A simple score: Importance × Uncertainty ÷ Cost-to-test, or use ICE with “Impact” defined as decision value.

Example (hypothetical)

Experiment Assumption Importance (1–5) Uncertainty (1–5) Cost (days) Score
Fake-door for “weekly plan” Parents want weekly plans 5 4 2 5×4÷2 = 10
Price test ₹99 vs ₹149 Willingness to pay 4 4 10 4×4÷10 = 1.6
Prototype test of onboarding Users understand setup 3 3 5 3×3÷5 = 1.8
Run the fake-door first: the answer decides whether the other tests matter.

4.9 Roadmap planning

A roadmap communicates intended outcomes and likely sequence. Formats: Now / Next / Later (outcome-based, no dates), quarterly themes, timeline (for committed dates). Keep committed items separate from exploratory bets and show dependencies and confidence.

From your course notes (Lecture 13)

Ask engineers about complexity, testing, risks and dependencies, then explain trade-offs to business stakeholders. Collaboratively explore scope or sequencing rather than assuming a visible change is technically simple. A roadmap is an evolving plan, not a guarantee.

4.10 Case-solving structure (product design and improvement questions)

From your course notes (Lectures 8, 11, 36)

Clarify the problem before proposing features. In an interview ask about scope, users and constraints; in written work, state assumptions. Then describe the user, their need, the proposed solution and trade-offs. Pick one user problem and investigate it before suggesting features. For community products, define the desired behaviour (useful conversations), not just clicks; measure meaningful participation, retention and safety together; and filtering is imperfect — avoid promising parents a completely safe experience. Treat each solution as a hypothesis.

4.11 Exercises with model answers

Exercise 1 · Compute and challenge RICE

Score: A) Reach 10,000, Impact 2, Confidence 80%, Effort 4. B) Reach 3,000, Impact 3, Confidence 100%, Effort 1. C) Reach 50,000, Impact 0.5, Confidence 50%, Effort 5. Rank them and say what would change your mind.

Model answer

A = 10,000×2×0.8÷4 = 4,000. B = 3,000×3×1.0÷1 = 9,000. C = 50,000×0.5×0.5÷5 = 2,500. Ranking: B > A > C. B wins on low effort and high confidence despite small reach. Challenge: is B's reach limited to a niche that doesn't serve this quarter's goal? Would C's reach justify a cheap test to raise confidence? If B's effort is really 3, its score drops to 3,000 and A wins — so I'd verify the effort estimate with engineering.

Exercise 2 · Pick a framework

A regulator requires a new consent screen by 30 June. Marketing wants a referral feature; support wants better refund tracking. How do you decide the order?

Model answer

The consent screen is mandatory — take it off the top and schedule it first (legal deadline). Then compare referral vs refund tracking with RICE or WSJF: referral's value depends on growth goals and CAC; refund tracking reduces support cost and complaints (risk reduction). Check dependencies (consent flow may touch the same onboarding screens). Present the trade-off with numbers and agree on a review date.

Exercise 3 · Five Whys + test

“Our app's rating fell from 4.4 to 4.1 last month.” Do a five-whys chain and name the data that would verify each “why”.

Model answer (example)
  1. Why did the rating fall? Many 1-star reviews mention payment errors → verify with review tagging. 2. Why payment errors? A new gateway SDK was released on the 12th → check release dates and error logs. 3. Why were they not caught? No test for bank redirect flow on Android 14 → check QA coverage. 4. Why no test? Test matrix excludes new OS versions → review the matrix. 5. Why? No owner for compatibility testing → process gap. Fix: hotfix SDK; add the OS to the matrix; assign an owner. Validate each step with evidence, not assumption.

4.12 Interview perspective

“How do you prioritise a roadmap?” — structure and model answer

What it tests: judgement, communication, humility. Structure: (1) goals and constraints; (2) gather and size opportunities; (3) mandatory work; (4) choose a framework fit for the decision (e.g., RICE) and show a few scores; (5) sensitivity and dependencies; (6) stakeholder alignment and a review cadence. Model answer: “I start with the quarter's goal — say, checkout completion. I list candidate problems with evidence and size them. I take mandatory items first, then score the rest with RICE using agreed definitions, and check how sensitive the ranking is to confidence and effort. I map dependencies, then share a one-page recommendation with trade-offs and what we're not doing, and revisit it each month as we learn.” Common mistakes: naming a framework without applying it; ignoring dependencies; treating scores as truth.

“A key stakeholder insists their feature goes first. What do you do?” — 60-second answer

“I'd first understand the problem behind the request and its evidence and urgency. Then I'd show where it sits against our goals using the same framework we use for everything — with numbers — and the cost of delaying it versus the alternatives. If it still doesn't win, I'd offer options: a smaller version, a time-boxed discovery, or a workaround, and agree a date to revisit. I'd document the decision and who made it.”

4.13 Key takeaways

  • Frame the problem with user, task, barrier, evidence, metric, guardrail.
  • RCA tools (Five Whys, fishbone, Pareto, first principles, systems thinking) generate hypotheses to test — not answers.
  • Frameworks encode values: RICE (reach-weighted), ICE (speed), MoSCoW (scope), Kano (expectations), weighted scoring (strategy), WSJF (timing).
  • Always do sensitivity checks, map dependencies, take mandatory work first and record what you're not doing.
  • An MVP is a learning vehicle; choose the cheapest type that tests the riskiest assumption.
  • Roadmaps are outcome-oriented, evolving plans.

4.14 Check your understanding

Check your understanding

RICE for Reach 20,000, Impact 1, Confidence 80%, Effort 2 equals…

  1. 8,000
  2. 16,000
  3. 32,000
  4. 40,000
Why: 20,000 × 1 × 0.8 ÷ 2 = 8,000.

In RICE, increasing Effort…

  1. Increases the score
  2. Decreases the score
  3. Has no effect
  4. Only affects Reach
Why: Effort is the denominator, so more effort lowers the score.

A regulatory deadline item should usually be…

  1. Scored with RICE like everything else
  2. Taken off the top as mandatory work
  3. Deferred until after features
  4. Dropped if its score is low
Why: Mandatory legal, security or contractual work is scheduled regardless of score.

Which describes a Kano 'must-be' feature?

  1. Its absence dissatisfies but presence is just expected
  2. More of it always raises satisfaction
  3. It delights when unexpected
  4. Customers don't care
Why: Must-be features are expected basics: absent = dissatisfied; present = neutral.

WSJF is computed as…

  1. Value ÷ effort
  2. Cost of Delay ÷ job size
  3. Reach × Impact
  4. Time ÷ cost
Why: Weighted Shortest Job First divides Cost of Delay by job size.

An MVP is best described as…

  1. The cheapest version of the full product
  2. The smallest useful version or experiment to learn about a key assumption
  3. A prototype only
  4. A public launch
Why: MVPs are defined by what they let you learn; they may be non-public and need not be a prototype.

  • Intercom: RICE prioritization — the original RICE write-up.

Module 5

UX and Design Collaboration

Understand UX craft well enough to review designs, run usability tests, and work productively with product designers.

≈ 10 h study

About the screens in this module

All wireframes are illustrative, simplified sketches made for teaching. They are not screenshots of any real company's interface and must never be presented as such.

5.1 UX versus UI

From your course notes (Lecture 16)

UI is the interface people see and use: text, controls, layout, colour, typography. UX is the complete experience of achieving a goal, including usability, accessibility, waiting, trust, service and what happens when something goes wrong. A large readable Pay button is UI. A checkout that clearly shows the total, works with a screen reader and explains a failed payment is part of UX.

UX (experience) UI (interface)
Scope The whole journey, before/during/after the screen Visual and interactive layer
Questions Can people achieve their goal? Do they trust it? Is it clear, consistent, accessible, attractive?
Artefacts Research, journeys, flows, prototypes, test findings Style guides, components, high-fidelity screens
Failure looks like Users abandon, get lost or distrust Inconsistent, hard to read or hard to tap

5.2 Design Thinking and Human-Centred Design

Design Thinking is a human-centred, iterative approach to problem solving with five stages (Stanford d.school): Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test. Human-Centred Design (HCD), standardised in ISO 9241-210, emphasises understanding users, tasks and environments; involving users throughout; evaluating with users; iterating; considering the whole user experience; and using multidisciplinary skills.

From your course notes (Lecture 16)

A possible design sequence is: define the problem and requirements, map the flow, sketch or wireframe, build a prototype, test, revise and implement — iterative, not mandatory. Include users with varied needs and abilities. A wireframe shows structure; a prototype lets people experience or test interactions.

5.3 Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics

Jakob Nielsen's ten general principles for interaction design are a fast way to review any screen (a heuristic evaluation).

# Heuristic Meaning Example (checkout)
1 Visibility of system status Keep users informed with timely feedback “Processing payment…” spinner with a timeout message
2 Match between system and real world Speak the user's language “Delivery fee”, not “ancillary charge code 4”
3 User control and freedom Easy undo/exit “Edit cart” and “Cancel” always available
4 Consistency and standards Follow conventions Same “Pay” button position on every step
5 Error prevention Prevent problems before they occur Disable “Pay” until a payment method is chosen; confirm address
6 Recognition rather than recall Make options visible Show saved cards, not “enter the last four digits”
7 Flexibility and efficiency of use Shortcuts for experts “Order again”, saved addresses
8 Aesthetic and minimalist design Remove irrelevant info Hide secondary promotions during payment
9 Help users recognise, diagnose, recover from errors Plain-language errors with a fix “Your card was declined. Try another card or UPI.”
10 Help and documentation Searchable, task-focused help Link to refund FAQ from the order screen

From your course notes (Companion ch. 3; Picture lesson)

Review visibility of status, clear labels, error recovery, keyboard and screen-reader access, colour contrast and understandable prices. A design review (heuristic evaluation) can find possible problems but does not replace testing with real users. An AI review is a useful draft, not a substitute.

How to run a heuristic evaluation: 3–5 evaluators review independently against the list, rate each problem's severity (0 cosmetic … 4 catastrophe), then consolidate. It is cheap and fast but misses problems real users hit.

5.4 Laws of UX that every PM should know

5.4.1 Jakob's Law

Users spend most of their time on other sites/apps, so they expect yours to work the same way. Implication: follow conventions (cart icon top-right, logo links home) unless you have a strong, tested reason. Innovate on value, not on basic mechanics.

5.4.2 Hick's Law

The time to choose increases with the number and complexity of choices.

Hick–Hyman law: T = b × log₂(n + 1) T = decision time; n = number of equally likely choices; b = empirically fitted constant

Illustrative calculation (b = 0.1 s, a made-up constant for illustration)

7 menu options: T = 0.1 × log₂(8) = 0.1 × 3 = 0.30 s. 15 options: T = 0.1 × log₂(16) = 0.1 × 4 = 0.40 s. Doubling the options adds one bit, not double the time — but real interfaces also add scanning and comprehension costs. Implication: group, prioritise, progressively disclose; don't hide key actions.

5.4.3 Fitts's Law

The time to reach a target depends on distance and size: closer and larger targets are faster to hit.

Fitts's law (Shannon form): T = a + b × log₂(D / W + 1) D = distance to target; W = target width (along the movement axis); a, b = constants Index of difficulty ID = log₂(D / W + 1)

Worked example

A button 40 px wide at a distance of 400 px: ID = log₂(400/40 + 1) = log₂(11) = 3.46 bits. Making it 80 px wide: ID = log₂(6) = 2.58 bits — about 25% lower. For touch, thumb reach zones and minimum target sizes (≈ 44×44 pt iOS guidance; 48×48 dp Android/Material guidance; WCAG 2.2 requires at least 24×24 CSS px as a minimum) matter more than the formula. Implication: make primary actions large and in easy reach; keep destructive actions small and apart.

5.4.4 Gestalt principles

How people perceive visual groups:

Principle Idea Use
Proximity Close items are grouped Space between form sections
Similarity Similar items are related Same style for all primary buttons
Common region Items in a shared boundary are grouped Card around the order summary
Continuity Eyes follow smooth lines Aligned lists and stepper progress
Closure We complete incomplete shapes Minimal icons
Figure–ground We separate focus from background Modal overlays dim the page
Focal point Distinct items draw attention One highlighted primary CTA

5.4.5 Cognitive Load Theory

Working memory is limited. Intrinsic load is the inherent difficulty of the task; extraneous load is added by poor design (clutter, confusing labels); germane load is effort that builds understanding. Designers reduce extraneous load: chunk information, use progressive disclosure, defaults, recognisable patterns and consistent layouts. Miller's “7±2” is often over-quoted — treat it as a reminder that capacity is small, not as a design rule.

5.5 Information architecture, user flows and task flows

  • Information architecture (IA) organises content so people can find it: structure, navigation, labelling, search. Methods: card sorting (how users group items), tree testing (can users find items in your proposed structure?).
  • A user flow maps paths and decisions through the product toward a goal; a task flow is one task in detail, typically for a single user type.

From your course notes (Lecture 5; Companion ch. 3)

A journey can contain many flows. Include branches: valid address, invalid address, payment failure, retry and cancellation — and label the desired outcome for each. Start/end markers and connectors make the sequence readable. Use the appropriate level of detail; a functional flow, not backend architecture.

5.6 Wireframes and prototypes: low to high fidelity

Fidelity What it is Use for Risk
Sketch / paper Hand-drawn boxes Exploring many ideas in minutes Hard to share remotely
Low-fi wireframe Grey boxes, real labels, no visual polish Layout, flow, content priority People critique visuals instead
High-fi mockup Real visual design Brand, UI details, stakeholder review Looks “finished”; invites premature sign-off
Interactive prototype Linked screens with transitions Usability tests, stakeholder demos Not connected to a real backend; may mislead about feasibility

From your course notes (Companion ch. 17; Lecture 16)

“Show an estimated total before checkout.” In scope: item cost and an estimate based on the address. Out of scope: changing the fee policy. Acceptance: label estimates, refresh when the address changes, and show a clear fallback when the fee service fails. Ask design about empty, loading, error, keyboard and accessible states. A prototype is not necessarily connected to a real backend.

5.6.1 Clickable prototype example

A clickable prototype for the redesign would link: Cart (redesign) → Pay → Confirmation, plus a branch Cart (fee unavailable) → Retry → Cart (redesign). In Figma: duplicate frames, name them, switch to Prototype mode, drag a connection from the button to the next frame, set the trigger (On click) and animation (Instant/Smart animate), then present and share a view-only link. Test it with 5 participants using a task such as: “Order this meal and tell me the total you expect to pay before you tap pay.”

5.7 Design systems, responsive design and mobile vs web

  • A design system is a shared library of design tokens (colours, spacing, type), reusable components, patterns and guidelines — plus code. Benefits: consistency, speed, accessibility baked in. As a PM: don't request one-off components without a reason; use existing ones; contribute needs via the system's process.
  • Responsive design adapts layouts to screen sizes (breakpoints; fluid grids; flexible images). Design mobile-first, then enhance.
  • Mobile vs web UX:
Mobile app Responsive web
Interaction Touch, gestures, thumb reach; smaller screens Mouse/keyboard and touch
Capabilities Camera, push notifications, biometrics Limited by browser; no install friction
Constraints App-store review, OS versions Cross-browser testing, performance on slow networks
Design focus One main task per screen, bottom navigation Wider layouts, persistent navigation

From your course notes (Companion ch. 17; Extra topic 14)

Avoid changing a shared production library without permission. Review variations, reusable components and responsive layouts with your designer; compare decisions to acceptance criteria and record unresolved questions in the PRD.

5.8 Accessibility

Accessibility means people with different abilities can perceive, understand and use the product. WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, currently 2.2) is organised around four principles — Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust — with conformance levels A, AA, AAA (AA is the common target).

From your course notes (Extra topic 14)

Inclusive design also considers varied devices, language, connectivity, literacy and circumstances. Accessibility is an ongoing product quality concern, not a finishing decoration. A form should use labels in addition to colour, have visible keyboard focus, describe errors in text and work with assistive technology; a delivery estimate must not rely only on a red or green indicator. Involve people with disabilities; use automated checks alongside manual and assistive-technology testing; ask qualified specialists about applicable standards and legal obligations.

Contrast ratio is (L₁ + 0.05) ÷ (L₂ + 0.05), where L is relative luminance (lighter ÷ darker). WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (≥ 24 px, or ≥ 18.66 px bold) and for UI component boundaries.

Worked check — contrast of common text colours on white (computed)

Text colour Ratio on white AA normal text (4.5:1)?
#101828 (navy) 17.75 : 1 Pass
#2563EB (royal blue) 5.17 : 1 Pass
#667085 (grey) 4.97 : 1 Pass
#767676 4.54 : 1 Pass (barely)
#777777 4.48 : 1 Fail
#949494 3.03 : 1 Fail (large text/UI only)
#10B981 (emerald) 2.54 : 1 Fail — white text on this green is also 2.54 : 1

This is why this handbook uses a deeper green (#047857) for filled buttons with white text: the brand emerald alone does not meet AA for text.

PM accessibility checklist: semantic structure and labels · keyboard operability and visible focus · contrast · text alternatives for images · captions for video · target sizes · error messages in text with guidance · no information by colour alone · respects reduced motion · tested with a screen reader on key flows · accessibility acceptance criteria in every story.

5.9 Usability testing

A usability test observes representative users attempting realistic tasks. Typical: 5–8 participants per round — Nielsen and Landauer's model estimates one user finds ~31% of problems, so five users find about 1 − (1 − 0.31)⁵ ≈ 84%, which is why iterating with small rounds beats one big test (the figure is a model for finding problems, not for estimating rates).

Task wording: bad — “Click the fee breakdown.” Good — “You're about to pay for this meal. How much will you be charged in total? Tell me what you're looking at.” Measures: task success, time on task, errors, confidence, plus SUS (System Usability Scale, 10 questions; average across products ≈ 68 on a 0–100 scale).

From your course notes (Lecture 16; Picture lesson)

Observe real people completing a task. Make a prototype, test with users with varied needs, improve and retest. The session contrasts discovering a problem with testing whether people can navigate a proposed design. A design review can find possible problems but does not replace testing with real users.

5.10 A/B testing in UX

A/B tests measure behaviour at scale (completion rates, clicks to goal), not understanding. Use usability tests to learn why, A/B tests to learn how much. Avoid testing tiny cosmetic differences with small traffic; test meaningful hypotheses and pair with guardrails (complaints, errors). See Module 7 for the statistics.

5.11 Design critique and working with product designers

Design critique is structured feedback on a design against goals — not personal taste. Good format: goal and constraints → what's being reviewed → feedback framed as observations tied to user/goal (“I notice… it may cause…”) → questions → decisions. Avoid solutioneering in comments.

From your course notes (Lecture 16)

The instructor described modifying a designer's file without coordination, causing inconsistencies and confusion. Agree on ownership, explain user and business context, use the design system and resolve disagreements through evidence. The claim that PMs should never edit Figma and that UI is solely a developer's responsibility is too rigid; roles depend on the team. Designers contribute to solutions; PMs can learn and create designs when appropriate.

How to be a great partner to designers

  1. Bring the problem and evidence, not a solution. 2. Involve them in discovery from day one. 3. Share constraints early (tech, legal, timing). 4. Give specific, user-centred feedback. 5. Protect time for exploration and for accessibility and edge states. 6. Respect craft: ask “what are you optimising for?”. 7. Decide together what to test.

5.12 Figma fundamentals for PMs

From your course notes (Companion ch. 17)

Figma Design is a collaborative design tool. A frame represents a screen or container; text, shapes and components form the interface; a component is a reusable element; a prototype connects screens to illustrate a flow. Editing rights and features depend on the team and plan. Beginner exercise: create a personal file, add a phone-sized frame, place a heading, meal card, price and button; duplicate the frame and change it to show the total fee; in prototype mode connect the button to the next frame, preview and test it. PM workflow: use comments to describe the user problem and evidence (“Three test participants missed the total; could we make it visible before payment?”). Share prototype links with appropriate permissions.

Figma concept What it is PM relevance
Frame Screen/container Check screens match the flow
Auto layout Responsive spacing rules Explains how content grows (long names, translations)
Component & variants Reusable element with states (default, hover, error, disabled) Ensures states are designed
Styles / variables Colour, type, spacing tokens Consistency, theming
Prototype Clickable flow Testing and demos
Comments Contextual feedback Give specific, evidence-based feedback
Dev Mode Specs and code snippets for engineers Handoff clarity

5.13 Journey mapping, onboarding and checkout optimisation

  • Onboarding — get users to their first meaningful value quickly: reduce steps, defer non-essential fields, use progressive profiling, show progress, explain permissions when needed (just-in-time), offer a sample/empty-state starter.
  • Checkout — show the total early, minimise fields, offer guest checkout and saved payment methods, give clear error recovery, keep the primary action consistent.

5.14 Error states and empty states

  • Error states: say what happened, why (if useful), and how to fix it; preserve user input; offer a way forward; log for diagnosis. Avoid blame (“Invalid input!”) and codes alone.
  • Empty states: teach the product — explain the benefit, show the primary action, optionally sample data.
  • Loading states: skeleton screens beat endless spinners; give time estimates for long tasks.
State Weak Strong
Payment error “Error 502” “We couldn't reach your bank. Your card hasn't been charged. Try again or use UPI.”
Empty orders Blank “No orders yet. Your first order will appear here. Browse popular meals →”
Offline Frozen app “You're offline. Showing saved items; ordering resumes when you're back online.”

5.15 UX metrics

Google's HEART framework (Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success) with the Goals–Signals–Metrics process helps choose UX metrics.

Other UX measures: task success rate, time on task, error rate, SUS, CSAT (satisfaction), CES (effort), NPS (recommendation — widely used, with limitations as a UX measure), accessibility issue count, support contacts per 1,000 orders.

5.16 Design handoff

A good handoff is a conversation, not a file drop: walk through the flow, states (empty/loading/error/offline), responsive behaviour, accessibility, copy, analytics events, and edge cases. Provide: final frames, component references, spacing/typography specs (Dev Mode), prototype link, acceptance criteria, open questions, and an agreed QA review (design reviews the build before release).

Handoff checklist: all states designed · copy final (or flagged) · accessibility requirements listed · events named · animation specs · assets exported · decisions logged · QA owner named · definition of done includes design review.

5.17 Exercises with model answers

Exercise 1 · Heuristic evaluation

Evaluate the “Before” checkout screens against the 10 heuristics. List three violations with severity.

Model answer

(1) Visibility of system status — the final cost isn't visible until payment (severity 3: causes abandonment). (2) Match with the real world / consistency — “fees are calculated at payment” hides a concept users need now (severity 2). (3) Error prevention — no way to preview the total before committing (severity 3). Also note heuristic 9: no designed failure state if fee calculation fails. Recommend the “After” design and test it.

Exercise 2 · Apply Fitts's law

A primary button is 48 px wide and 500 px from the thumb's resting point. What is the index of difficulty? What happens if you widen it to 96 px?

Model answer

ID = log₂(500/48 + 1) = log₂(11.42) ≈ 3.51 bits. With 96 px: log₂(500/96 + 1) = log₂(6.21) ≈ 2.64 bits — about 25% easier. In practice also move it into the thumb zone and keep a ≥ 44 px height.

Exercise 3 · Accessibility check

Your error text is #949494 on white, 14 px. What is wrong and how do you fix it?

Model answer

Contrast is ~3.03:1; normal text needs ≥ 4.5:1. Fix: darken to ≈ #767676 (4.54:1) or darker (e.g., #595959 = 7.0:1); don't rely on colour alone — add an icon and the text “Error:”. Test with a screen reader that the error is announced and associated with the field.

Exercise 4 · Plan a test

You redesigned onboarding. Write three realistic tasks and two metrics for a usability test with 6 users.

Model answer

Tasks: (1) “You've just downloaded the app. Set it up so it can deliver to your office.” (2) “Find a vegetarian meal under ₹300 and add it to the cart.” (3) “Check what you'd pay in total.” Metrics: task success rate, time on task, errors/hesitations, confidence rating (1–5), SUS at the end. Pre-define success (e.g., ≥ 5 of 6 complete task 3 unaided).

5.18 Interview perspective

“How would you improve the checkout experience of a food-delivery app?” — structure

1) Clarify goal (completion? AOV? trust?) and users. 2) Map the journey and find the biggest friction with data (funnel by step/device) and research. 3) Hypotheses: fees shown late, payment failure recovery, form length. 4) Solutions with trade-offs (show fee early; guest checkout; retry). 5) Prioritise (impact/effort/risk). 6) Design considerations: states, accessibility, honest fallbacks. 7) Test: usability test then A/B with guardrails. Model answer highlights: “I'd start with the funnel to find where users leave, then interview people who abandoned. If fees surprise them, I'd test showing a full breakdown in the cart with 'estimate' labels and a clear fallback. Primary metric: checkout completion; guardrails: complaints and payment errors; segment by new vs returning users.” Mistakes: jumping to UI changes without evidence; ignoring failure states and accessibility.

“How do you work with designers when you disagree?” — 60-second answer

“I start by getting aligned on the user problem and the success metric. Then I ask what the designer is optimising for and share the evidence I have. If we still disagree, we agree on a quick test — a usability session or A/B — and a decision rule in advance. I give feedback as observations tied to the user, not preferences, and make sure the final decision is documented.”

5.19 Key takeaways

  • UX = whole experience; UI = the interface layer.
  • Use heuristics and the laws of UX (Jakob, Hick, Fitts), Gestalt and cognitive load to review designs quickly.
  • Design all states: empty, loading, error, offline, success.
  • Accessibility is a quality requirement: check contrast, keyboard, labels, target sizes.
  • Usability tests with ~5–8 users per round find most problems; A/B tests measure behaviour at scale.
  • Partner with designers by bringing problems and evidence, respecting ownership and the design system.
  • Make handoff a conversation with states, events, accessibility and QA agreed.

5.20 Check your understanding

Check your understanding

Which statement correctly contrasts UX and UI?

  1. UI is the whole experience; UX is the buttons.
  2. UX is the whole experience; UI is the interface people see and use.
  3. They are the same.
  4. UX applies only to mobile apps.
Why: UX covers the full experience of achieving a goal, including usability, trust and failure handling; UI is the visual and interactive layer.

Hick's law says decision time…

  1. Decreases with more options
  2. Increases with the number and complexity of choices
  3. Is constant
  4. Depends only on colour
Why: More (and more complex) choices take longer to process; group and prioritise options.

Fitts's law implies a primary mobile button should be…

  1. Small and far from the thumb
  2. Large and within easy reach
  3. Hidden in a menu
  4. Red
Why: Time to reach a target falls as it gets closer and larger.

Normal body text needs at least what contrast ratio for WCAG AA?

  1. 2 : 1
  2. 3 : 1
  3. 4.5 : 1
  4. 21 : 1
Why: WCAG 2.2 AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI components.

Why run several small usability rounds rather than one large one?

  1. It is cheaper per participant only
  2. Each round finds most problems, you fix them, then retest to find the next layer
  3. Statistics require it
  4. Designers prefer it
Why: Small samples find most usability problems; iterating compounds the benefit.

A good error message…

  1. Shows an error code only
  2. Blames the user
  3. Explains what happened and how to recover, in plain language
  4. Is hidden
Why: Heuristic 9: help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors.

5.21 Recommended resources

  • Nielsen Norman Group: 10 usability heuristics and heuristic evaluations.
  • Laws of UX — concise write-ups of Jakob's, Hick's, Fitts's laws and more.
  • W3C: WCAG 2 overview and How to Meet WCAG (Quick Reference).
  • Figma Help: Share files and prototypes.
  • Google HEART framework (Rodden, Hutchinson, Fu).
  • Stanford d.school: Design Thinking Bootleg.
Module 6

Effective Communication and Stakeholder Management

Lead without authority — structure your thinking, write clear PRDs, align stakeholders, negotiate trade-offs and communicate with every function.

≈ 9 h study

About the dialogues

Conversations in this module are illustrative scripts written to model technique. They are not transcripts of real meetings.

6.1 Why communication is the PM's core tool

PMs rarely have formal authority over the people who build, sell or support the product. Influence comes from clarity, evidence, trust and consistency. Most PM failures are communication failures: unclear problems, unshared trade-offs, surprises, or decisions nobody wrote down.

Principles

  1. Start with the answer (then support it).
  2. Know your audience — what decision do they need to make, and what do they care about?
  3. Make trade-offs explicit — options, cost, benefit, risk.
  4. Separate facts, assumptions and opinions — label each.
  5. Write it down — decisions, owners, dates.
  6. No surprises — share bad news early, with a plan.
  7. Listen more than you talk — especially with customers and engineers.

6.2 Structured problem-solving communication

6.2.1 The Pyramid Principle and SCQA

Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle: lead with the governing thought (answer), group supporting arguments (ideally mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, MECE), and support each with evidence. SCQA frames the opening: Situation → Complication → Question → Answer.

SCQA opening (hypothetical)

Situation: Checkout completion is 70% and is our largest growth lever this quarter. Complication: 30% of users leave at the payment step, and research says the fee surprises them. Question: What should we change first? Answer: Show the full fee breakdown in the cart, tested as an A/B experiment over two weeks.

6.2.2 Executive summaries

An executive summary fits on one screen: the ask/decision, the recommendation, why (2–3 bullets with numbers), risks and mitigations, what you need (people, money, decision by date). Put it at the top of every doc.

Executive summary template

Decision needed by 15 May: approve 2 engineers for 6 weeks to test early fee display. Recommendation: run an A/B test; ship only if checkout completion rises ≥ 2 points with no rise in complaints. Why: the payment step loses 30% of starters; 6/8 users cite fee surprise; est. +2,160 orders/month (range 720–4,320). Risks: fee estimate inaccuracy → label as estimate, fallback text; delay to loyalty work by 3 weeks. Not doing: loyalty redesign until Q3.

6.2.3 STAR and PREP

  • STAR (behavioural answers): Situation, Task, Action, Result — with your actions and a real result (or say it wasn't measured).
  • PREP (quick opinions and updates): Point, Reason, Example, Point — great for meetings and 60-second answers.

From your course notes (Lectures 18, 24)

Use STAR for experience-based interviews: explain the Situation, your Task, the Actions you personally took, and the Result, ideally with evidence. The instructor called the last part “reaction” but explained it as the result. Tell the story naturally; do not invent outcomes. If results were not measured, say so rather than inventing numbers.

PREP in a stand-up (hypothetical)

Point: We should delay the loyalty launch by a week. Reason: payment errors spiked 3× after Tuesday's release. Example: 412 failed attempts yesterday vs ~130 normal. Point: let's fix payments first, then launch loyalty next Wednesday.

6.3 Storytelling with data

Data persuades when it answers a question for a specific audience. Principles (in the spirit of Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's Storytelling with Data):

  1. Lead with the takeaway as the chart title (“Checkout loses most users at payment”), not “Funnel Q1”.
  2. Choose the right chart: trend → line; comparison → bar; part-to-whole with few parts → stacked bar; distribution → histogram; relationship → scatter. Avoid 3D and pie charts with many slices.
  3. Remove clutter; highlight the one thing that matters with colour.
  4. Give context: baseline, target, comparison period, sample size.
  5. Show uncertainty (ranges, confidence intervals).
  6. End with the action you want.

6.4 Stakeholder mapping and influence

Stakeholder mapping identifies who matters and how to engage them. The power–interest grid: manage closely (high power, high interest), keep satisfied (high power, low interest), keep informed (low power, high interest), monitor (low, low).

Decision-rights frameworks

  • RACI — Responsible (does the work), Accountable (one person owns the outcome), Consulted (two-way input), Informed (kept updated).
  • DACI — Driver (runs the decision process), Approver (one person decides), Contributors, Informed. Useful for product decisions.

Influence without authority — what actually works: shared goals (“we both want fewer failed payments”), evidence, reciprocity (help others hit their goals), early involvement (“co-authors defend what they wrote”), credibility through follow-through, and making it easy to say yes (clear asks, small first steps).

6.5 Cross-functional collaboration

Partner What they need from you What you need from them Common friction
Engineering Clear problem, priorities, early involvement, stable scope Estimates, risks, technical options Late requirement changes; dates set without them
Design Problem, evidence, constraints, time to explore Flows, prototypes, research partnership Solution-first requests; skipping research
Data / Analytics Questions, decisions, tracking needs early Definitions, analysis, experiment design Ad-hoc requests with no decision attached
Marketing / PMM Positioning inputs, launch dates, user value Messaging, launch plans, market feedback Late notice; overpromising
Sales Roadmap context, honest timelines Customer feedback, deal blockers Promising features to close deals
Support / Ops Release notes, known issues, training Ticket trends, customer pain Launches without support readiness
Legal / Compliance Early sight of data use and claims Risk assessment, approvals Brought in at the last minute

6.6 Negotiation and conflict resolution

Negotiation principles (from Getting to Yes, Fisher & Ury): separate the people from the problem; focus on interests, not positions; invent options for mutual gain; use objective criteria; know your BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement).

Interests, not positions (hypothetical)

Position (Sales): “We need custom reports for Client X by June.” Interest: keep a renewal worth ₹40 lakh; client's finance team needs monthly numbers. Options: scheduled CSV export (2 weeks), template report in existing tool (1 week), full custom reports (3 months). Objective criteria: revenue at risk, number of other clients asking, engineering cost. Outcome: ship the scheduled export now; evaluate custom reports in Q3 planning.

Conflict modes (Thomas–Kilmann): competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating.

PMs default to collaborating for important, high-trust issues; compromising for time-bound trade-offs; accommodating on low-stakes items to build goodwill; avoid only for trivia.

A conflict-resolution sequence: (1) restate each side's interest until they agree you understood; (2) agree on the shared goal and decision criteria; (3) lay out options with evidence; (4) decide — or escalate together with a joint summary; (5) document and move on.

6.7 Decision-making meetings

  • Before: circulate a one-page decision brief 24–48 hours ahead (context, options, recommendation, evidence, open questions); state the decision type (decide, consult, inform).
  • During: confirm the decision and decider; walk through options and trade-offs; invite dissent explicitly (“what would make this wrong?”); decide or agree what information is missing.
  • After: within 24 hours send the decision, rationale, owner, next steps and review date.

From your course notes (Extra topic 11)

Before a meeting, share a one-page decision brief. During the meeting name the options, trade-offs and open questions. Afterward record the decision, accountable owner, rationale and next review date. Disagreement is useful when it reveals an overlooked risk.

6.8 Writing PRDs

A PRD aligns the team on the problem and intended solution. It is a living document, sized to the team's needs.

From your course notes (Lecture 14; Companion ch. 4, 19)

The demonstrated PRD includes objective, target users, goals, success metrics, requirements, design links, out-of-scope items and open questions. Choose metrics that reflect the particular problem (business, user and technical measures); sample targets are not validated forecasts. Use AI for a first draft, not a source of truth — check invented assumptions, numbers, privacy and accuracy before sharing. A Confluence page can link to Jira items and design files; version history explains what changed; access permissions should match the audience. Discuss estimates without blame: ask engineers about complexity, testing, risks and dependencies, then explain trade-offs.

Mini-PRD: Show estimated total before checkout (hypothetical)

Problem. First-time mobile buyers abandon at payment; 30% of checkout starters leave at that step; 6 of 8 interviewees said the fee surprised them. Goal. Checkout completion for first-time buyers 70% → 76% this quarter; guardrail: complaint rate ≤ 1.3%; payment-error rate unchanged. In scope. Item total + estimated delivery/platform fees and taxes in the cart; “est.” labels; refresh on address change; fallback “Estimate unavailable” with retry. Out of scope. Changing the fee policy; personalised fees. User story. As a first-time buyer, I want to see my estimated total in the cart so that I can decide before I start paying. Acceptance criteria (Gherkin). Given an eligible address, when the user opens the cart, then show item price, estimated fees, taxes and estimated total. Given the fee service fails, when the cart loads, then show “Estimate unavailable” and a keyboard-accessible Retry, and never display an invented fee. Given the user changes the address, when the cart reloads, then the estimate refreshes within 2 seconds (p95). Non-functional. WCAG 2.2 AA; no PII in analytics events; works on 3G within 3 s (p95). Analytics. fee_displayed {fee_amount, is_estimate, source}; fee_estimate_failed {error_code}. Rollout. Feature flag; A/B 50/50; 14 days; kill switch owner: Eng lead. Open questions. Should the fee estimate include surge? Legal wording for “estimate”?

6.8.1 User stories and acceptance criteria

  • User story: As a [user], I want [capability] so that [benefit].
  • INVEST checklist: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
  • Acceptance criteria: testable conditions, often written Given / When / Then.
  • Definition of Ready (criteria before work starts) vs Definition of Done (quality criteria for completed work).

6.8.2 Writing one-pagers

A one-pager pitches an idea before a full PRD: problem, why now, who, proposed approach, expected impact (with range), cost, risks, the ask. If you can't write it on one page, the idea isn't clear yet. (Amazon popularised the related PR/FAQ — a mock press release and FAQ written before building — as a way to test whether the customer benefit is compelling.)

6.8.3 Jira and Confluence in the workflow

From your course notes (Lecture 13; Companion ch. 18, 19)

Jira helps teams track work items, workflows and delivery: projects contain work; boards present items by status; teams use stories, tasks, bugs and epics — terminology and workflows vary. A sprint is a Scrum time-box, not a mandatory feature of every team. Beginner exercise: create a work item “Show estimated total before checkout” with user, outcome, scope and acceptance criteria; move it through the existing workflow. Review boards for blocked and ageing items; discuss causes rather than treating story points as individual productivity. Confluence organises pages in spaces; a page can hold a PRD, decision log, research summary or launch checklist; link Jira items; record the decision and date when scope changes; pages are not automatically safe for every audience.

6.9 Engineering collaboration

  • Involve engineers in discovery — they often see the simplest solution.
  • Ask for estimates as ranges with assumptions, not commitments on the spot.
  • Story points are relative effort for a team's planning — not a productivity score and not comparable across teams.
  • Trade scope, not quality: offer smaller slices before asking for overtime.
  • Respect technical debt — reserve capacity; understand the cost of delay of not fixing it.
  • Be available during the sprint to answer questions quickly.

Dialogue — negotiating scope with an engineering lead (illustrative)

PM: “Our goal is to stop the fee surprise for first-time buyers this quarter. What's the simplest version you'd build?” Eng lead: “Showing a static fee is easy. A live estimate needs the pricing service — three weeks, and it's flaky at peak.” PM: “What if v1 shows the estimate when the service responds within 500 ms and otherwise ‘Estimate unavailable’? Would that cut the time?” Eng lead: “Then it's about ten days. We'd add a cache later.” PM: “Great. Let's take that, put it behind a flag and A/B it. I'll update the PRD and note the cache as a follow-up. Anything else risky?” Eng lead: “Analytics events — let's define them now so QA can check them.” Why it works: goal first, asks for the simplest option, trades scope not quality, records the follow-up.

6.10 Communicating with every function — dialogue examples

With senior leadership (illustrative)

VP: “Why isn't loyalty on the Q2 roadmap?” PM: “Short answer: checkout completion is a bigger, faster lever. We lose 30% of buyers at payment; fixing that is worth an estimated 2,000+ orders a month, and it takes 6 weeks. Loyalty only helps people who complete checkout. I'd like your approval to run the checkout test first, and I'll bring a loyalty proposal to the Q3 review with the test results.” Technique: answer first, number, trade-off, specific ask, follow-up date.

With design (illustrative)

PM: “Six of eight users missed the fee. I'm not attached to any layout — what are the options you see?” Designer: “A breakdown in the cart, or a sticky total bar.” PM: “Can we test both with five users next week and decide using task success?”

With analytics (illustrative)

PM: “The decision is whether to ship early fee display. I need: completion per eligible user by variant, complaint rate, and a power estimate for detecting +2 points.” Analyst: “At 70% baseline that's about 8,000 users per arm.” PM: “Then we run 14 days. Can we pre-register the metric definitions in the doc?”

With operations / support (illustrative)

PM: “From Monday, 50% of users will see an estimated fee in the cart. Here's the help article and three macros. If customers say ‘the fee changed’, tag it fee_estimate — I'll review tags daily during the test.”

With a customer (illustrative)

Customer: “Your app always surprises me with fees.” PM: “I'm sorry — that's exactly what we're trying to fix. Could you walk me through the last time it happened? What did you expect to see?” (Listen; don't defend; don't promise dates.) “Thank you. We're testing a change that shows the full estimate earlier; may I follow up to get your feedback?”

6.11 Handling conflicting priorities and difficult stakeholders

Conflicting priorities: bring them to a common yardstick (the goal and a framework such as RICE or cost of delay), make trade-offs visible, escalate jointly if needed with a one-page options paper, and record the decision.

Difficult stakeholders — patterns and responses

Pattern Response
The HiPPO (highest-paid person's opinion) Ask for the goal behind the idea; propose a test; show data respectfully
The bulldozer (“just build it”) Acknowledge urgency; show cost of delay of displaced work; offer a smaller slice
The silent blocker 1:1 conversation; ask what would make them comfortable; involve early
The scope-creeper Refer to the agreed scope and decision log; queue new asks for the next cycle
The customer-promiser (sales) Shared rule: no commitments without PM sign-off; give roadmap themes, not dates

From your course notes (Extra topic 11)

Stakeholders have different incentives: sales may want a customer request, engineering may need reliability work, users may want a faster experience. Clarify the shared outcome, evidence, constraints and decision rights instead of promising every request.

6.12 Customer empathy

Empathy is understanding the customer's situation and feelings well enough to make better decisions — not agreeing with every request. Practise it through regular customer calls, listening to support calls, reading tickets, using the product as a new user, and shadowing operations.

6.13 Giving and receiving feedback

SBI model: Situation (when/where), Behaviour (observable, not judgement), Impact (effect on you, team, user). Then ask, listen and agree next steps.

SBI (illustrative)

“In yesterday's review (S), the PRD's success metric changed from completion to clicks without a note (B). Engineering built tracking for the old metric and lost a day (I). Could we add a change log to the PRD so everyone sees updates?”

Receiving feedback: thank, clarify, don't defend in the moment, decide what to act on, close the loop.

6.14 Leadership communication and executive product reviews

Executives want: the decision you need, how it serves the strategy, the numbers, the risks, and what you're not doing. Prepare for an exec review:

  1. One-page memo at the top (or a 6-page narrative memo in memo-culture companies).
  2. Metrics vs targets with honest status (green/amber/red with reasons).
  3. Learnings — what surprised you, what you stopped.
  4. Decisions needed — clearly listed.
  5. Appendix for detail; anticipate the three hardest questions.

Delivering bad news: state it plainly, the impact, the cause (if known), what you're doing, what you need, when you'll update next.

6.15 Exercises with model answers

Exercise 1 · Rewrite an update with the Pyramid Principle

Original: “We did lots of analysis this week. We looked at funnels, did interviews, talked to payments, and engineering thinks it's 2 months. Fees might be a problem. Also loyalty is pending.”

Model answer

“Recommendation: test showing the delivery fee in the cart, starting next sprint. Why: (1) 30% of checkout starters leave at payment; (2) 6 of 8 interviewees cite fee surprise; (3) engineering estimates a simplified v1 at ~2 weeks (full live estimate ~2 months). Ask: approve the two-week v1 and an A/B test; loyalty moves to Q3.”

Exercise 2 · Acceptance criteria

Write three Given/When/Then criteria for “saved addresses”.

Model answer

Given a logged-in user with no saved addresses, when they complete an order with a new address, then offer “Save this address” (unchecked by default). Given a user with saved addresses, when they open checkout, then show up to 5 most recent addresses with the last used pre-selected. Given a saved address fails validation, when it is selected, then show a plain-language error and an Edit option without losing the cart.

Exercise 3 · Stakeholder map

For launching a fintech card-application redesign, place six stakeholders on a power–interest grid and give one engagement action each.

Model answer (example)

Manage closely: Head of Risk (co-design KYC changes), Compliance (review copy and consent). Keep satisfied: CFO (monthly KPI summary). Keep informed: Customer Support (training and macros), Marketing (launch messaging). Monitor: partner bank's ops team (notify of timeline). Re-map after the pilot.

6.16 Interview perspective

“Tell me about a time you influenced without authority.” — STAR model answer outline

S: Team wanted to build a feature a large client requested; I believed checkout reliability was more urgent. T: Align sales, engineering and my VP on priorities. A: Pulled funnel data and support tags, quantified lost orders, met sales to understand the client's real need, proposed a 2-week workaround for the client, and presented options with a recommendation. R: We fixed payment retries first; failed-payment recoveries rose (state the real measured number — or say it wasn't measured); the client accepted the workaround and renewed. Learning: start with shared goals and offer options. Mistake to avoid: inventing results or describing only what the team did.

“How would you communicate a delayed launch to executives?” — 60-second answer

“I'd tell them as soon as I know, in one message: the launch will slip by two weeks; the cause is a payment-gateway certification we underestimated; the impact is roughly X orders and no customer-facing risk; options are to launch without the new payment method or wait; my recommendation is to wait because the old flow is the main pain point; and I'll update them every Friday until launch. Then I'd document the learning for future estimates.”

6.17 Key takeaways

  • Answer first (Pyramid/SCQA); support with MECE reasons and evidence.
  • Use STAR for stories and PREP for quick points; never invent outcomes.
  • Make decision rights explicit (RACI/DACI) and write decisions down.
  • Negotiate on interests, with options and objective criteria.
  • PRDs are living alignment tools: problem, metrics, scope, testable requirements, risks.
  • Tailor to each function's needs; no surprises.

6.18 Check your understanding

Check your understanding

The Pyramid Principle recommends…

  1. Building up to the conclusion at the end
  2. Starting with the answer, then grouped supporting arguments
  3. Listing all data first
  4. Using only charts
Why: Lead with the governing thought, then MECE support and evidence.

In DACI, who makes the final decision?

  1. Driver
  2. Approver
  3. Contributors
  4. Informed
Why: The Approver decides; the Driver runs the process.

Which is a well-formed acceptance criterion?

  1. The page should be fast.
  2. Given an eligible address, when the cart opens, then show the estimated total.
  3. Make the cart better.
  4. Users will like it.
Why: Acceptance criteria are specific and testable, often Given/When/Then.

Focusing on interests rather than positions means…

  1. Agreeing to every request
  2. Understanding the need behind a demand to find better options
  3. Refusing to negotiate
  4. Escalating immediately
Why: Interests reveal options that satisfy the underlying need.

Story points are best described as…

  1. A measure of individual productivity
  2. Relative effort estimates for a team's planning
  3. Hours of work
  4. Comparable across all teams
Why: Story points are team-relative planning estimates, not productivity scores.

6.19 Recommended resources

  • Barbara Minto, The Pyramid Principle — publisher page.
  • Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, Storytelling with Data.
  • Fisher, Ury & Patton, Getting to Yes — Harvard Program on Negotiation.
  • Atlassian: DACI decision-making framework.
  • Atlassian Support: Create a Jira work item and Use Jira and Confluence together (from your course notes).
  • Center for Creative Leadership: SBI feedback model.
Module 7

Product Analytics and Metrics

Choose the right metrics, calculate them correctly, run experiments you can trust, and turn data into decisions.

≈ 12 h study

About the data in this module

Every number is hypothetical or synthetic. Hand-worked examples use round numbers so you can follow the arithmetic. SQL examples run against the synthetic files in datasets/ (users.csv, events.csv, orders.csv, …) and every output shown was produced by actually running the query. None of it is real company data, and no benchmark here should be quoted as an industry norm.

7.1 Product analytics fundamentals

Product analytics is the practice of measuring how people use a product so that teams can find problems, size opportunities, test changes and verify outcomes.

Level 1 · Beginner

A metric is a number that describes something about your product. Analytics is choosing the right numbers, calculating them the same way every time, and using them to decide what to do next.

Every useful metric needs five parts defined — otherwise two people will calculate it differently and argue:

Metric definition = event/population + numerator + denominator + time window + exclusions Example: Checkout completion = users who placed an order ÷ users who started checkout, same 7-day window, excluding internal test accounts and bots.

From your course notes (Lecture 21)

Define what is being measured, for whom and over what period, and compare against a relevant baseline or target. Users and revenue alone are not sufficient measures of every product's success. Correlation alone does not prove that a change caused an outcome. If an outcome misses its target, check data quality, user feedback, usability and context before removing a feature; revisit a metric when it no longer measures the intended outcome — not merely to make results look better.

7.2 Choosing KPIs

A KPI (key performance indicator) is a metric chosen to assess progress toward an important goal. Not every metric is a KPI.

Concept Meaning Example (food ordering)
Leading indicator Early signal that predicts a later result; you can influence it quickly Share of new users who place a first order within 7 days
Lagging indicator Result that confirms what already happened 90-day retention, quarterly revenue
Input metric A driver the team directly controls Payment success rate, time-to-first-order
Output / outcome metric The result the inputs are meant to move Orders per active customer
Guardrail metric Must not get worse while you optimise something else Complaint rate, refund rate, cancellation rate
Vanity metric Looks good, drives no decision Total registered users (all time)

7.2.1 The North Star Metric and metric trees

A North Star Metric (NSM) is a single measure of the recurring value users get from the product that also supports sustainable business results. It focuses teams; it never replaces guardrails.

From your course notes (Extra topic 3)

A north star is a team's chosen measure of recurring value delivered, not a universal number. A metric tree breaks a high-level outcome into smaller drivers so a team can investigate changes. Pair it with guardrails such as refunds and delivery complaints. A single metric never tells the entire story. Do not claim causality merely from a breakdown.

How to choose an NSM — a checklist

  1. Does it reflect value delivered to the user (not just value captured by the company)?
  2. Is it tied to a repeatable behaviour (not a one-off)?
  3. Is it sensitive enough that a good team can move it in a quarter?
  4. Can it be measured reliably today?
  5. Does it predict long-term business health (retention, revenue)?
  6. Can you name two guardrails that stop gaming it?

Level 3 · Senior PM

NSMs fail when they become targets without guardrails (Goodhart's law): optimising “time in app” can produce addictive design and wellbeing harm. Senior PMs pressure-test an NSM by asking “how could a team hit this number while harming users or the business?” and add the guardrail that blocks that path. They also revisit the NSM when strategy or product stage changes.

7.3 AARRR (Pirate Metrics)

AARRR examines the path from discovering a product to recommending it: Acquisition → Activation → Retention → Revenue → Referral.
