From your course notes (Lecture 25)

  • Activation should be an early action showing meaningful value — first payment is only one example; the right event depends on the product.
  • Retention can mean returning or continuing to receive value; recurring subscription payment is one example, not the only one.
  • Funnel arithmetic: if 800 of 1,000 visitors complete a step, conversion is 80% and drop-off 20%. If 600 of 800 return, retention is 75% and loss 25%.
  • Churn needs a defined starting group, behaviour and time period; non-payment alone does not mean every free user has churned.
  • The lecture's “20–30% ideal activation” and one-to-one referral claims are not universal benchmarks.
  • Analytics shows where behaviour changes; interviews and tests help explain why.

7.3.1 Acquisition and activation

  • Acquisition metrics: visits, sign-ups, installs, cost per acquisition by channel, share of traffic by channel. Always compare channels on quality (activation and retention), not just volume.
  • Activation: pick an event that correlates with long-term retention and represents real value. Test it by comparing retention of users who did vs did not reach it — remembering correlation is not causation (see below).
  • Time-to-value: how long from sign-up to the activation event. Shortening it usually raises activation.

Worked example · defining activation (hypothetical)

For a reading app, candidate events: signed up, opened a book, finished a first chapter, read on 3 different days in week one. The team compares 4-week retention of users who did each. Hypothetically, “finished a first chapter” predicts retention far better than “opened a book,” so it becomes the activation event. The next step is an experiment to see if nudging users toward finishing a first chapter actually improves retention — not an assumption.

7.4 Funnel analysis and drop-off

A funnel counts how many distinct users (or sessions) get through an ordered series of steps. Step conversion compares each step with the previous one; overall conversion compares with the top.

Step conversion = users at step n ÷ users at step n−1 Drop-off = 1 − step conversion Overall conversion = users at last step ÷ users at first step

Hypothetical worked funnel (10,000 visits)

Step Users Step conversion Drop-off % of top
Visits 10,000 – – 100%
Menu viewed 6,200 62.0% 38.0% 62.0%
Added to cart 2,480 40.0% 60.0% 24.8%
Checkout started 1,736 70.0% 30.0% 17.4%
Order placed 1,388 80.0% 20.0% 13.9%

Interpretation: the largest absolute loss is visit → menu (3,800 users) and the lowest step conversion is menu → cart (40%). The best place to investigate is not automatically the biggest percentage drop; weigh how fixable each step is and how many users it affects.

From your course notes (Companion ch. 5)

Of 300 checkout starters, 240 complete: 80% completion, 20% abandonment. Cart-to-order of 240 ÷ 400 = 60%. These use different starting populations, so their percentages should not be mixed.

Funnel pitfalls

  • Sessions vs users: counting sessions can inflate steps for repeat visitors. State which one you use.
  • Strict vs loose order: must a user hit steps in order, within X minutes?
  • Time window: a user who adds to cart today and buys tomorrow — is that a conversion?
  • Segmenting is essential: an overall funnel can hide that mobile-web users convert at half the rate of app users.

Interview perspective — “Checkout conversion dropped. What do you do?”

  1. Clarify the metric definition and window. 2. Check data quality (tracking change? outage?). 3. Segment: platform, app version, geography, payment method, new vs returning, channel. 4. Compare to seasonality. 5. Look at internal changes (releases, price/fee, promo, partner outage) and external ones (competitor, holiday). 6. Form hypotheses, rank by likelihood × impact, propose the first checks. Always say what you would look at first and why.

7.5 Engagement: DAU, WAU, MAU and stickiness

DAU = distinct users with a qualifying action on a given day WAU / MAU = same over a 7-day / 28–30-day window Stickiness = DAU ÷ MAU (average DAU over the period ÷ MAU for the same period)

“Active” must mean a meaningful action (e.g., viewed a menu or placed an order), not merely “opened the app”.

Worked example

Average DAU = 12,000; MAU = 48,000 → stickiness = 25% — on average a monthly user is active about 7.5 days a month (0.25 × 30). Whether 25% is good depends entirely on how often the product's job occurs: a banking app opened monthly differs from a messaging app used daily.

7.6 Retention, cohorts and churn

Retention measures how many users in a defined cohort are still active in a later window. A cohort groups users by a shared starting event (e.g., signup week).

Retention (week k) = cohort users active in week k ÷ cohort size Churn rate (period) = customers lost during the period ÷ customers at start of the period Net revenue retention (NRR) = (start MRR + expansion − contraction − churned MRR) ÷ start MRR

From your course notes (Extra topic 4)

Of 100 users who signed up in week one, 25 order again in a specified later seven-day window → 25% for that window. Users who ordered on day one but never returned are not “retained” unless your definition says so. State cohort start, qualifying action, time zone and exact return window. A correlation between activation and retention does not prove the activation action causes retention.

7.6.1 Reading a cohort heatmap

The heatmap below uses the synthetic dataset cohort_retention_weekly.csv: each row is a signup-week cohort; each column is the share of that cohort that placed a delivered order k weeks after signup.

How to read it: (1) Across a row — the shape of decay and whether it flattens. (2) Down a column — are newer cohorts better after a product change? (3) Diagonals show calendar effects (holiday, outage). Small cohorts produce noisy cells.

Retention pitfalls

  • Survivorship: averaging only active users hides churn.
  • Mixed definitions: “active” in Week 1 vs “ordered” in Week 1.
  • Blended cohorts: comparing a fresh paid-ads cohort to an organic one without segmenting.
  • Small samples: see the caption above.

7.7 Monetisation metrics: GMV, AOV, ARPU, ARPPU

GMV = Σ value of orders in the period (define: before/after discounts, refunds, cancellations) AOV = total order value ÷ number of orders (same definition, same period) ARPU = revenue in the period ÷ active users in the period ARPPU = revenue in the period ÷ paying users in the period

From your course notes (Lecture 31)

AOV = total order value ÷ number of orders for a chosen period; it does not by itself measure profit or user happiness. Example: ₹200, ₹300, ₹400 → ₹900 ÷ 3 = ₹300. Compare similar customers; check discounts and delivery costs; a higher AOV alone does not prove improved profitability or experience.

Worked example — GMV is not revenue

A marketplace processes 100,000 delivered orders at an AOV of ₹400 → GMV ₹40,000,000. The platform's net revenue is only what it keeps: commission, fees, ad income less the discounts it funds. Quoting GMV as “revenue” inflates the picture.

Worked example — ARPU vs ARPPU

Revenue ₹2,400,000; monthly active users 48,000; paying users 9,600. ARPU = 2,400,000 ÷ 48,000 = ₹50. ARPPU = 2,400,000 ÷ 9,600 = ₹250. Payer conversion = 9,600 ÷ 48,000 = 20%. Note ARPU = payer conversion × ARPPU (0.20 × 250 = 50). A freemium PM can raise ARPU by converting more users or by raising what payers spend — different levers, different risks.

7.7.1 Decomposing AOV (the quick-commerce case)

AOV = items per order × average price per item

To raise AOV, a team can raise items per order (relevant add-on suggestions, bundles, free-delivery thresholds) or price per item (assortment, premium options). The course case compared a quick-commerce AOV with a competitor's.

From your course notes (Lecture 31)

Participants discussed fee thresholds, inexpensive add-ons, near-expiry discounts, bundles and loyalty rewards. These were hypotheses, not validated causal findings. Check contribution margin, discount and delivery costs, conversion, repeat purchase and customer trust — not AOV alone. Assess whether each idea genuinely helps customers rather than encouraging unwanted spending.

7.8 Unit economics: contribution margin, CAC, LTV, payback

Unit economics looks at the money earned and spent for one unit — an order, a customer, a subscription.

Contribution margin = revenue − variable costs attributable to the unit CAC = acquisition spend ÷ new customers acquired (define which costs) LTV (simple) = monthly contribution per customer ÷ monthly churn rate Payback period = CAC ÷ monthly contribution per customer

Worked example — contribution per order

Line ₹ per order
Average order value 400
Commission (20% of AOV) 80
Delivery fee collected 30
Platform fee 5
Platform revenue per order 115
Delivery partner cost −70
Payment processing (2% of AOV) −8
Support cost allocation −6
Promotion funded by the platform −15
Contribution per order 16 (4.0% of AOV; 13.9% of revenue)

Without the ₹15 promotion, contribution would be ₹31. If the promotion lifts orders by less than the contribution it burns, it destroys value. More orders at negative contribution make the business worse.

From your course notes (Extra topics 6, 7)

Contribution margin is not net profit. With ₹100 revenue and ₹65 attributable cost, contribution is ₹35 (35%); with a ₹15 promotion it falls to ₹20. Campaign example: ₹10,000 spent to acquire 100 qualified customers → simple CAC ₹100; at ₹40 contribution per month, simple undiscounted payback is 2.5 months only if that contribution persists and other costs are excluded. Avoid blindly copying LTV-to-CAC benchmarks.

Worked example — LTV, CAC and payback

Monthly contribution per paying customer ₹120; monthly churn 5%; CAC ₹800. LTV (simple) = 120 ÷ 0.05 = ₹2,400. LTV : CAC = 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0. Payback = 800 ÷ 120 = 6.7 months. Sensitivity: if churn is 8% instead of 5%, LTV = 120 ÷ 0.08 = ₹1,500 and the ratio falls to 1.9 — churn is the lever the whole calculation hangs on. Real LTV models discount future cash and use cohort retention curves rather than a constant churn.

Level 3 · Senior PM

Executives care about payback period and cash as much as LTV : CAC, because LTV is a forecast while cash is real. Present base, low and high scenarios, state which costs are in CAC (paid media only vs fully loaded), and show how sensitive the answer is to churn and to retention flattening. Never present a precise LTV to two decimals from three months of data.

7.9 Experiment design and A/B testing

An A/B test randomly assigns eligible users to control (current experience) and variant (change), then compares a pre-agreed metric. Random assignment is what makes the groups comparable, so differences can be attributed to the change.

From your course notes (Lecture 27, Companion ch. 6)

  • A/B testing compares variants against a defined outcome; it differs from alpha/beta release testing.
  • Specify hypothesis, target users, control and treatment, primary metric, guardrails, sample requirements and duration; randomly assign eligible users; compare rates using consistent definitions.
  • Choose the unit of randomisation and make sure one person is not repeatedly switching groups. Compare completed orders per eligible user, not just clicks.
  • A higher observed conversion is not automatically a reliable winner: consider uncertainty, sample size, practical impact, implementation cost, accessibility, safety and compliance.
  • A preference poll is not an A/B test. Confidence level does not mean the probability a variant will work, and no test proves safety with 100% certainty.
  • If traffic is too low, run usability research or a different appropriately sized test instead of claiming proof.

When not to A/B test: too little traffic; irreversible or safety/legal changes; strong network effects (a marketplace treatment can contaminate control — consider geo or switchback tests); changes whose value only appears over months.

7.10 Hypothesis testing, p-values and confidence intervals

7.10.1 The idea

  • Null hypothesis (H₀): there is no real difference between control and variant.
  • Alternative (H₁): there is a difference.
  • p-value: if H₀ were true, how often would you see a difference at least this large purely by chance? It is not the probability that the variant works, and it does not measure the size or importance of the effect.
  • Significance level α: the threshold you fix in advance (commonly 0.05). If p < α, you reject H₀.
  • Confidence interval (CI): a range of effect sizes consistent with the data; a 95% CI is produced by a procedure that captures the true effect in 95% of repeated experiments. It tells you how big the effect might be.

Fully worked example — early fee display

Control: 10,000 eligible users, 7,000 complete an order (70.0%). Variant (fee shown early): 10,000 users, 7,250 complete (72.5%).

Step 1 — difference: 72.5% − 70.0% = +2.5 percentage points (relative lift 2.5 ÷ 70 = 3.6%).

Step 2 — pooled proportion: p̂ = (7,000 + 7,250) ÷ 20,000 = 0.7125.

Step 3 — standard error (pooled): SE = √[ p̂(1 − p̂) × (1/10,000 + 1/10,000) ] = √(0.7125 × 0.2875 × 0.0002) = 0.006401.

Step 4 — test statistic: z = 0.025 ÷ 0.006401 = 3.906.

Step 5 — p-value (two-sided): p ≈ 0.00009 → far below 0.05, so we reject H₀.

Step 6 — 95% CI for the difference (unpooled SE = 0.006398): 0.025 ± 1.96 × 0.006398 = [+1.25, +3.75] percentage points.

Decision: the effect is statistically distinguishable from zero and the plausible range is positive. Check the guardrail: complaints were 118 vs 121 per 10,000 users (1.18% vs 1.21%) — no meaningful change. Then ask about practical significance: is +1.2 to +3.8 points of completion worth the cost of shipping and maintaining the change? (Dataset: ab_test_checkout.csv.)

Two-proportion z-test p̂ = (x₁ + x₂) / (n₁ + n₂) SE = √[ p̂ (1 − p̂) (1/n₁ + 1/n₂) ] z = (p₂ − p₁) / SE 95% CI for difference = (p₂ − p₁) ± 1.96 × √[ p₁(1−p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1−p₂)/n₂ ]

From your course notes (Lecture 27)

The classroom example compared 23/100 with 37/100 and showed how a stricter significance threshold changes the conclusion. Check it: p̂ = 0.30, SE = √(0.3 × 0.7 × 0.02) = 0.0648, z = 0.14 ÷ 0.0648 = 2.16, two-sided p ≈ 0.031. That is significant at α = 0.05 but not at α = 0.01 — the same data, a different threshold, a different conclusion. With only 100 users per arm, the 95% CI is very wide (about +1.4 to +26.6 points), so the data is also consistent with a small effect. Statistical significance is not a guarantee, and a small sample gives imprecise estimates.

7.10.2 Type I and Type II errors, and power

H₀ true (no real effect) H₀ false (real effect)
Reject H₀ (“we found an effect”) Type I error (false positive), probability α Correct — probability = power (1 − β)
Do not reject H₀ Correct Type II error (false negative), probability β
  • Power is the probability of detecting a real effect of a given size. Conventional target: 80%.
  • MDE (minimum detectable effect) is the smallest effect worth detecting; smaller MDE → much bigger sample.

7.10.3 Sample size

n per arm = (z_{1−α/2} + z_{power})² × [ p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂) ] ÷ (p₂ − p₁)² α = 0.05 two-sided → z = 1.96; power 80% → z = 0.8416

Worked example — sizing the checkout test

Baseline 70%; we care about detecting +2 points (72%). n = (1.96 + 0.8416)² × [0.70×0.30 + 0.72×0.28] ÷ 0.02² = 7.849 × 0.4116 ÷ 0.0004 ≈ 8,077 users per arm. Other MDEs (same baseline, α = 0.05, power 80%): +1 point needs ≈ 32,600 per arm; +5 points needs ≈ 1,250 per arm. Halving the MDE roughly quadruples the sample.

7.10.4 Practical rules for trustworthy experiments

  • Fix the sample size or use a sequential method designed for peeking. Stopping the moment p < 0.05 inflates false positives (the “peeking problem”).
  • Run full weekly cycles to cover weekday/weekend behaviour.
  • Check sample ratio mismatch (SRM): if you planned 50/50 and observed 52/48 with large counts, assignment may be broken and results untrustworthy.
  • Pre-register one primary metric; treat others as secondary. Testing many metrics or segments without correction creates false positives (multiple comparisons).
  • Separate statistical from practical significance. A tiny, “significant” lift may not justify the cost; a larger, “non-significant” one may merit a bigger test.
  • Novelty effects: an early lift may fade. Where stakes are high, hold out a group longer.

Interview perspective

“How would you know if an A/B result is real?” → fixed hypothesis and metric; adequate power; random assignment verified; check guardrails and SRM; look at the CI, not just the p-value; consider practical impact, cost and risk; and if traffic is too low, use qualitative research or a longer or larger test.

7.11 Correlation versus causation

Two things moving together does not mean one causes the other. Causes of misleading correlation: confounding (a third factor drives both), reverse causation, selection bias, and Simpson's paradox.

Worked example — Simpson's paradox from an unbalanced split

A team compares two checkout designs but, due to a faulty rollout, the variant gets mostly desktop traffic.

Segment Control (conv / users) Variant (conv / users)
Desktop (high converting) 60 / 200 = 30.0% 232 / 800 = 29.0%
Mobile (low converting) 64 / 800 = 8.0% 15 / 200 = 7.5%
Overall 124 / 1,000 = 12.4% 247 / 1,000 = 24.7%

The variant looks twice as good overall yet is slightly worse in both segments. The overall gap comes from the traffic mix, not the design. The cure is correct randomisation (and segment-aware analysis), not trusting the aggregate.

From your course notes (Lecture 21; Extra topic 4)

Correlation alone does not prove causation. A relationship between activation and retention may be useful but does not prove the activation action causes retention. To test causality, run an experiment.

7.12 Segmentation in analytics

Always ask “for whom?” Useful cuts: acquisition channel, platform/app version, geography, new vs returning, plan/tier, cohort, device class, behavioural segments (power users vs casual). Use the synthetic data to see it:

7.13 Event instrumentation and data quality

Instrumentation is adding tracking so product behaviour becomes data. Do it from a tracking plan written before development.

Event name Fires when Key properties Owner
checkout_started User opens the checkout screen cart_value, item_count, platform Checkout team
fee_displayed A delivery fee/estimate is shown fee_amount, is_estimate, source Pricing
payment_attempted User taps Pay method, amount Payments
payment_succeeded / payment_failed Gateway responds method, error_code (no card data) Payments
order_placed Backend confirms the order order_id, amount Orders

A well-formed event (illustrative):

{
  "event": "checkout_started",
  "timestamp": "2026-03-14T18:22:05+05:30",
  "anonymous_id": "a1b2-c3d4",
  "properties": { "cart_value": 520, "item_count": 3, "platform": "ios" }
}

Data quality checklist

  • Naming convention (object_action, snake_case) and a single owner of the schema.
  • Test in staging before release; compare dashboard totals with the authoritative system (orders table).
  • Deduplicate (retries, double fires) and handle bots/internal traffic.
  • Time zones and clock skew: define the reporting zone.
  • Late and lost events: mobile events batch and can arrive late; define a lag window.
  • Privacy: minimise personal data; never put card details, emails or phone numbers into analytics events; honour consent and retention rules.

From your course notes (Lecture 35; Companion ch. 9)

Do not send personal identifiers such as email addresses or phone numbers to Google Analytics — privacy and platform rules apply. Request a tracking plan before development, test events in staging, compare dashboards with the authoritative order system, minimise personal data, limit access, honour retention rules, and never send card details to an analytics event. Decide what you want to learn before setting up the tool; low use alone is not enough reason to remove a feature.

7.14 SQL for Product Managers

Many PM interviews and day-to-day questions need basic SQL. These queries run against the synthetic dataset (users, events, orders). They use portable SQL; date functions differ by database (SQLite uses strftime, PostgreSQL uses DATE_TRUNC, BigQuery uses DATE_TRUNC / FORMAT_DATE).

From your course notes (Lecture 34)

Relational databases organise data in tables of rows and columns; SQL lets an authorised user select, filter and combine data. SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Country='UK' AND City='London' — AND requires both conditions, OR either. Check whether cancelled orders, time zones or missing values change the answer, and do not expose personal details unnecessarily. Contrary to a claim in the lecture, many PMs do query data and some interviews test SQL or joins.

1 · Basics: GMV, AOV and counts (delivered orders only)

SELECT COUNT(*)                 AS delivered_orders,
       SUM(amount_inr)          AS gmv_inr,
       ROUND(AVG(amount_inr),2) AS aov_inr
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'delivered';

Result: 320 | 122874 | 383.98. (GMV here excludes cancelled orders — a definition you must state.)

2 · Cancellation rate

SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS cancel_pct
FROM orders;

Result: 334 | 14 | 4.19.

3 · Monthly active buyers and GMV (GROUP BY)

SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)       AS active_buyers,
       SUM(amount_inr)               AS gmv_inr
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

Result: 2026-01 | 55 | 23128, 2026-02 | 107 | 45400, 2026-03 | 136 | 54346.

4 · Funnel by distinct users

SELECT event_name, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users
FROM events
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY users DESC;

Result: app_open 792 → view_menu 716 → add_to_cart 423 → checkout_start 322 → payment_success 284. Step conversions: 716/792 = 90.4%, 423/716 = 59.1%, 322/423 = 76.1%, 284/322 = 88.2%. This counts users who ever reached a step, so it is not a strict ordered funnel.

5 · JOIN: which acquisition channels produce buyers?

SELECT u.acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS users,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS buyers,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id), 1) AS buyer_pct
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id AND o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel
ORDER BY buyer_pct DESC;

Result: organic 370/142 (38.4%), search_ads 130/49 (37.7%), referral 106/32 (30.2%), paid_social 194/51 (26.3%). A LEFT JOIN keeps users with no orders; an INNER JOIN would silently drop them and overstate conversion.

6 · Repeat purchase (subquery)

SELECT COUNT(*) AS buyers,
       SUM(CASE WHEN n >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS repeat_buyers,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN n >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS repeat_pct
FROM (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS n
      FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY user_id);

Result: 274 | 44 | 16.1.

7 · Window function: rank customers by spend

SELECT user_id, SUM(amount_inr) AS spend,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(amount_inr) DESC) AS rnk
FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY rnk
LIMIT 5;

Result: U0648 (1,229), U0483 (1,210), U0246 (1,160), U0665 (1,040), U0751 (1,039).

SQL habits PMs should build: state the metric definition in a comment; check row counts before and after JOINs (duplicates inflate sums); filter to the right status; be explicit about time zones; never SELECT * on personal data; sanity-check totals against an authoritative dashboard.

Practice: write the query (answers)

Q: Average discount per delivered order? SELECT ROUND(AVG(discount_inr),2) FROM orders WHERE status='delivered'; Q: GMV by city, highest first? SELECT city, SUM(amount_inr) AS gmv FROM orders WHERE status='delivered' GROUP BY city ORDER BY gmv DESC; — Result: Mumbai 40,089; Delhi 34,279; Bengaluru 34,022; Pune 14,484. Q: Users who started checkout but never paid? Use checkout_start users minus payment_success users (e.g. NOT IN or LEFT JOIN … WHERE p.user_id IS NULL).

7.15 Excel for product analytics

Excel is enough for quick funnels, cohorts and A/B maths.

Task Formula
Step conversion =C3/C2
AOV =SUM(Amount)/COUNT(OrderID)
Conditional sum / count =SUMIFS(Amount, Status,"delivered", City,"Mumbai"), =COUNTIFS(Status,"cancelled")
Retention % =ActiveInWeek/CohortSize
z for two proportions =(p2-p1)/SQRT(pp*(1-pp)*(1/n1+1/n2)) where pp=(x1+x2)/(n1+n2)
Two-sided p-value =2*(1-NORM.S.DIST(ABS(z),TRUE))
Pivot table Insert → PivotTable: rows = channel, values = count of orders, average of amount
Lookup =XLOOKUP(user_id, Users[user_id], Users[city])

Build a tracking sheet per experiment: hypothesis, dates, n, conversions, z, p, CI, guardrails, decision. It doubles as a decision log.

7.16 Dashboards and tools: Power BI, Mixpanel, Amplitude, GA4

Tool Best for Notes
Mixpanel / Amplitude Event-based product analytics: funnels, retention, cohorts, user paths, segmentation, often with experimentation add-ons Needs a good tracking plan; self-serve for PMs
Google Analytics 4 (GA4) Web/app traffic and acquisition; events with parameters; “key events” (formerly called conversions) Do not send personal identifiers; sampling and thresholds can apply to reports
Power BI Business dashboards over many sources (SQL, Excel, APIs) with a data model and DAX measures Good for exec reporting; refresh schedule and access control matter
SQL + notebooks Custom analysis, joins, reproducible work Needs data access and review
Spreadsheet Fast calculations and small tests Easy to break silently; document formulas

From your course notes (Lecture 35)

The instructor demonstrated setting up an analytics property and web data stream, adding a tracking tag and viewing recent users and page activity. Compare activity across pages and time periods but validate definitions, data quality and sample size before deciding what to change. Reconcile metric definitions when reports disagree. Setup screens change; follow current official documentation.

A simple Power BI measure (DAX), to show the idea:

Conversion Rate = DIVIDE( DISTINCTCOUNT(Orders[user_id]), DISTINCTCOUNT(CheckoutStarts[user_id]) )

Dashboard design rules: start with the decision; one headline metric per question; show the trend and the target; include definitions and “last refreshed”; put guardrails next to the metric they protect; avoid pie charts for more than 3–4 parts; annotate releases and incidents.

7.17 Experiment readout template (worked example)

Readout: Early fee display (hypothetical)

Decision requested: Ship early fee display to 100% of users? Recommendation: Yes, with a 5% holdout for 4 weeks. Hypothesis: Showing the delivery fee in the cart (not only at payment) will increase checkout completion by reducing surprise. Design: randomised by user; 10,000 eligible per arm; 14 days; primary = completed orders ÷ eligible users; guardrails = complaint rate, payment failures, AOV. Result: 70.0% → 72.5% (+2.5 pts; 95% CI +1.25 to +3.75; z = 3.91; p < 0.001). Complaints 1.18% vs 1.21% (n.s.). No SRM detected (10,000 vs 10,000). Segments (exploratory, not powered): directionally positive on new and returning users. Risks / caveats: novelty effect possible; estimate accuracy depends on the fee service; two-week window. Next steps: staged rollout; monitor the estimate error rate; re-run on high-fee cities.

7.18 Source-flagged corrections

  • The lecture's 20–30% “ideal” activation and referral claims are not universal benchmarks.
  • A single page-load time cannot by itself establish API latency; browser rendering, network and other components also contribute.
  • A preference poll is not an A/B test; confidence level is not the probability a variant will work.
  • A confidence interval is not a probability statement about a single experiment's true value (frequentist interpretation).
  • GMV ≠ revenue ≠ profit. Define each.

7.19 Exercises with model answers

Exercise 1 · Funnel diagnosis

A funnel shows: Visit 20,000 → Product page 12,000 → Cart 3,000 → Checkout 2,100 → Order 1,680. (a) Compute step conversions. (b) Which step is lowest? (c) Name three hypotheses and the data you would pull for each.

Model answer

(a) 60.0%, 25.0%, 70.0%, 80.0%; overall 8.4%. (b) Product page → Cart at 25%. (c) H1: add-to-cart is hard to find on mobile — segment by device and check click heatmaps/events. H2: prices or fees not clear until cart — compare with sessions where a fee estimate was shown earlier; run a usability test. H3: wrong traffic mix (new channel bringing low-intent users) — split by acquisition channel. State the largest absolute loss is Visit→Product page (8,000), but the product page is a browsing step; the cart step is more actionable.

Exercise 2 · Is the test result real?

Control: 4,000 users, 600 conversions. Variant: 4,000 users, 660 conversions. Compute the lift, z-statistic, p-value and 95% CI. Would you ship?

Model answer

p₁ = 15.0%, p₂ = 16.5%; diff = +1.5 pts (relative +10%). Pooled p̂ = 1,260/8,000 = 0.1575; SE = √(0.1575 × 0.8425 × (2/4,000)) = 0.008141; z = 0.015/0.008141 = 1.84; p ≈ 0.066 (two-sided) → not significant at 0.05. Unpooled SE = √(0.15×0.85/4,000 + 0.165×0.835/4,000) = 0.008155 → 95% CI ≈ −0.1 to +3.1 pts, which includes zero. Do not claim a win; the effect might be real but the test is underpowered for a 1.5-point effect (roughly 9,250 per arm would be needed at 80% power). Options: extend the test to the planned size, or accept the uncertainty if the change is cheap and reversible.

Exercise 3 · Unit economics

Subscription: ₹300/month price; gross margin 70%; monthly churn 6%; CAC ₹1,500. Compute LTV (simple), LTV:CAC and payback. Which assumption would you stress-test?

Model answer

Monthly contribution ≈ 300 × 0.70 = ₹210. LTV = 210 ÷ 0.06 = ₹3,500. LTV:CAC = 3,500 ÷ 1,500 = 2.33. Payback = 1,500 ÷ 210 = 7.1 months. Stress-test churn (e.g., 9% → LTV ₹2,333, ratio 1.56) and whether churn is really constant — real cohorts usually churn faster in month 1 and flatten.

Exercise 4 · Pick a North Star

Choose an NSM for a language-learning app and name two guardrails and one way the team could game it.

Model answer

NSM: learners who complete ≥ 3 lessons per week (value = actual learning). Guardrails: lesson quality rating / test scores; 30-day retention; complaints about notification spam. Gaming: making lessons trivially short or sending aggressive streak-guilt notifications to inflate lesson counts — hence the quality and wellbeing guardrails.

7.20 Interview perspective

“How would you measure the success of a new feature?” — structure

1) Goal and user: what outcome and for whom. 2) Primary metric (outcome), 3) input/leading metrics that explain it, 4) guardrails, 5) how you will measure causally (A/B or phased rollout), 6) timeframe and success threshold, 7) segments to check, 8) decision rule (ship, iterate, stop). Close with what you would do if the result is inconclusive.

“Our retention is dropping. How do you investigate?” — 60-second answer

“I'd first confirm the definition and whether it's real — check tracking and seasonality. Then I'd see which cohorts: new vs old users, by channel, platform, geography. If new cohorts are weaker, I'd look at acquisition quality and onboarding changes; if everyone is weaker after a date, at releases or competitor moves. I'd pair the quantitative cut with 5–8 interviews of recently churned users to learn why, form two or three hypotheses, and test the cheapest first. I'd also check guardrails so a fix doesn't hurt revenue or satisfaction.”

7.21 Key takeaways

  • A metric is only as good as its definition (event, numerator, denominator, window, exclusions).
  • Use leading + lagging metrics, an NSM with a metric tree, and guardrails.
  • Funnels, cohorts and segmentation show where things change; research and experiments show why and whether it works.
  • GMV ≠ revenue ≠ profit. Check contribution margin and CAC payback before celebrating growth.
  • Experiments need pre-registered metrics, adequate power, clean randomisation and guardrails. p-values are not the probability a variant works; CIs show effect size.
  • Correlation is not causation — Simpson's paradox is the standard warning.
  • Instrument from a tracking plan, validate data quality, and keep personal data out of analytics events.

7.22 Check your understanding

Check your understanding

A funnel has 800 of 1,000 visitors completing a step. What are step conversion and drop-off?

  1. 80% and 20%
  2. 20% and 80%
  3. 100% and 0%
  4. Cannot tell without revenue
Why: Step conversion = 800 ÷ 1,000 = 80%; drop-off = 1 − 0.80 = 20%.

AOV is best defined as…

  1. Total revenue ÷ number of users
  2. Total order value ÷ number of orders
  3. Profit ÷ orders
  4. GMV ÷ MAU
Why: AOV = total order value ÷ number of orders for the same period and definition. It says nothing by itself about profit.

A test gives p = 0.03. Which statement is correct?

  1. There is a 97% chance the variant is better.
  2. If there were truly no difference, results this extreme would occur about 3% of the time.
  3. The effect is large.
  4. The result will replicate 97% of the time.
Why: A p-value is a probability about the data under the null hypothesis. It is not the probability the variant works and says nothing about effect size.

Which change makes the required sample size per arm increase the most?

  1. Halving the minimum detectable effect
  2. Raising power from 80% to 85%
  3. Doubling traffic
  4. Using one more guardrail
Why: Sample size scales roughly with 1/(effect size)², so halving the MDE roughly quadruples the sample.

LTV (simple) = ₹120 ÷ 0.05 is ₹2,400. If churn rises to 8%, LTV becomes…

  1. ₹960
  2. ₹1,500
  3. ₹2,400
  4. ₹3,840
Why: 120 ÷ 0.08 = ₹1,500. LTV is very sensitive to churn.

In Simpson's paradox, the overall result is reversed relative to every segment because of…

  1. Rounding
  2. Unequal segment mix between groups
  3. Too many users
  4. Using a two-sided test
Why: When the variant gets a different mix of high- and low-converting segments, the aggregate can mislead; proper randomisation and segmenting fix it.

Which should NOT be sent as an analytics event property?

  1. cart_value
  2. platform
  3. card_number
  4. item_count
Why: Card details (and typically emails and phone numbers) must never go into analytics tools.

7.23 Recommended resources

  • Google Analytics Help — events, key events, privacy.
  • Mixpanel Docs · Amplitude Docs — product analytics concepts and setup.
  • Power BI documentation — dashboards and DAX.
  • Evan Miller: A/B testing tools and sample-size calculator — practical references for sample size and sequential testing.
  • Kohavi, Tang, Xu — Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments — the standard book on online experimentation.
  • SQLBolt — free interactive SQL lessons.
Module 8

Product Launch, Growth, and Monetization

Plan launches, design growth loops, run growth experiments, price and package, reduce churn and scale responsibly.

≈ 10 h study

About the numbers

All growth, pricing and churn figures are hypothetical and chosen for clear arithmetic. They are not benchmarks for any industry or company.

8.1 Go-to-market planning and launch objectives

Go-to-market (GTM) coordinates how the right users discover, adopt and get support for a product: audience, positioning, pricing, channels, sales and support readiness, timing and measurement (Module 2 covers the strategy). A launch is one event within GTM — not the end of product work.

From your course notes (Lecture 23; Extra topic 10)

Start with the business case and timing, define the audience and proposition, choose pricing and explain the rationale, plan distribution and launch support, set measurable success metrics and adjust the roadmap using feedback after launch. Pilot an early feature with a small group, train support, prepare a help article, monitor completion, confusion and complaints; if accuracy fails, pause or roll back; expand only after the team reviews results. Assign owners for product, engineering, support, analytics, operations and communications; distinguish an internal pilot from a public launch; name a rollback owner. In the cricket-equipment exercise, the instructor pushed learners to consider partner incentives, sponsorship costs and likely return — not just list channels.

Launch objectives should be outcome-based and time-bound:

Weak objective Strong objective
“Launch the subscription” “Reach 2,000 paying subscribers in 60 days at CAC ≤ ₹600 with refund rate < 3%”
“Get press coverage” “Drive 15,000 qualified visits from launch content; 8% start a trial”
“Make users happy” “Activation (first plan created) ≥ 45% within 7 days; CSAT ≥ 4.2/5”

8.1.1 Launch tiers

Not every release deserves a big launch. Tier them:

Tier What Example Effort
Tier 1 New product or major capability; market-facing New credit card; paid plan Full GTM: PR, sales enablement, campaigns, support training
Tier 2 Significant feature for existing users Early fee display; new integrations In-app announcement, help docs, email to relevant segment
Tier 3 Improvements and fixes UI polish; performance Release notes

8.1.2 Product launch checklist

8.2 Positioning and market segmentation at launch

Re-use Module 2's positioning statement and choose a beachhead segment: a narrow group with acute need, reachable cheaply, whose success creates references for the next segment. Messaging should lead with the job and outcome (“Know your total before you pay”), not the feature (“Fee breakdown component”).

8.3 Beta testing and pilot launches

  • Alpha: internal or very small trusted group; find major bugs.
  • Closed beta: invited external users; usability, value and reliability; often with feedback channels and NDAs.
  • Open beta: anyone can join; scale and edge cases.
  • Pilot: a real launch in a constrained scope (one city, one customer, 5% of traffic) with success criteria and a go/no-go decision.
  • Staged rollout / canary: gradually increase exposure (1% → 5% → 25% → 100%) while watching guardrails.

From your course notes (Lecture 27)

A/B testing is different from alpha and beta release testing: alpha/beta reveal problems and gather feedback; A/B testing compares variants against a defined outcome with random assignment.

8.4 Product adoption

Everett Rogers' diffusion of innovations model segments adopters by timing: innovators (2.5%), early adopters (13.5%), early majority (34%), late majority (34%), laggards (16%). Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm argues the jump from early adopters to the early majority is the hardest because the majority wants proven, complete solutions and references.

Adoption metrics: activation rate, time-to-value, feature adoption rate (users of feature ÷ eligible users), depth (frequency of use), breadth (number of features used), accounts with ≥ N active seats (B2B).

8.5 Growth funnels and growth loops

A funnel is linear (acquire → activate → retain → monetise → refer). A growth loop is circular: the output of one cycle becomes input to the next, so growth compounds.

8.5.1 Viral coefficient (K-factor)

K = invites sent per user × conversion rate of invites Total users from an initial cohort N (K < 1) ≈ N ÷ (1 − K)

Worked example

Each new user sends 3 invites; 10% of invites convert → K = 0.3. From 1,000 seed users: 1,000 + 300 + 90 + 27 + … ≈ 1,000 ÷ (1 − 0.3) = ≈ 1,429 users. Virality amplifies other channels rather than replacing them unless K > 1, which is rare and usually temporary. Cycle time matters as much as K: a loop that turns weekly compounds far faster than one that turns quarterly.

8.6 Growth experimentation

Growth teams run a pipeline of experiments: generate ideas from funnel data and research → prioritise (ICE) → design (hypothesis, metric, guardrails, sample size) → run → analyse → document → next. Keep a public experiment log with results, including failures.

Good growth experiments are tied to a funnel step, have a single primary metric, enough traffic for the effect size (Module 7), and guardrails that protect users.

8.7 User acquisition

Channel Strengths Weaknesses Watch metric
Organic search / content Compounding, low marginal cost Slow to build Organic sign-ups, rankings
App-store optimisation Captures intent Competitive; algorithms change Store conversion rate
Paid social / search Fast, targetable Costly; can attract low-intent users CAC, payback, retention by channel
Referral High trust, low CAC Depends on product love K-factor, referred retention
Partnerships Access to trusted audiences Incentive alignment, dependency Partner-sourced activation
Sales (B2B) Large contracts Expensive, slow Win rate, sales cycle, ACV
Community / events Loyalty, feedback Hard to scale Engagement, referrals

Compare channels on quality, not volume: activation, 30/90-day retention, contribution and payback — not just installs.

8.8 Lifecycle marketing

Messages (email, push, in-app, SMS) timed to the user's stage: onboarding (help reach first value), engagement (habit-building tips, relevant content), expansion (upgrade when they hit limits), win-back (lapsed users with a reason to return). Respect consent and frequency caps; measure incrementality with holdout groups — many “opens” would have happened anyway.

8.9 Product-led growth (PLG)

PLG makes the product the main driver of acquisition, conversion and expansion: self-serve sign-up, fast time-to-value, a free tier or trial, in-product upgrade prompts at moments of value or limits, and natural virality (sharing, collaboration). The PM's levers: activation design, usage limits that align with value, pricing page clarity, product-qualified leads (PQLs) for sales-assist.

8.10 Retention strategies and referral mechanisms

Retention strategies: improve activation (the biggest lever for most products); build habits around a real recurring need; deliver ongoing value (new content, personalisation); reduce friction (saved preferences, reorder); proactive support; win-back flows; loyalty programmes that reward genuine value (not just discounts).

Referral mechanisms: double-sided rewards (both get value), referral at moments of delight (after a successful delivery), easy sharing, fraud controls (self-referral, fake accounts), and measuring referred users' retention, not just referral counts.

8.11 Pricing, subscriptions and freemium

From your course notes (Lecture 26; Extra topic 5)

Pricing is how much and on what terms; monetisation is the broader way a product earns revenue. Consider value, costs, competition and willingness to pay — not cost alone. Models include subscription, freemium, advertising, affiliate, usage-based, licensing and transaction fees, and they can be combined. A paid user is not automatically a happy user — watch activation, repeat use, revenue, refund requests and fairness together. A free trial should disclose when payment begins and how to cancel.

8.11.1 Freemium vs premium (economics)

Worked example — is the free tier paying for itself?

100,000 free monthly active users; 3% convert to paid → 3,000 subscribers × ₹299 = ₹8,97,000/month revenue. Serving costs: free users ₹2/month each → ₹2,00,000; paid users ₹20/month each → ₹60,000. Contribution before acquisition: ₹8,97,000 − ₹2,60,000 = ₹6,37,000/month. If conversion fell to 1.5%, revenue halves to ₹4,48,500 and contribution drops to ₹4,48,500 − (₹2,00,000 + ₹30,000) = ₹2,18,500. The PM's job: find the free/paid boundary where free users experience real value and paying users clearly get more.

8.11.2 Pricing psychology and packaging (use ethically)

  • Good–better–best tiers with a clear “most popular” anchor.
  • Value metric: charge on the unit that tracks customer value (seats, projects, transactions).
  • Annual discounts improve cash flow and retention.
  • Avoid dark patterns: hidden fees, forced continuity without notice, hard-to-cancel flows — they damage trust and may be illegal in some places.

8.12 Conversion optimisation, cross-selling and upselling

  • Conversion optimisation (CRO): identify the leakiest step (Module 7 funnels), research why, test fixes. Typical checkout fixes: show total early, fewer fields, guest checkout, trust signals, saved payment methods, clear errors.
  • Upsell: move a customer to a higher tier (more value). Cross-sell: add a related product (e.g., add-on dessert, insurance with a card). Make offers relevant and timely; measure attach rate, AOV, refunds and complaints.

From your course notes (Lecture 31)

In the quick-commerce AOV case, ideas included cart recommendations, transparent discounts on near-expiry items, bundles, thresholds and loyalty rewards — assess whether each genuinely helps customers rather than encouraging unwanted spending. Higher AOV alone does not prove better profitability or experience.

8.13 Monetisation experiments

Price tests, packaging tests, paywall placement, trial length, discount offers. Special care: price tests can feel unfair if customers see different prices — consider testing on new users or by geography, or test packaging rather than price; check local laws; measure long-term retention and refunds, not just conversion.

Example (hypothetical) — trial length

7-day vs 14-day trial for a SaaS tool, randomised by new sign-up. Primary metric: paid conversion at day 30; guardrails: refund rate, day-60 retention. Result interpretation must wait until day 60 for the 14-day arm — define the analysis window in advance.

8.14 Churn reduction

  • Voluntary churn: customer chooses to leave (value, price, competitor, need ended). Tools: exit surveys + interviews, save offers that address the reason (pause, downgrade), product fixes for top reasons.
  • Involuntary churn: payment failures (expired cards, insufficient funds). Tools: dunning (smart retries, reminders, card-updater services), grace periods.

8.15 Growth metrics

Net revenue retention (NRR) = (Start MRR + expansion − contraction − churned MRR) ÷ Start MRR Gross revenue retention (GRR) = (Start MRR − contraction − churned MRR) ÷ Start MRR SaaS quick ratio = (new MRR + expansion MRR + reactivation MRR) ÷ (churned MRR + contraction MRR)

Worked example

Start MRR ₹100 lakh; expansion ₹12 lakh; contraction ₹3 lakh; churned ₹5 lakh; new ₹15 lakh; reactivation ₹1 lakh. NRR = (100 + 12 − 3 − 5) ÷ 100 = 104% — existing customers grew revenue even after churn. GRR = (100 − 3 − 5) ÷ 100 = 92%. Quick ratio = (15 + 12 + 1) ÷ (5 + 3) = 28 ÷ 8 = 3.5 — revenue added is 3.5× revenue lost.

8.16 Case study from your course: ride-hailing surge pricing

From your course notes (Lecture 15)

Design hypothetical surge-pricing logic with an AI component. A useful goal balances availability, driver earnings, affordability and trust. Groups considered drivers, requests, location, time, weather, festivals and events; distinguish the ordinary fare from a temporary surcharge; make assumptions explicit. Ideas: use historical demand and weather to anticipate busy periods, alert customers and help drivers move toward demand. Test price changes with guardrails: measure ride completion, cancellations, driver earnings, affordability and trust; price caps and local rules may matter. A participant's idea of charging more based on low phone battery or repeat booking behaviour is an unverified proposal — exploiting urgency or personal data undermines trust and raises privacy, fairness and legal concerns.

8.17 Launch retrospectives and scaling

Retrospective (blameless): goals vs results (with data), what went well, what didn't, surprises, decisions to keep/change, owners and dates. Hold it 2–4 weeks after launch and publish it.

Scaling a product: (1) prove retention in the beachhead before expanding; (2) industrialise operations (support, onboarding, fraud); (3) harden reliability and observability (Module 9); (4) localise (language, payments, regulation); (5) expand segments and channels one at a time; (6) protect unit economics as you grow.

From your course notes (Extra topic 13)

An incident is an event that disrupts a service or harms users. Define alert thresholds and owners before release; track failed orders and recovery; maintain an incident timeline; follow up with actionable prevention items. Never assume an incident is over merely because the dashboard looks better for a few minutes.

8.18 Practical launch plans

8.18.1 Fintech: launching a digital credit card application (hypothetical)

Phase Key activities Gate criteria
Readiness Regulatory and compliance approvals; KYC vendor integration; credit-risk policy; fraud rules; disclosures and consent copy reviewed Compliance sign-off; security and privacy review complete
Employee pilot Staff apply with real KYC; manual review of every decision No critical defects; approval decisions match policy
Limited pilot 2% of eligible traffic; staged by region; human review of edge cases Completion ≥ target; fraud rate within limit; complaint rate stable
Scale Increase traffic weekly; marketing campaigns; partner channels Unit economics within plan; ops queue SLA met
Optimise A/B test document-upload UX, pre-fill, status tracking Experiments show completion lift without risk increase
Metrics: application start → submit → approve → activate (first transaction); time to decision; drop-off by step; fraud rate; cost per approved account; complaints. Guardrails: credit losses, fraud, regulatory breaches.

8.18.2 B2B SaaS: launching a paid tier (hypothetical)

Phase Activities
Beta 20 design-partner accounts; usage telemetry; weekly feedback calls; pricing interviews
Pricing Value metric choice (seats vs projects); good–better–best tiers; pricing page test
GA launch Docs and help centre; in-app upgrade prompts at limits; sales enablement for large accounts; webinar
Post-launch Conversion funnel by plan; expansion; churn reasons; NRR tracking
Metrics: trial → paid conversion, time-to-value, PQL → won rate, expansion MRR, NRR, support tickets per account.

8.18.3 Consumer app: launching in a new city (hypothetical)

Phase Activities
Pre-launch Supply onboarding (restaurants, couriers) to minimum density; localisation; payment methods
Soft launch Invite-only waitlist; referral codes; monitor delivery times and cancellations
Public launch Local partnerships, app-store optimisation, targeted ads with CAC caps
Scale Expand zones only where wait times and contribution meet targets
Metrics: first-order conversion, repeat within 14 days, delivery time, cancellation rate, contribution per order, CAC payback. Guardrails: rider/courier earnings, complaints, safety incidents.

8.19 Exercises with model answers

Exercise 1 · K-factor

Users send 2 invites each; 25% convert. Seed = 5,000. Estimate total users after the loop exhausts. How would halving cycle time change things?

Model answer

K = 2 × 0.25 = 0.5 → total ≈ 5,000 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 10,000. Halving cycle time doesn't change the eventual total when K < 1, but you reach it twice as fast — which matters for compounding with other channels and for time-bound goals.

Exercise 2 · NRR and quick ratio

Start MRR $200k; new $30k; expansion $20k; contraction $10k; churn $14k; reactivation $4k. Compute NRR, GRR, quick ratio.

Model answer

NRR = (200 + 20 − 10 − 14) ÷ 200 = 196 ÷ 200 = 98%. GRR = (200 − 10 − 14) ÷ 200 = 88%. Quick ratio = (30 + 20 + 4) ÷ (14 + 10) = 54 ÷ 24 = 2.25. Growth relies on new logos; existing customers shrink slightly — focus on churn reasons and expansion paths.

Exercise 3 · Launch plan

Draft a one-page launch plan for “early fee display” (Tier 2).

Model answer outline

Objective: +2 pts checkout completion, complaints ≤ 1.3%. Audience: all app users (A/B 50/50, then ramp). Readiness: flag, events validated, help article, support macros, fee-service fallback tested. Rollout: 1% internal → 5% canary → A/B 14 days → 100% with 5% holdout. Comms: in-app tooltip; no press. Monitoring: completion, payment errors, complaints daily. Rollback owner: Eng lead. Retro: 3 weeks after ramp.

8.20 Interview perspective

“How would you grow a product's revenue by 20%?” — structure

Decompose revenue: users × conversion × ARPPU (or orders × AOV × take rate). Find the biggest, most fixable lever with data (funnel, cohorts, segments). Generate options per lever (acquisition, activation, retention, pricing/packaging, upsell/cross-sell). Prioritise by impact, confidence, effort and risk. Set metrics and guardrails (refunds, complaints, churn). Sequence experiments. Mention unit economics: growth that loses money per unit is not success.

“Our churn went up. What do you do?” — 60-second answer

“First, confirm it's real and which churn — voluntary or payment failures — and for which cohorts and plans. Payment-failure churn can often be cut quickly with smarter retries and reminders. For voluntary churn, I'd segment by reason using exit surveys and talk to recently churned customers, then check whether activation or a recent change explains it. I'd pick the biggest addressable reason, test a fix — product change, better onboarding, or a pause/downgrade option — and track churn by cohort plus guardrails like refunds and complaints.”

8.21 Key takeaways

  • Launch = one step in GTM; tier launches and gate rollouts with criteria and a kill switch.
  • Growth loops compound; funnels don't. K-factor < 1 amplifies, not replaces, other channels.
  • Compare channels on quality and payback, not volume.
  • PLG depends on time-to-value and upgrade prompts at moments of value.
  • Model freemium economics explicitly; free users cost money.
  • Distinguish voluntary vs involuntary churn; track NRR, GRR and quick ratio.
  • Monetise fairly — avoid dark patterns; watch refunds and trust.

8.22 Check your understanding

Check your understanding

Users send 4 invites each and 5% convert. What is K?

  1. 0.2
  2. 0.8
  3. 4.05
  4. 20
Why: K = invites per user × conversion = 4 × 0.05 = 0.2.

NRR above 100% means…

  1. No customers churned
  2. Revenue from existing customers grew after expansion, contraction and churn
  3. New customers grew fast
  4. Prices were raised
Why: NRR measures revenue from the starting cohort including expansion, contraction and churn; it excludes new customers.

Which is involuntary churn?

  1. Customer switches to a competitor
  2. Card expires and renewal payment fails
  3. Customer finds it too expensive
  4. Customer no longer needs it
Why: Involuntary churn comes from payment failures rather than a choice to leave.

A staged rollout primarily helps you…

  1. Avoid measuring results
  2. Limit blast radius and check guardrails before full exposure
  3. Skip QA
  4. Run a price test
Why: Gradual exposure with gates and a kill switch limits damage from unexpected problems.

In PLG, the best moment for an upgrade prompt is…

  1. Immediately at sign-up
  2. At a random time
  3. When the user hits a limit after getting real value
  4. Never
Why: Upgrade prompts convert best at moments of demonstrated value or need.

8.23 Recommended resources

  • Reforge: Growth loops are the new funnels.
  • OpenView: Product-led growth resources.
  • Geoffrey Moore, Crossing the Chasm — overview (Wikipedia).
  • Stripe: Reduce involuntary churn (Billing docs).
  • Lenny's Newsletter — growth and pricing essays.
Module 9

Tech 101 and System Design for PMs

Understand how software works well enough to ask the right questions, make trade-offs with engineers, and explain systems in interviews.

≈ 12 h study

About the architectures

Diagrams are simplified teaching architectures, not descriptions of how any named company actually builds its systems. Numbers are illustrative.

Why a PM needs this

You don't write production code, but you decide what gets built and you trade off cost, speed, risk and quality with engineers. Knowing the moving parts lets you ask good questions (“what happens if the payment provider times out?”), spot risks early and explain your product credibly in interviews.

9.1 How the internet works (the 60-second version)

  • IP address: numeric address of a machine. DNS: the internet's phone book (name → IP).
  • TCP/IP: reliable delivery of data packets. HTTP: the request/response language of the web. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS, which encrypts data in transit and verifies the server's identity.

From your course notes (Lecture 33)

HTTPS protects data in transit using TLS. Consider authorisation, sensitive data handling and error recovery as part of any integration.

9.2 Frontend, backend and client–server architecture

From your course notes (Lecture 29; Companion ch. 7)

The frontend presents the interface (HTML structures content, CSS styles it, JavaScript adds behaviour; React and Angular are examples of frontend tools). The backend applies rules, connects services and stores or fetches data — it includes application logic, not just databases. Databases store information; infrastructure runs the services. Hosting makes the application reachable; a domain is its readable address. Dev and staging are test environments; production serves real users. Ask engineers where data is stored, which systems are required, what happens on timeout or retry, how user access is checked, and request explicit release and rollback plans. A visible button alone is not proof that an order or payment actually happened.

9.3 APIs, REST, GraphQL and JSON

An API (Application Programming Interface) is a contract for how one piece of software asks another for data or an action.

From your course notes (Lecture 33; Companion ch. 8)

An API is a contract for communication: a request names an action or asks for data; a response returns information or an error. Agree the endpoint, method, authentication, expected fields and response format; different providers may use JSON or XML, requiring mapping and validation. REST is an architectural style; SOAP is a protocol using XML messages. A testing tool can send requests and inspect status, data and latency — validate both expected and failure cases. A 200 response alone does not prove the returned data is correct. An API need not be one-to-many; a website URL and its API endpoint need not match. A webhook is an event notification sent to an endpoint instead of the client repeatedly asking.

REST organises an API around resources (nouns) with standard HTTP methods; GraphQL exposes a typed schema where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one query.

REST
GET  /restaurants/42/menu            → menu items
POST /orders            {cart...}    → 201 Created, {order_id}
GET  /orders/9001                    → order status

GraphQL (one request, client chooses fields)
query {
  order(id: "9001") { status eta restaurant { name } items { name qty } }
}
REST GraphQL
Shape Many endpoints, fixed responses One endpoint, client-specified fields
Strengths Simple, cacheable, widely understood Avoids over/under-fetching; great for complex UIs
Weaknesses Multiple round-trips; over-fetching Caching and rate-limiting are harder; query cost control needed
PM question “Do we need new endpoints for this screen?” “Does the schema already expose these fields? Any expensive queries?”

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a common text format of key–value pairs and lists:

{
  "order_id": "9001",
  "status": "out_for_delivery",
  "eta_minutes": 12,
  "items": [ { "name": "Veg biryani", "qty": 1, "price_inr": 260 } ],
  "fees": { "delivery_inr": 45, "platform_inr": 5, "is_estimate": false }
}

9.3.1 HTTP methods and status codes

Method Typical meaning Idempotent?
GET Retrieve Yes (no side effects)
POST Create / trigger an action No (repeating may create duplicates)
PUT Replace a resource Yes
PATCH Partially update Not necessarily
DELETE Remove Yes

Actual behaviour depends on the API contract. Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as once — vital for payments (use idempotency keys so a retried “charge” doesn't charge twice).

Code Meaning PM implication
200 OK / 201 Created / 204 No Content Success Still validate the data
301 / 302 Redirect SEO, deep links
304 Not Modified Use your cached copy Performance
400 Bad Request / 422 Unprocessable Client sent invalid data Better validation and error copy
401 Unauthorized Not authenticated (missing/invalid credentials) Sign-in flow
403 Forbidden Authenticated but not allowed Permissions model
404 Not Found Resource doesn't exist Empty states, broken links
409 Conflict State conflict (e.g., duplicate) Concurrency design
429 Too Many Requests Rate limit hit Back-off, quotas, pricing tiers
500 / 502 / 503 / 504 Server, gateway, unavailable, timeout Retries, fallbacks, status page, incident

9.4 Authentication, authorisation and OAuth

  • Authentication (authN): who are you? (password, OTP, passkey, biometrics, SSO).
  • Authorisation (authZ): what are you allowed to do? (roles, permissions, scopes).
  • OAuth 2.0: a standard for delegated authorisation — letting an app access a user's resources at another service without sharing the password, via scoped access tokens. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 for “Sign in with…”.

From your course notes (Lectures 46, 49; Companion ch. 8)

API access can use tokens or OAuth, not necessarily passwords. Keep API keys on the server or in approved secret storage — never in a public frontend or screenshot. CORS is a browser security mechanism for controlling cross-origin requests, not a synonym for all communication between a UI and an API.

9.5 Databases, SQL vs NoSQL, and data modelling

From your course notes (Lectures 29, 34, 35; Companion ch. 9)

Relational, NoSQL and vector databases serve different needs; vector indexes store embeddings for similarity search but do not replace all other databases. Data does not automatically move from relational to NoSQL to vector storage as a product grows, and not all AI applications need vector databases. CRUD (create, read, update, delete) describes common operations; specify what users can do, who can do it and how information is protected.

Type Model Good for Examples
Relational (SQL) Tables with rows/columns, joins, ACID transactions Orders, payments, accounts — anything needing consistency PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server
Document JSON-like documents Flexible profiles, catalogues MongoDB, Firestore
Key–value Key → value Caching, sessions Redis, DynamoDB
Wide-column Rows with flexible columns at huge scale Time-series, event logs Cassandra, Bigtable
Graph Nodes and edges Social graphs, fraud rings Neo4j
Search Inverted index Full-text search Elasticsearch, OpenSearch
Vector Embeddings + similarity index Semantic search, RAG pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate

ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) guarantees matter for money: a payment and its ledger entry must succeed or fail together.

Data modelling defines entities, attributes and relationships — often drawn as an ER diagram:

9.6 Cloud computing: AWS, Azure and GCP

Cloud computing rents computing resources on demand. Service models: IaaS (virtual machines, storage), PaaS (managed platforms/databases), SaaS (finished software), plus serverless (run code without managing servers; pay per use).

Capability AWS Microsoft Azure Google Cloud
Virtual machines EC2 Virtual Machines Compute Engine
Serverless functions Lambda Azure Functions Cloud Run functions
Object storage S3 Blob Storage Cloud Storage
Managed relational DB RDS / Aurora Azure SQL Database Cloud SQL / AlloyDB
Containers / Kubernetes EKS / ECS AKS GKE
Message queue / pub-sub SQS / SNS Service Bus Pub/Sub
CDN CloudFront Azure Front Door / CDN Cloud CDN
Data warehouse Redshift Synapse / Fabric BigQuery

PM questions: What does it cost per user/transaction? Which region holds the data (residency rules)? What are the provider's SLAs? Are we locked into proprietary services? Product names and offerings change — check current documentation.

9.7 Monolith vs microservices

Monolith Microservices
Structure One deployable application Many small services, each owning a capability and its data
Pros Simple to build, test, deploy early; fewer network calls Independent scaling and deployment; team autonomy; fault isolation
Cons Hard to scale teams; one bug can take everything down; slow deploys at size Distributed-system complexity: network failures, data consistency, observability, ops cost
Good default for Early products, small teams Large orgs with clear domain boundaries

Level 3 · Senior PM

Microservices are an organisational scaling tool as much as a technical one (Conway's law: systems mirror communication structures). A PM should ask what a migration buys the customer (speed of change, reliability) and fund it explicitly — not let it silently consume a year of roadmap.

9.8 Caching, load balancing, queues, event-driven systems, webhooks and CDNs

  • Caching: keep frequently used data in fast storage (memory) to cut latency and load. Trade-off: staleness — when must the cache refresh?
  • Load balancer: spreads requests across servers; removes unhealthy ones; enables horizontal scaling.
  • Message queue: producers put work on a queue; consumers process it later — smooths spikes and decouples services (e.g., send confirmation emails asynchronously).
  • Event-driven architecture: services publish events (“OrderPlaced”) that others subscribe to; adds flexibility, complicates tracing.
  • Webhook: an HTTP callback one system sends to another when an event happens (“payment succeeded”). Receivers must verify signatures, handle duplicates and out-of-order events, and reconcile with their own records.
  • CDN (Content Delivery Network): servers near users cache static content (images, scripts, video) to reduce latency.

Worked example — cache effect on average latency

Cache lookup 5 ms; database 80 ms; cache hit ratio 90%. Average = 0.9 × 5 + 0.1 × (5 + 80) = 4.5 + 8.5 = 13 ms versus 80 ms without a cache. At a 50% hit ratio: 0.5 × 5 + 0.5 × 85 = 45 ms. Hit ratio is the lever; staleness is the risk (menus OK to cache for minutes; payment status not).

From your course notes (Companion ch. 8)

A payment provider may send a webhook after payment status changes; the backend verifies the signature and reconciles the event with its own order record. Retries must be safe: use idempotency or deduplication for repeated payment events. Ask what happens for 4xx client errors, 5xx server errors, rate limits and timeouts.

9.9 Scalability, reliability, availability, latency and throughput

  • Scalability: ability to handle more load by adding resources — vertical (bigger machine) or horizontal (more machines).
  • Reliability: the system does the right thing consistently (correct results, no data loss).
  • Availability: share of time the system is usable.
  • Latency: time to respond to one request; report percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not just averages.
  • Throughput: requests (or transactions) processed per second.
Allowed downtime = (1 − availability) × period Availability of components in series = A₁ × A₂ × … × Aₙ Little's law: concurrent requests in flight (L) = arrival rate (λ) × time in system (W)
Availability Downtime per year Per 30-day month
99% 87.6 hours 7.2 hours
99.5% 43.8 hours 3.6 hours
99.9% (“three nines”) 8.76 hours 43.2 minutes
99.95% 4.38 hours 21.6 minutes
99.99% (“four nines”) 52.6 minutes 4.32 minutes

Worked example — dependencies multiply

Checkout needs the API (99.95%), the database (99.99%) and the payment gateway (99.9%). In series: 0.9995 × 0.9999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.99840 → 99.84%, about 14 hours of downtime a year — worse than any single component. Mitigations: redundancy (second gateway), graceful degradation (queue the order; retry), and clear user messaging.

Worked example — why percentiles matter

20 response times (ms), sorted: 80, 85, 90, 92, 95, 98, 100, 102, 105, 110, 115, 120, 125, 130, 140, 150, 180, 220, 400, 900. Mean = 3,437 ÷ 20 = 171.9 ms. Median (p50) ≈ 110–115 ms. p95 (19th value, nearest-rank) = 400 ms. p99 = 900 ms. The mean hides that 1 in 20 users waits ≥ 400 ms. Set targets on p95/p99 for user-facing flows.

Little's law example: 200 requests/second × 0.25 s average time in system = 50 requests in flight — useful for sizing connection pools and worker counts.

9.9.1 Rate limits

APIs limit how many requests a client can make (e.g., 100/minute) to protect capacity and enforce fairness or pricing tiers. Exceeding limits returns 429 often with a Retry-After header. PM implications: quotas per plan, back-off and retry design, batching, and partner contracts (third-party API limits can cap your feature).

9.10 Security fundamentals

  • Principles: least privilege, defence in depth, secure defaults, encrypt in transit (TLS) and at rest, validate all input, log security events, rotate secrets.
  • OWASP Top 10 (web risks such as broken access control, injection, cryptographic failures, security misconfiguration, vulnerable components) is the standard checklist.
  • Common PM-visible issues: broken authorisation (user A can see user B's order by changing an ID), exposed API keys in frontends or repos, weak password resets, missing rate limits on OTP/login.
  • Card data: handling card numbers brings PCI DSS obligations; most products use a payment provider's hosted fields/tokenisation to stay out of scope.

From your course notes (Companion ch. 24)

Never commit passwords or API keys. If a secret is exposed, tell the responsible team and rotate it; deleting it from the latest file does not necessarily remove it from history.

9.11 Privacy and compliance basics

  • Data minimisation, purpose limitation, consent, retention limits, user rights (access, correction, deletion) are common principles.
  • Regimes you may meet: GDPR (EU), India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, CCPA/CPRA (California), sector rules (banking/KYC, health). Payment card data: PCI DSS.
  • PM practice: privacy review for new data uses; no PII in analytics events; data-residency questions in vendor selection; get qualified legal advice for interpretation.

9.12 System architecture diagrams

When drawing a system in an interview or doc: clients → edge (CDN, gateway) → services → data stores → external providers, then annotate data flows, sync vs async calls, failure points and where PII lives. Label assumptions. Keep it to 6–12 boxes.

9.13 Technical debt and engineering estimation

From your course notes (Extra topic 12)

Technical debt is the future cost of a technical shortcut or outdated implementation; not every bug or maintenance item is technical debt. A PM should understand its effect without pretending to estimate technical work alone. Record dependencies on the roadmap, track blockers, reserve capacity for reliability where evidence supports it, define release criteria and a rollback path.

Estimation: ask for ranges with assumptions (“5–8 days if the pricing API is stable”), break work down, identify unknowns (spikes), and track estimate accuracy over time — not to blame, but to plan. Common traps: anchoring on the PM's wish date; ignoring testing, review and deployment; forgetting non-functional work.

9.14 Agile delivery, CI/CD and feature flags

  • CI (Continuous Integration): code changes are merged frequently and automatically built and tested.
  • CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment): every change that passes tests is releasable (delivery) or automatically released (deployment).
  • Feature flags: turn features on/off (or for a percentage/segment) without redeploying — enabling staged rollouts, A/B tests and kill switches. Clean up stale flags (they are a form of tech debt).

From your course notes (Lecture 29; Companion ch. 24)

An IDE helps developers edit code; repositories support version control; CI/CD pipelines build, test and deploy across environments. A repository holds project files and history; a branch isolates work; a commit records a snapshot; a pull request proposes changes for review. Learn protected branches, CODEOWNERS, automated tests and CI/CD at a conceptual level.

9.15 Observability

Observability = being able to understand what a system is doing from its outputs: logs (events), metrics (numbers over time), traces (a request's path across services). Reliability targets:

  • SLI (service level indicator): a measured value, e.g., % of checkout requests succeeding within 2 s.
  • SLO (objective): the target, e.g., 99.9% over 30 days.
  • SLA (agreement): a contractual promise with consequences, usually looser than the SLO.
  • Error budget: 100% − SLO. At 99.9% per 30 days the budget is 43.2 minutes; if it's spent, prioritise reliability over features.

From your course notes (Extra topic 13)

Define alert thresholds and owners before release; maintain an incident timeline; run a blameless review focused on what happened, contributing conditions, impact and prevention; the PM helps quantify user impact and coordinate communication.

9.16 Technical trade-offs a PM should recognise

Trade-off Example decision
Consistency vs availability During a network partition, show possibly stale menu (available) vs refuse orders (consistent)? (CAP theorem)
Latency vs cost Add caching/replicas (faster, costlier)
Build vs buy Own the search engine or use a managed service
Sync vs async Confirm payment instantly vs queue and notify
Flexibility vs simplicity Generic rules engine vs hard-coded rules
Speed vs quality Ship behind a flag with known gaps vs harden first

9.17 System design examples

The format for each: requirements → core components → data flow → key risks → PM decisions/metrics.

9.17.1 1 · Payment processing

Key risks: double charges on retry; webhook lost/duplicated/out of order; timeouts leaving status unknown (“pending”); fraud; refunds. PM decisions: show “payment pending” states honestly; retry UX (another method, saved cart); refund SLA; success-rate SLO by method; reconciliation ownership. Metrics: payment success rate (by method/bank), time-to-confirm, duplicate-charge reports, refund time, chargeback rate.

9.17.2 2 · Food delivery

Key risks: restaurant doesn't accept; ETA errors; courier shortages at peak; menu/price staleness. PM decisions: order state machine and customer messaging; batching policy; ETA confidence ranges; cancellation rules. Metrics: order acceptance time, on-time rate, ETA error (p50/p90), cancellations by cause, contribution per order.

9.17.3 3 · Ride-hailing

Components: rider app, driver app (location every few seconds), location service (geospatial index), matching/dispatch, pricing (base + surge), trip service, payments, safety (SOS, trip sharing), ratings. Key challenges: real-time location at scale, fair and fast matching, dynamic pricing with guardrails, fraud, safety. PM metrics: ETA to pickup, match rate, cancellation rate (rider and driver), surge frequency, driver utilisation and earnings, safety incidents.

9.17.4 4 · Notifications

Components: event producers → notification service (templates, user preferences, rate limits, quiet hours) → channel providers (push, SMS, email, WhatsApp) → delivery receipts. Key risks: spam/fatigue, duplicate sends, wrong user, timezone errors, provider outages, consent. PM decisions: priority tiers (transactional vs marketing), frequency caps, opt-outs, fallbacks (push → SMS for critical). Metrics: delivery rate, open/click, opt-out rate, complaints, time-to-deliver for transactional messages.

9.17.5 5 · Customer onboarding (fintech KYC)

Key risks: high drop-off at document upload; vendor latency/outages; false rejections (bias, poor image quality); fraud; data protection. PM decisions: progressive onboarding (collect only what is needed now), save-and-resume, camera guidance, manual-review SLAs, adverse-action explanations. Metrics: step completion, time to decision, auto-approval rate, manual review backlog, fraud rate, complaints.

9.18 Exercises with model answers

Exercise 1 · Status codes

Users report “Something went wrong” on checkout. Logs show many 429 and some 504 responses from the pricing API. Explain each and propose product actions.

Model answer

429 = rate limit exceeded — our calls to the pricing API exceed the quota (perhaps at peak or due to retries). Actions: cache fee estimates for a short TTL, batch requests, add exponential back-off, negotiate a higher tier. 504 = gateway timeout — the upstream didn't respond in time. Actions: shorter timeout with the “Estimate unavailable” fallback, monitor p95 latency, alerting. Product: replace the generic error with specific, honest copy and a retry.

Exercise 2 · Availability maths

A booking flow depends on four services at 99.9% each. What's the combined availability and yearly downtime? Suggest two mitigations.

Model answer

0.999⁴ ≈ 0.996 → 99.6%, about 0.004 × 8,760 ≈ 35 hours/year. Mitigations: make non-critical dependencies asynchronous (e.g., send confirmation email via queue), add redundancy/fallback for the most critical one, cache read-only data.

Exercise 3 · Explain a system in an interview

In 90 seconds, explain how an order moves through a food-delivery system.

Model answer

“The customer app sends the cart to our API gateway, which routes it to the order service. The order service validates items and prices from the catalogue, asks the payment service to charge via the payment provider using an idempotency key, and saves the order. It publishes an OrderPlaced event; the restaurant tablet gets the order, and the dispatch service matches a courier using live locations and an ETA model. Status events update the customer through the notification service. Key risks are payment failures, restaurant non-acceptance and ETA errors; we track acceptance time, on-time rate and cancellations.”

9.19 Interview perspective

“Design a notification system” (technical PM) — what interviewers test and a structure

Tests: requirements thinking, trade-offs, user empathy, scale awareness — not code. Structure: clarify use cases (transactional vs marketing), scale (users, messages/day), channels, latency needs → components (producers, queue, notification service with preferences/caps/templates, channel providers, receipts) → data (preferences, logs) → failure handling (retries, dedup, fallbacks) → abuse/spam controls and consent → metrics (delivery, opt-outs, complaints) → phased rollout. Mistakes: jumping into tech names without requirements; ignoring user fatigue and consent.

“What happens when you type a URL and press enter?” — 60-second answer

“The browser resolves the domain via DNS to an IP address, opens a TCP connection and a TLS handshake for HTTPS, then sends an HTTP GET request. The request may be served by a CDN cache; otherwise it reaches a load balancer and an application server, which may query databases or other services and return HTML or JSON with a status code. The browser parses and renders the page, fetching CSS, JavaScript and images — often from a CDN. Each hop adds latency and is a potential failure point, which is why we use caching and monitor percentiles.”

9.20 Key takeaways

  • Think in requests and responses; every network hop adds latency and failure modes.
  • Know HTTP methods/codes, authN vs authZ, OAuth scopes and idempotency.
  • Pick databases by access pattern and consistency needs; vector DBs complement, not replace, transactional stores.
  • Reliability maths: dependencies multiply; report p95/p99 latency; manage error budgets.
  • Caches, queues, webhooks and CDNs trade freshness, complexity and cost for speed and resilience.
